#5795. $150 Billion More Paid by Americans for Gas This Year Than Last

Since the beginning of America’s war against Iran, Americans have paid an additional $150+ billion for gas and diesel than they did last year during the same time period, according to a study from Brown University. Global gas prices have risen because supply has been disrupted (Iran having one of the top oil reserves in the world). Americans are paying upwards of $6 a gallon even though American oil companies have not had their own supply chains disrupted the way crude from the Middle East has.

The result? Windfall profits for big oil at the expense of American citizens.

In the leadup to his election in 2024, Donald Trump asked about 20 oil executives at Mar-a-Lago to raise $1 billion for his campaign, promising to reverse dozens of Biden-era regulations if elected. The industry seems not to have raised the full $1 billion, but oil interests still gave tens of millions to Trump-aligned committees. The policies put in place by the Republican party, who has had control of congress and the White House since the last election, have been very pro oil & gas, whether they were anti-EV, anti-solar, anti-energy efficiency, anti-fuel efficiency, anti-wind, or just flat out subsidies to oil and gas.

They ended many of the Biden Administration’s clean energy policies. They ended the Solar For All Program (or tried to). They ended residential and commercial solar tax credits. They signed Executive Order 14315 to terminate wind and solar production and investment tax credits and impose additional restrictions. They made solar development on Federal lands more difficult. On his first day in office, Trump signed a memo withdrawing federal offshore areas from new and renewed wind leasing – but the rule didn’t apply to oil and gas. They ended wind tax credits. They kneecapped the federal standards for vehicle fuel efficiency. They tried to eliminate Energy Star, a program that costs the government $32 million a year and saves Americans $14 billion a year. They weakened Home Energy Rebate programs, SPECIFICALLY stipulating that they could not be used to replace polluting gas furnaces (that increase childhood asthma by more than 15%) with energy efficient electric options. They even tried to make it illegal for future legislators to improve energy efficiency legislation. Then, as if that wasn’t enough, they just gave our tax dollars to the fossil industries, allocating about $190 billion in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade from the OBBBA.

If this isn’t quid pro quo, I guess I don’t understand what quid pro quo is. But the Iran War took it to a whole new level.

Since it began on February 28, as Americans have spent about $150 billion more on gasoline and diesel, U.S. oil and gas companies earned more than $130 billion in profit from April through September, nearly triple what they earned a year earlier, according to the New York Times.

We can’t say the war was fought for the industry. The president has said his focus is stopping Iran from getting a nuclear weapon. But we can say who is paying at the pump and who is collecting.

Connect the dots however you like, but connect them before you vote. Add it to the roughly $50 billion that US taxpayers have directly spent on the war, and untold more that has percolated through the rest of our economy due to inflationary pressure from rising energy costs, and it’s safe to say it’s well over $200 billion that this war has cost us, alongside the unquantifiable cost in human lives and suffering.

Wars fought for oil are nothing new. But there are things about this conflict that are new.

Oil shocks focus the mind, and this week’s reporting shows how fast the world outside the US is moving to get away from oil dependency. CleanTechnica’s analysis argues that global oil demand is on track to fall by 2–3 million barrels a day this year, the first drop not caused by a recession or pandemic, as high prices push consumers away from fuel. You can see it in China, where gas-car sales fell 49% in September and EVs hit a record 67% share. Europe is also answering, with affordable small EVs like the Smart #2 and an electric Citroën 2 CV at about €15,000. In Australia, a Chinese-built electric semi is already hauling cement for about half the price of its rivals, and Africa’s e-mobility leaders are talking about building vehicles rather than just importing them. Drivers who’ve switched are happy too: 82% of XPeng owners in a 4,000-person European survey said they’d recommend the brand, versus a 53% average.

Every driver, trucker, and country that electrifies becomes less exposed to the next oil shock. The question for the U.S. is how fast it joins in. And this election will go a long way toward answering that question.

Not everyone knows the difference between four-wheel drive and all-wheel drive. They sound similar and interchangeable, but the terms describe distinct drivetrains, each designed for specific purposes. The Jeep we looked at yesterday was 4WD, a drivetrain that ties all four wheels together when needed through a central locking differential for low-speed maneuvering through mud and over rocks.

By contrast, today's 2001 Audi A4 Quattro Avant is permanently activated AWD and is intended not for off-roading but for more secure handling and power application in inclement weather. For Audi, at least, this drivetrain is time-tested and rally-proven. Their personalities are further differentiated by their looks: the Jeep being brutish and basic while the Audi is one of the most handsome and elegant small estates ever offered for sale.

This one, in Cactus Green with the coal mine black interior that was favored by German carmakers back in the day, comes with a clean title, 175,020 miles under its Cactus Green belt, and an extensive list of refurbishment and renewal that has left it looking like Cinderella before the ball.

The paint still shines; there are no significant dings or dents beneath that top coat, and the headlamp lenses show only minor clouding. Surprisingly, the interior is in even better shape, looking almost as-new thanks to several replacement parts and general care and cleaning. Plenty of other work has gone into this A4's care and feeding. That included replacing several suspension components and wheel bearings, all set at factory ride height. Most importantly, the engine has received a ton of maintenance, starting with a timing belt and water pump replacement (a plus because this is an interference engine). That work continued to the exhaust, which had the catalytic converter, O2 sensor, and mounting hardware replaced. Another major update was converting the A/C from R12 to R134. New rotors and pads, plus chasing down a number of electrical gremlins, round out the major mechanical work.

#5793. Hyundai's XRT Off-Road Division Is On The Right Path But A Step Behind

There's nothing more in vogue right now than automakers soft-roader-ing their crossovers for weekend warrior types who enjoy a bit of camping or a dirt road every once in a while. Honda has TrailSport, Subaru has Wilderness, Toyota has TRD, GMC has AT4, and so on and so forth. Of course one of the largest automakers in the U.S. would want to get in on the action, so Hyundai spun up its own off-road sub-brand a few years back: XRT, which stands for Extreme Rugged Terrain.

What started out as more of a trim and appearance package on vehicles like the first-gen Palisade and fourth-gen Tucson and Santa Fe has evolved into offering styling changes with a bit of added capability when the going gets bumpy. With the introduction of Hyundai's XRT Pro trim on the Palisade and upcoming fifth-gen Tucson, that idea gets taken up another notch. However, after spending a day with both the 2026 Santa Fe XRT and 2026 Palisade XRT Pro off-roading in rural Missouri, I'm not totally sure Hyundai is all the way there yet. That's not to say the Korean automaker isn't on the right path and won't keep improving expeditiously, but as it stands right now, it may be just a step or two behind.

Full Disclosure: Hyundai flew me out to Bentonville, Arkansas, put me up in a very nice hotel and fed me, all so I could sample the 2026 Santa Fe XRT and 2026 Palisade XRT Pro.

It can be sort of tricky to evaluate the capability of a soft-roader like Hyundai's XRT fleet. Technically, both the Palisade XRT Pro and Santa Fe XRT were able to do everything that was thrown at them on this program, but they both lacked a bit of the sure-footedness I just experienced in Honda's Passport TrailSport, and that was on a far more technical and challenging course. That being said, what I did with the XRT siblings is probably 10 times as grueling as what the average Hyundai owner will do with their SUVs. There's also the issue of tires. While the Passport TrailSport is fitted with beefy General Grabber A/T Sport all-terrain rubber, the Santa Fe XRT makes do with less-aggressive Continental TerrainContact A/Ts, which leads to a good bit of wheel slippage.

Still, both XRTs do an admirable job of tackling trails, though rock crawlers they are not. The Palisade XRT Pro I drove was certainly the more capable of the two, thanks to its electronic limited-slip differential in the rear and a 360-degree camera that helped overcome its sheer size, but it never felt particularly at home, even if it did tackle every obstacle without much protest.

I say much protest because, while the car didn't get stuck at any point, the 4,575-pound crossover didn't exactly seem happy, and that especially goes for its Hyundai-built 8-speed transmission. While the naturally aspirated 3.5-liter V6 provided enough power (287 horsepower and 260 pound-feet of torque) to get up just about anything despite a lack of low-end oomph, I could tell that the 8-speed was none too pleased. I couldn't hear it on the road, but when switching to the Sand setting in its Trail drive mode, there was a noticeable whine coming from it on the throttle. A temperature readout in the gauge cluster also served as a constant reminder it was, uh, hot, and when I got out of the car, there was an unmistakable smell of hot transmission wafting through the air. From a functional standpoint, the XRT Pro didn't skip a beat, which is certainly a testament to the rest of the Palisade's drivetrain and its 8.4 inches of ground clearance; it bottomed out far less than I expected it to.

It's a similar story with the Santa Fe XRT. It may lack the e-LSD and all-out grunt of the Palisade, but it does make up for that somewhat with more low-end grunt courtesy of a torquey turbocharged 2.5-liter inline-4 that pumps out 277 hp and 311 lb-ft of torque. This drivetrain lent itself far better to the old-school way of getting yourself unstuck: give 'er some gas. Sure, there are 10 fewer horses than the Palisade's V6, but an extra 51 torques is massive.

Still, you can tell the Santa Fe is a far less luxury-oriented product than the Palisade, and I got bumped around a hell of a lot more than I did in the Palisade. Obviously, there's a price delta to consider, as the Santa Fe XRT starts at $43,940 including destination, and the Palisade XRT Pro has a far more costly $51,820 entrance price.

Currently, there are four XRT models on sale: the two I've been talking about, and then the Santa Cruz XRT and the Ioniq 5 XRT. I've driven the Ioniq and had a pretty good time with it, but came away feeling it was more of a styling exercise than anything else. Sure, it can handle some dirt, but that's just about it. While all these models do come with all-terrain tires, a bit more ground clearance, upped towing capacity, better approach and departure angles, and functional front recovery hooks, they're without a doubt behind industry frontrunners like Honda TrailSport and Subaru Wilderness when it comes to real capability.

I believe that's because XRT, as a brand, is so new. Hyundai's still trying to find its footing in an ever-more crowded world. It promises that its next product, based on the fifth-generation Tucson, will be its best yet, and far more than an appearance package. Even though the Tucson won't have the e-LSD of the Palisade XRT Pro, despite sharing the "Pro" moniker, it will have skid plates, all-terrain tires, 8.3 inches of ground clearance, some sick body cladding, and Hyundai's new off-road software called Smart Terrain Assist.

That program has the ability to analyze the terrain ahead of you, determining traction and slip conditions. From there, it provides visual guidance via green, orange or red "stuck zones," and shows the driver the best route to take. It works in concert with Automatic Terrain Detection (which has auto, snow, mud, sand and rock modes) with intelligent mode switching to remove any guesswork from off-roading. Clearly, Hyundai wants to make it as friendly to first-time off-roaders as possible.

Lest we forget, this same team is working on the body-on-frame Hyundai Boulder SUV, which will likely be powered by a hybrid or EREV drivetrain. It shares underpinnings with a future body-on-frame truck Hyundai is also working on, and it's targeted specifically at the American market.

While I'm not sure Hyundai's XRT division is quite the cream of the crop just yet when it comes to soft-roading — it might be a bit too focused on aesthetics, rather than actual performance — there's little doubt in my mind that it'll get to the front of the pack sooner rather than later. Just look at what this massive company has done with its N performance division, or what it has done with Genesis when it comes to luxury. When Hyundai puts its mind to something, it gets the job done, and I don't expect XRT to be any different.

#5792. What Recessionmobile Should Automakers Build?

Folks, it certainly feels like there's a recession right around the corner. The AI stocks are tumbling, nothing else in the economy is doing anything, we're teetering on the edge of an auto debt crisis — things are bad. But, no matter how broke we all get, we all still have to get to work. That brings us to the topic of today's question: What recession-mobiles should automakers start building?

A good recessionmobile should be practical, reliable, and most importantly economical. Think the Cruze and Focus of the post-recession era, cars that just get you from point A to poitn B without pretending to do anything more. We've all got places to get to, and we all want to do that for as little cash as possible — especially with fuel prices where they are. What should automakers start designing now, so they're ready to hit the market with new cost-effective products when everything hits the fan?

I think, for this try at a recession, we've got to give it up on the whole idea of four-wheeled transportation. We've tried it, and cars are just too much to move around for the one or two people aboard. Plus, when we're all broke, we won't exactly be making Costco hauls — who needs all the cargo space of a Traverse? The Honda Cub is the vehicle we all need, but other companies should try their hand at it too. Give us a Suzuki, a Triumph, a Toyota version of tiny, efficient transportation.

I think more companies should make Super Cubs for the recession, but what do you think? Leave your responses in the comments below, and I'll pick my favorites out later this week. Bonus points for some real in-depth reasoning as to why you think your pick would be the ideal vehicle for getting us all through the next once-in-a-lifetime financial crisis.

#5791. Trump Wants More Attention For His New Algae Biofuel Showcase

US President Donald Trump has famously transformed the magnificent Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool into a high profile showcase for the algae biofuel industry, and he stands firm in his faith that the tiny green microalgae can produce renewable fuels at scale. In fact, on Monday, November 2, the President held his all-important closing message for the 2026 midterm election cycle right there at the Reflecting Pool. Hey, maybe Trump knows something about algae biofuel…

The Reflecting Pool is a massive body of shallow water that extends from the foot of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington, DC. Situated on filled ground in former marshlands, the Reflecting Pool provides a golden opportunity to showcase the ability of the domestic biofuel industry to take advantage of the built infrastructure, rather than taking up valuable farmland with conventional energy crops like corn or soybeans.

Although algae cultivation was probably not the original intention of the Reflecting Pool, it has been a perennial host to algae ever since its construction in the 1920’s, with the humid environment and temperate climate of DC lending a hand.

In earlier years, the Pool was drained and refilled twice a year to control the growth. By the 1990’s, the structure was clearly sinking into the marshes, sparking calls for a major structural overhaul and the addition of a water circulating system.

The soup-to-nuts rehab was completed in 2012, and yet the algae persisted. Finally, when Trump took office for the second time in January of 2025, he lit upon a brilliant idea of turning lemons into lemonade. The Reflecting Pool would be re-made as a monument to the domestic algae biofuel industry.

By the summer of 2026, the transformation was complete and the algae were thriving, as confirmed by satellite imagery. Others mocked, but the President stood by the plan. After all, biomass is a key element in his “American Energy Dominance” policy, and where better to showcase biofuel than in the nation’s capitol, to be seen and admired by millions of tourists.

And so, that explains why Trump chose the Reflecting Pool as the seemingly incongruous scene of his Election Day eve closing message, as reported somewhat incredulously by The Guardian among many others.

“On the eve of a consequential election day, with polls indicating that most voters feel the US president has grown too focused on building projects in the nation’s capital, he stood in front of the newly opened reflecting pool to discuss – in detail – changes to the pool’s pipe, the grass surrounding the area and granite,” observed The Guardian.

Algae biofuel surfaced regularly on the pages of CleanTechnica in the early 2000’s, with the high oil content and rapid growth cycle of algae being the attractions along with the potential for developing next-generation farming and extraction systems leading to a competitive renewable energy resource (see more algae background here).

Not much progress has been made since then, and stakeholders in the field have weathered much skepticism if not downright mockery. A seal of approval from the President of the United States of America is just what the industry needs to get to the next level.

Indeed, a fresh round of activity has surfaced in recent years, with the UK firm HutanBio being one example. The startup aims to generate profitability by leveraging the carbon-capturing angle of algae farming.

Earlier this year Hutan signed an MOU (Memorandum of Understanding) with the Irish firm Utopia World Investment and the biodiesel refiner Wakud International to scale up its algae farming system, with Oman being the location. “Our unique microalgae strain, Sphaerica, is grown in seawater, on non-arable coastal land, using CO₂ and sunlight creating a genuinely low-carbon biocrude stream that the industry currently lacks and urgently needs,” HutanBio says of itself.

As described by HutanBio, Sphaerica yields up to ten times more oil than typical algae biofuel strains. Hutan expects the high level of productivity to dovetail with Oman’s high level of solar radiation, enabling it to leapfrog over its competitors.

The Oman operation is set for operation at a demonstration scale before the end of 2027, which is just around the corner. Meanwhile, Japanese automaker Mazda is also beginning to crack the algae code.

On October 7, Mazda announced that its microalgae biofuel research program has nailed down support from NEDO, the New Energy and Industrial Technology Development Organization of Japan. The Mazda program is in early stages, with scale-up expected by the 2030’s. If all goes according to plan, Mazda will use its homemade algae biofuel to factory-fill the tanks of every diesel vehicle that rolls off its assembly lines.

Evidently Mazda does not anticipate that drivers can pump out algae biofuel at any corner gas station for their next fill-up. Still, it’s another sign that that years-long research programs are finally leading to commercial application.

For a glimpse into the future, check out newly published research from the Saitama University in Japan. Where conventional systems involve cultivating algae, drying it, and processing it to remove oils, the Saitama team has developed a strain of cyanobacteria (commonly known as blue-green algae) that can express free fatty acids outside of the cell and deposit them directly into a culture medium. Among other benefits, the Saitama system does not require destroying the algae with each harvesting cycle.

As for the US, ExxonMobil was the standard-bearer for early stage algae biofuel research throughout the early 2000’s. By 2017, the company was confident enough to put up millions for an elaborate advertising blitz that showcased its efforts to the world.

Or not, as the case may be. In 2019, Massachusetts State Attorney General Maura Healey filed suit against Exxon, alleging that the biofuel ads were deceptive. “Specifically, the complaint alleges that Exxon systematically and intentionally has misled Massachusetts investors about material climate-driven risks to its business and has deceived consumers about the central role its fossil fuel products play in causing climate change,” AG Healy’s office explained.

Exxon subsequently dropped the program altogether, but the lawsuit persists. Among the details coming to light is a deposition by an Exxon scientist who worked on the algae program. Under questioning by attorneys with the AG’s office, the scientist asserted that the claims in Exxon’s ads were “patently false,” and that he said as much to the company.

It’s too bad Exxon dropped the ball before Trump had a chance to pick up the algae biofuel torch. Oh, well. We’ll always have the Reflecting Pool…

Photo: The Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool has been host to thriving populations of algae ever since its construction in the 1920’s (cropped, courtesy of National Parks Service).

This score is crucial to how your ads perform and how much they cost. But what does it mean for realtors, and what constitutes a great Google Quality Real Estate Score? Let's dive in.

Google Ads Quality Score is essentially a measurement of the quality and relevance of both your keywords and PPC ads. It is a dynamic metric, assigned on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being the best possible score. It is used by Google to determine your cost per click (CPC) and your ad rank in the ad auction process.

Quality Score is calculated based on three primary components: click-through rate (CTR), ad relevance, and landing page experience.

For any industry, including real estate, a good Quality Score is generally around 7 or above. However, in the competitive world of real estate, striving for an even higher Quality Score could give you an advantage. So, for realtors, a great Quality Score might be considered 8 or above.

That said, keep in mind that a high-Quality Score is not an end in itself. It's a sign that your ads are relevant, and your landing pages provide a good user experience, but it's still just one factor in the overall success of your Google Ads campaigns.

#5789. Surprise, Surprise: Short-Sighted Automakers Back Trump's Fuel Economy Standards Rollback

Good morning! It's Tuesday, November 3, 2026, and this is The Morning Shift, your daily roundup of the top automotive headlines from around the world, in one place. This is where you'll find the most important stories that are shaping the way Americans drive and get around.

The Alliance for Automotive Innovation, a group representing some of the biggest automakers in the world, including General Motors, Toyota, Hyundai, Ford, Stellantis and Volkswagen, said it was backing the Trump administration in a legal challenge to its sharply lower vehicle fuel economy standards that had been filed by California, New York and two dozen other states, cities and counties around the country. I'll tell ya what, I'm not surprised, but I'm sure those automakers will be once those fuel economy rollbacks are changed in the next administration (whenever that comes).

Last month, the U.S. Department of Transportation said it was finalizing a fleet-wide fuel economy average of 34.9 mpg by 2031. That's down from the 50.4 mpg mark that was set by the Biden administration in 2024. The group argued that automakers require "certainty and stability" in standards. From Reuters:

It added that if the standards were set aside, it "would affect automakers' ​business, endangering the capital investment planning, product development, and performance validation for hundreds of ​new vehicle models intended for the US market."

The states said the Trump administration was ignoring the presence ‌of millions ⁠of electric vehicles, "leading to a flawed, dramatically distorted analysis of the 'maximum feasible' fuel economy level." The automaker group said the court should reject those arguments.

The revised Trump administration standards seek to reverse Biden's push toward greater fuel efficiency and electric vehicles. A coalition of environmental ​and consumer groups ​also filed a separate ⁠lawsuit challenging the new rules.

The Transportation Department said the regulation reduces manufacturers' average cost per vehicle to comply by $1,289 but increases fuel ​costs by more than $1,600 over the life of the vehicles.

The department ​said the ⁠rule would increase US gasoline consumption through 2050 by 4.6%, or about 121 billion gallons, compared with the Biden rules but also boost new car sales.

The American Petroleum Institute, an oil ⁠and natural ​gas industry trade group, also filed in support of ​the Trump administration's rules, saying they ensure the government sets standards that "do not force consumers to purchase vehicles that ​consume less fuel than they would otherwise choose."

Automakers can talk all they want about being environmentally sustainable and eco-friendly, but at the end of the day, it's very clear that what it all comes down to is the bottom line. It'll certainly be interesting to see what the fallout will be once a new, more eco-conscious administration enters the White House in a few years' time.

That same group, the Alliance for Automotive Innovation, is currently on a heater. Not only are they going after fuel economy standards. They're also continuing their push to get Congress to ban the import of Chinese EVs to the U.S. Automakers have been whining about this for years at this point, and now they'd like the bill to pass when lawmakers return next week for a quick session following today's midterm elections.

Back in September, the Senate sponsors of a bipartisan bill to effectively ban Chinese-made vehicles from entering the U.S. agreed to delay the effort to fast-track the bill until November, despite the fact it had overwhelming support from other congresspeople who apparently aren't a fan of a free market or freedom of choice for the consumer. There are some officials who believe that if Dems win control of Congress, there may not be enough time to approve the ban before the session ends in December. Whatever will these OEMs do??? From Reuters:

"We need to ​protect the US market from a flood of Chinese imports that carry ​surveillance risk and disadvantage current manufacturers that have made generational investments in ⁠American communities," said John Bozzella, who heads the Alliance for Automotive Innovation.

"Given the ​obvious national security risk and China's pattern of unfair behavior, Congress should protect ​our defense and advanced manufacturing base and stop Chinese automakers from doing here what they've gotten away ‌with ⁠in Europe," Bozzella said.

Bozzella said in the first eight months of 2026, the EU imported more than 1.1 million vehicles from China — more than all of 2025.

A Senate committee passed the bill, which has significant momentum, in July and a House version now tops 100 co-sponsors. ​Automakers and legislative aides ​hope to win full ⁠passage this year.

A regulation imposed by the former ​Biden administration ⁠in early 2025 effectively banned Chinese automakers from selling or building passenger vehicles in the US because they could send sensitive driver data to China. Washington also maintains more ⁠than 100% ​tariffs on Chinese electric vehicles.

The Chinese foreign ministry ​has previously urged the United States "to respect the laws of the market economy and principles of fair competition," ​criticizing previous proposals against Chinese companies as "unreasonable suppression."

President Trump, wildcard that he is, sparked a hell of a lot of worry among key stakeholders when he said he would accept Chinese automakers building cars in the U.S., but so far no one has taken him up on the offer.

Of course, the whole "national security angle of this story is just steeped in irony. After all, I'm writing this article on my Chinese-made laptop, and you're reading it on your Chinese-made phone.

#5788. Residual Disease in Spondyloarthritis: What's Being Missed by DMARDs?

— It's common for symptoms to stick around even if inflammation is resolved by medication

In spondyloarthritis (SpA), the wealth of biologic and disease-modifying anti-rheumatic drug (DMARD) options still leaves some patients unsatisfied with their treatment outcomes, most likely due to residual disease.

This year, the flurry of drug development in SpA continued, including promising phase II-III trial data released for the selective Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor filgotinib and the anti-interleukin (IL)-17A monoclonal antibody vunakizumab in axial SpA (axSpA).

Assessment of SpondyloArthritis International Society (ASAS) improvements of 40% or better (ASAS40) occurred in 35% to 40% of filgotinib recipients versus 18% to 21% of placebo recipients, while ASAS improvements of 20% or better (ASAS20) were reported for 65.6% of vunakizumab patients versus 42.5% of placebo patients.

The trials were deemed successful despite ASAS responses falling well short of 100%, in line with what is acceptable for the many medications already on the market for varying subsets of SpA.

"It is common to have persistent symptoms despite treatment of inflammation. Firstly, when you look at the results from successful clinical trials for most DMARDs approved for axSpA ... ASAS40 response is achieved by about 40% to 55% of patients," Abhijeet Danve, MD, MHS, of the Yale School of Medicine in New Haven, Connecticut, told MedPage Today. "That informs us that patients will have residual symptoms despite treating the inflammation adequately."

ASAS40 and ASAS20 are subjective measures of health recovery in terms of patient global assessment of the disease, spinal pain, function, and inflammation: ASAS40 is defined as a ≥40% improvement and an absolute improvement from baseline of two or more units in at least three of the four domains without any worsening in the remaining domain, and ASAS20 is defined as a ≥20% improvement and an absolute improvement from baseline of one or more units in at least three of the four domains and no major worsening in the remaining domain.

A major issue of tracking progress in SpA is the reliance on patient-reported outcomes and the lack of a good objective measure of disease activity.

"Frequently, there is contribution from the nociplastic pain," Danve noted. "Some of the spinal symptoms can be from concomitant degenerative disc disease or facet arthritis, and distinguishing between the pain from the degenerative and inflammatory components is difficult owing to lack of specific monitoring biomarkers."

Lianne Gensler, MD, of the University of California San Francisco, stressed that there will never be a physical exam that shows inflammation of axial joints of the spine and sacroiliac joints specifically. "It's a huge problem in our field because we don't have a physical exam ... that really clearly says, 'Oh, like rheumatoid arthritis, this patient has ongoing joint swelling.'"

"The closest you can come to that is an MRI," she told MedPage Today, "but that one alone is not specific" and "you can't do an MRI every time a patient has symptoms."

SpA is itself a heterogeneous family of diseases characterized by inflammation in the spine and/or the entheses, the joint-like connective tissues where tendons and ligaments insert into bones. AxSpA is one manifestation affecting the spine, commonly causing lower back pain and stiffness, and can be split into radiographic (i.e., ankylosing spondylitis [AS]) or non-radiographic subsets, while peripheral SpA, a sister condition, can cause limb discomfort such as heel pain and plantar fasciitis.

Generally, pharmacological treatment of these sometimes-overlapping SpA conditions means initial therapy with nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, and in some cases glucocorticoids, before the patient resorts to the various DMARDs on the market. In a 2026 guideline update, the American College of Rheumatology endorsed tumor necrosis factor inhibitors and IL-17 blockers preferentially over JAK inhibitors for initial biologic DMARD treatment of AS and axSpA.

But what happens when patients still complain of residual symptoms after DMARD therapy?

"Many physicians who are treating patients don't recognize that these symptoms are not necessarily driven by objective inflammation, and there's a trigger response to change the treatment because a patient has residual symptoms. That's a huge problem," Gensler said.

"There's certainly some patients who can be treatment refractory, but most patients that have ongoing symptoms actually [have] other factors, whether it's damage, nociplastic pain, or comorbidities driving symptoms," such as depression and obesity, she noted.

In these cases of residual symptoms, Danve suggested physical therapy and regular exercise, as well as use of medications such as gabapentin, selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and muscle relaxants to help the nociplastic pain.

"Having right expectations is important to avoid rapid cycling through DMARDs," he said.

With residual disease being a major concern to researchers, several groups have recently tried to establish various terms to describe persistent symptoms and inadequate response to targeted therapies.

In 2025, ASAS released its consensus-based definition of difficult-to-manage (D2M) axial SpA: failure of at least two biologic or targeted synthetic DMARDs, suboptimal disease control, and the perception of problematic signs and symptoms by both rheumatologists and patients. Treatment-refractory disease is considered a subset within D2M that requires a history of treatment failure, the presence of objective signs of inflammatory activity, and the exclusion of non-inflammatory reasons for nonresponse.

Supporting the idea that many D2M symptoms are not coming from inflammation, Gensler cited her own group's research and estimated that treatment-refractory patients, who do have objective signs of inflammation, make up just 10% of the D2M pool.

She urged rheumatologists to "take a step back and say, 'Do I believe that the ongoing symptoms of disease activity are coming from inflammation?'"

They need to be "holistic" about assessing all the things that can drive symptoms and addressing them separately, she said, or getting patients to a clinician who will address them.

#5787. I Checked Out Tesla’s New Model YL, Standard Y, Model 3 In Person — Here’s What Surprised Me

I finally got to see the new Tesla Model YL, Model Y Standard, and Model 3 Standard in person a few weeks ago and wanted to give my thoughts on the three models. I drove the two Model Ys and just looked at the Model 3 Standard.  I was visiting relatives in Colorado and visited the Tesla dealer in Superior, Colorado (a very progressive part of Colorado). The dealer was very busy, but not quite as busy as I saw when the tax credit was expiring last year.

As I mentioned in this article 4 months ago, I’ve been a fan of the Model YL since it was announced in China, and finally in the US recently. As a parent of 3 kids and an owner of a series of 3 minivans over 30 years, I’m well aware of the criticism that Tesla doesn’t make a car suitable for large families. The Model X was a partial solution to this problem, but had two large flaws in my opinion.

So, I wanted to see if the Model YL solved these two issues with the Model X. The short is answer is that it solved the price issue but not the space issue. The premium launch edition at $61,990, with about $11,000 in free options, is plenty affordable — although, still a bit more than a minivan or a Grand Highlander. In fact, I optioned up a Model Y Premium with similar features (including the 3rd row) and it came out to about $60,000! So, this suggests the Model YL will be available for about $53,000 or approximately a $3,000 upcharge once they stop selling the Launch Edition (similar to the price difference in other global markets). On space, the Model YL is pretty similar to the Model X. Good enough for many families, but not as spacious as minivans, the Grand Highlander, or the Chevy Tahoe. You can see from the screenshot below that the Model YL is sold out for 2026, and the dealer was telling people to not expect them until March 2027.

I thought it would look more different than the regular Y. I found it difficult to tell the difference at a glance.

The second row was very comfortable, with heated and cooled seat and plenty of room and adjustable headrests. A significant upgrade to the second row of the regular Y!

The third row was a mixed bag. The seats are heated, but not cooled. It does have vents for both air conditioning and heat. It’s not as spacious as the first and second rows, but at 6′ 2″, I was comfortable and would be fine on a long drive. I did find it challenging to get to the 3rd row, since the second row didn’t slide forward like it does in many vehicles (including the regular Model Y). You are expected to sneak between the two seats in the second row, which works for most people, but older folks like me don’t like it.

Leg room was adequate (not not generous), but I was more comfortable putting one leg in the middle as shown. Had I moved up the second row, I would have had plenty of room, but then it would have been crowded. I was setting all three rows as best I could for 6-feet-tall people in all 3 rows. This is MUCH better than the 3rd row in the regular Model Y, which is only appropriate for children and small adults.

I was amazed I had an inch or two of space above my head in the 3rd row. I forgot to take any pictures of the first row. It does have an extra thigh support adjustment that is nice, but is mostly just like all of the other Model Y (great, but nothing new). Handling and accelerations were about the same as a Premium Model Y dual motor. The ride was a little softer (the YL has electronically controlled dampers, tuned for comfort) than the 2026 Model Y Premium (frequency dependent passive controlled dampers, tuned for a balance of comfort and handling) and much improved over my 2021 Model Y (conventional passive shock absorbers, great for handling but gives a harsh ride) and the 2026 Model Y Standard (retuned conventional passive shock absorbers, a balance between handling and ride). Full Self Driving (Supervised) was promoted by the sales advisor and was perfect on the short test drive.

The Model Y Standard reminded me most of my daughter’s 2024 Model Y Rear Wheel Drive. It is a little noisier and doesn’t ride as well as the premium model. It doesn’t have the ventilated seats and the premium audio, but for many, the $6,000 price difference makes up for that. For others, the Premium is well worth that cost. I did like the 18″ wheels that improve range and offer more sidewall for surviving large potholes. The Model Y Premium only offers 19″ and 20″ wheels. Full Self Driving (Supervised) worked perfectly on the test drive.

To adjust the seats, you use the screen, since there are not controls on the seats.

I didn’t drive the Model 3 Standard, but I want to make two points about it.

After seeing the Model YL, Model Y Standard, and the Model 3 Standard in person, the takeaway is clear: Tesla has made its most practical vehicles significantly more accessible without abandoning the core strengths that made the brand popular.

The Model YL addresses the long-standing complaint that Tesla lacked a true family hauler. While it still doesn’t match the passenger or cargo space of a minivan or large three-row SUV like the Grand Highlander or Tahoe, it is a meaningful improvement over the regular Model Y’s third row and far more usable for adults or even teenagers. At roughly $53,000 once the Launch Edition incentives end, it finally offers a realistic alternative to the much more expensive Model X or Rivian R1S (~$90,000 for comparable 6 seat layout) for families who want three rows without the premium price.

The Model Y Standard reinforces that Tesla can still deliver strong value at a lower price. It gives up ventilated seats, premium audio, and some refinement, but the $6,000 savings and more practical 18-inch wheels make it a sensible choice for some buyers. Meanwhile, the Model 3 Standard stands out as an even better relative deal than the original 2016 Model 3 that created such intense demand — more range, quicker acceleration, and Full Self-Driving capability at a price that remains extremely competitive in today’s market. I was disappointed when these models were announced a year ago, as I wrote about here, mainly because I felt Tesla promised a smaller car for under $30,000. However, all three of these vehicles have found their market in the US, as evidenced by the long waitlist to get all three and the lack of discounts and aggressive financing deals available.

Taken together, these three models show Tesla broadening its appeal. The company is no longer only competing at the premium end; it is also offering capable, reasonably priced options for both families and efficiency-focused buyers. For those who have been waiting for Tesla to better serve larger households or entry-level shoppers, the current lineup finally delivers more realistic choices.

#5785. The Jaguar Type 01's U.S.-Spec Bumper Is Fantastically Well Integrated

We may be long past the days of requiring extraordinarily ugly impact bumpers be affixed to cars sold in the U.S., with those laws extending to supercars like the Lamborghini Countach, cars that are driving around on American roads still aren't quite as smooth as they may be in other markets. Whether for insurance reasons like the Bugatti Chiron or to meet regulatory crash safety regulations, U.S.-spec versions of some cars (typically wild-looking, high-end ones) sometimes get bumpers that protrude slightly further out, or have bumperettes or bumper guards added on.

The latest victim of this is the Jaguar Type 01, except its little U.S.-spec bumperette solution is actually extremely well done, perfectly integrated with its outrageous styling. I got to see the Type 01 in person for the first time at the Las Vegas Concours over the weekend, and I love it even more in the metal than I already did in photos. Luckily our American-market modifications haven't ruined that.

At the bottom of the body-color strakes in the upright rear end, the Type 01 has a black bar stretching across the same width that houses the parking sensors, with the license plate holder sitting just below it along with a fang-like diffuser design. On the U.S.-spec Type 01, that black bar juts outward a little more dramatically, with angled sections at the ends instead of it being flat all the way across. The rest of the rear end design is exactly the same, and the protruding bumper flows so perfectly with the car's design, you probably wouldn't even notice it if the two cars were side by side.

There is one other difference between Euro- and U.S.-spec Type 01s you may have noticed. Here in America our cars need to have side marker lights and reflectors at front and the rear; usually automakers will integrated these as subtly as possible, maybe along the curve of the wheel arches, following the design of the bumper, or even putting them within the headlights and taillights themselves. Jaguar, though, decided to make them a more prominent part of the car's design.

The Type 01's side markers are squares, positioned low down in the corners of the front and rear bumpers where their lines are aligned with other lines of the car. Yeah, they stand out, and some people will find them to be an eyesore, but I actually like this placement. At least nothing else about the Type 01's lighting design had to be changed for the U.S. market — the headlight arrays are still ultra-thin, and the pair of full-width taillights are still hidden between those strakes.

Other than those two little details, the Type 01's design is identical across markets, which is a good thing. Love it or hate it, you've got to respect Jaguar really swinging for the fences here and creating production car with pure concept-y looks, like it traveled back in time to show off how wild cars will look in the future.

#5784. I Only Want The Gorgeous Mid-Engine BMW Sports Car Because I Care About Saving The Planet, Sir, I Promise

As we all do occasionally, I found myself browsing BMW i8 listings over the weekend. A clean i8 passed me on the road, and it looked so good, I had to check prices. I mean, we're talking about a mid-engine sports car with butterfly doors and a sweet carbon-fiber chassis, so they can't be that cheap. But the engine's essentially the same three-cylinder that's found in a Mini, and there's no manual, so they can't be that expensive.

The cheapest BMW i8 I could find with a clean title is listed for $33,299, or what those of us in the business call "the danger zone." That's juuuust cheap enough that a normal person could convince themselves it's a good idea to buy a depreciated luxury car, only to get hit with huge bills. Obviously, a normal person should never buy a heavily depreciated, low-volume German car that's incredibly complicated and already more than a decade old. Me, though? I think I might replace my Fiat 500e with an i8 when the lease is up.

Obviously, since the Fiat is a coupe, and I'm never having kids, it makes sense that I'd replace one coupe with another, but you're probably assuming I want the BMW i8 because it's a gorgeous mid-engine sports car that I can buy at an affordable price. That's incorrect. You see, I actually want the beautiful BMW with the carbon-fiber chassis because I'm a good person who cares about the environment. Yes, it offers great balance and agile handling in a comfortable, daily drivable package that looks like an exotic, but I need you to believe I only want the BMW i8 so I can help save the planet.

You can buy all sorts of cars for about $33,000, but as far as practical rides go, it's hard to beat the Honda Civic Sport Touring Hybrid. It's comfortable, offers pretty much all the bells and whistles, and its hybrid powertrain is rated at 49 mpg combined. That's the kind of good, responsible car you buy, and oh, isn't it nice it also has 200 horsepower and 232 pound-feet of torque? A hybrid Civic is the car someone my age probably should buy, but I just care about not giving kids asthma too much to get the reasonable Honda.

Remember, the BMW i8 is a hybrid, too. In fact, it's a plug-in hybrid. And because of that, despite making enough power for Car and Driver to hit 60 mph in 4.0 seconds flat, it's also incredibly fuel efficient. Keep that battery topped off, and it's rated at 76 MPGe, which is more than 49 mpg. The i8 also has 15 miles of electric-only while the Civic has none. You see, I can't buy the Honda because I can't afford to. I need the BMW and its sweet billionaire doors because it's so much more efficient.

Could you imagine driving a car that got less than 50 mpg? I certainly couldn't. I need to get at least 75 mpg to feel good about all the tire particles my car feeds the salmon, and the only car I can think of that meets my needs is the BMW i8. So if you really think about it, the two-door German and its laser headlights is just the more practical choice. That's not a slight at the Civic, either. I'm sure it's a very nice car if you like modern features and refinement. It's just not the car I need because it's not the BMW i8. And I need the BMW i8 because I care about saving the planet. You believe me, right? I need you to promise you believe me here.

#5783. Aluminum–Air Generators for Data Centres Face a Metal Logistics Test

California startup Voya Energy announced a $35 million financing round in August 2026 for generators that use prepared scrap aluminum, air and water to produce electricity without combustion. Its immediate opportunity includes replacing diesel backup equipment at data centres, where exhaust, noise and permitting can be genuine obstacles. The company also describes a larger market for firm power at grid-constrained sites, including systems operating around the clock. The electrochemistry is established, but delivering competitive electricity requires a materials supply chain that the generator specifications do not describe.

An aluminum–air cell consumes aluminum. It does not accept electricity through a charging cable and return to its original chemical state. Aluminum reacts with oxygen and water, producing electrical energy and aluminum hydroxide, sometimes called aluminum trihydrate. The generator needs more metal when the fuel is spent, and the hydroxide has to be collected, transported and either sold into another market or processed further. The aluminum brought to a data centre already embodies substantial electricity used earlier to turn aluminum compounds into metal. That upstream energy belongs in the assessment.

I encountered the same supply-chain issues when I examined Wright Electric’s aluminum–air aircraft proposal in 2021. Prepared aluminum would have needed delivery to airports, followed by collection and processing of spent material. Data centres avoid the aircraft weight constraint, while retaining the need for deliveries of prepared fuel and industrial handling of reaction products.

The operating schedule determines the size of that problem. Voya’s August announcement emphasizes diesel replacement while also describing larger, continuously available power installations. To test the larger proposition, I calculated the materials needed for a hypothetical 100 MW data centre supplied continuously by aluminum–air generation. Using the company’s reported 57% conversion efficiency and aluminum’s theoretical electrochemical energy, the system consumes roughly 520 metric tons of metal each day and produces about 1,500 metric tons of aluminum hydroxide. That becomes approximately 190,000 tons of incoming metal and 550,000 tons of outgoing material each year. The additional byproduct mass comes from oxygen and water incorporated in the reaction. These are scenario quantities, not measured operations at a Voya site.

An intermittent backup generator could consume orders of magnitude less aluminum annually than the continuous 100 MW case, changing the economics of deliveries and residue handling. Voya’s interest in low-grade contaminated scrap deserves examination, since some metal streams are difficult to sort into high-quality recycled products. Yet scrap is not automatically valueless because it is contaminated. Recycling aluminum into new metallic products uses approximately 95% less energy than making primary metal, and improving scrap recovery is itself an important industrial decarbonization opportunity. Buying that scrap as expendable fuel can compete with other recovery routes as their technology and economics improve.

Voya initially expects to sell aluminum hydroxide and proposes metal regeneration as a longer-term option. Those are different uses for the spent material. A 2026 lifecycle assessment modeled electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency of 29–35% for aluminum–air storage pathways involving regeneration. That finding is not a test result for Voya’s equipment, but it indicates how much additional electricity and processing could be needed to close the material loop. A company selling the hydroxide cannot also assume it will recover that same material for fuel without buying it back.

Voya’s published metal-price target leaves limited room for other costs. In a 2025 California Energy Commission submission, the company listed targets below $0.30/kWh for delivered electricity and $0.50 per pound for the metal fuel. At 57% conversion efficiency, the latter implies about $0.24/kWh for aluminum alone, before fuel preparation, generator capital, transport, residue handling or financing. Saleable hydroxide could provide an offset where purity, processing costs and buyers support it. The generation target remains a target, rather than a demonstrated commercial tariff.

There may be worthwhile applications for compact, noncombustion backup power where diesel is hard to permit and suitable scrap is readily available. Continuous power for large AI facilities calls for a much larger comparison with grid connections, generation and rechargeable batteries. The chemistry works, but the economics must account for every load of metal delivered, every load of residue removed and the electricity consumed upstream.

My TFIE Strategy Briefing assessment follows the aluminum through the generator, the possible recycling and regeneration routes, Voya’s cost targets and the very different material demands of backup and continuous generation.

#5782. How Did History's Deadliest Pathogen Infect a Private High School?

— Anatomy of a tuberculosis outbreak in the Bay Area

We heard about the outbreak by accident. In December 2025, I (Meyer) was chatting with a friend who has a teenager in a rival San Francisco high school. Our conversation turned to football first, then to prom.

"It's going great," the friend reported. "Well, except for the tuberculosis."

Tuberculosis (TB), caused by the slender, rod-shaped Mycobacterium tuberculosis, is one of humanity's great scourges. It's ancient, contagious, highly lethal, and thrives in impoverished settings. A well-funded private school is just about the last place we would expect to find a TB outbreak.

But my friend was right. About a month earlier, the San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH) issued a report describing a case of TB at Archbishop Riordan High School (ARHS). By March, that one case would balloon into hundreds more.

As a physician (Meyer) and a journalist (Hahm), we spent months wondering how history's deadliest infection overwhelmed a prestigious Bay Area school. On the outbreak's 1-year anniversary, we sat down with several parents and a student to find out.

The story of TB is one of the U.S.'s great triumphs. Until the 1800s, tuberculosis was the single greatest cause of American mortality, responsible for a quarter of all deaths. But by the early 1900s, public health initiatives that improved living and work conditions precipitated a drop in TB. After streptomycin was developed in the 1940s, case rates plunged. Between the 1950s and 1980s, annual TB mortality dropped from 20,000 to under 2,000. However, TB remains a leading cause of death globally due to overcrowding, malnutrition, limited healthcare, and, more recently, cuts to foreign aid.

Today, 77% of cases in the U.S. occur in foreign-born individuals, in whom TB incidence is 20 times greater than in U.S.-born individuals. In San Francisco, TB epidemiology mirrors national trends.

This, according to the parents we interviewed, is how the ARHS outbreak began -- with a student who had recently immigrated from a continent with high TB prevalence (Africa).

In September 2025, ARHS's index case of TB (patient zero) was evaluated by a medical provider, reporting 2 weeks of cough. As you might imagine, a cough is a fairly common complaint amongst high school students during flu season. The student's symptoms were not attributed to TB at that initial visit.

TB is a slow burning disease. Infection occurs when someone inhales its bacilli and, in about 5% of infected individuals, this results in the development of active TB with classic consumptive symptoms (cough, bloody sputum, night sweats). But most people don't develop symptoms immediately. Their immune system halts the infection and they remain both asymptomatic and non-contagious -- a state known as latent TB. But there's always a risk those dormant bacilli will reactivate into active TB -- about a 10% risk over a person's lifetime. In the U.S., 80% of active TB cases are due to reactivation, and among foreign-born individuals, 93% are. The good news is there's treatment for latent TB, and it's 90% effective at preventing progression to active disease.

However, there are still an estimated 13 million people with latent TB in the U.S. who, left untreated, represent a reservoir for ongoing transmission -- a sort of tuberculous tinderbox. And treatment of latent TB often falls through the cracks of the American health system: in one study, only half (48%) of foreign-born adults who tested positive for latent TB were offered treatment; in another, only 47% of patients who started treatment completed it.

In addition, in 2021, for the first time in 30 years, TB began quietly staging a comeback. Cuts to public health infrastructure, pandemic-related healthcare disruptions, and increased immigration all contributed to a recent and ongoing TB resurgence in the U.S.

Once someone has active TB, that person is contagious, but only moderately so -- in developed countries the R0 (the number of people typically infected by an individual with active TB) is generally well below 1. But transmission can increase -- a lot -- if there's extended, indoor contact between the infected and uninfected. Especially during the winter.

ARHS offers a boarding option, which is convenient for international students. This, according to the parents we interviewed, was where patient zero was living between the onset of cough in September and November -- when the student was finally referred to SFDPH for evaluation of active TB.

SFDPH began by screening patient zero's close contacts. This revealed an ominously high prevalence of TB infection. In December, mandatory testing of all ARHS students and staff was announced. Two additional cases of active and 50 cases of latent TB were confirmed in January. By late February, over 1,300 TB tests had been administered. And by March, a startling 18% of those tested -- 244 students and staff -- were positive for latent TB infection, in addition to eight cases of active TB.

All told, the fallout was massive: extensive, repeated, months-long testing; medical treatment for hundreds of students and staff; widespread school disruption, including cancellation of in-person classes; and considerable frustration and confusion amongst students and parents, who largely shouldered the cost of all that testing. By April, 96% of the latent and 100% of the active cases had started treatment, and the outbreak was considered contained.

The goal of any outbreak investigation is, first and foremost, to stop the outbreak. And then to learn from it. It's tempting to view the ARHS outbreak as an isolated anomaly -- but this would be learning the wrong lesson.

In April, the CDC published a review of 50 large TB outbreaks in the U.S. About a quarter were associated with congregate living settings, such as correctional facilities. In the remaining three quarters, the outbreak spread primarily via social networks. In all of them, 80% of cases occurred in U.S.-born individuals. The study is a bleak reminder that no one is completely safe from TB.

Could the San Francisco outbreak have been prevented? It's not clear. We don't know if patient zero was offered, initiated, or completed treatment for latent TB. We do know the initial diagnosis was missed and the student spent months with active TB in a congregate living setting before starting treatment. From there, the high-density, highly social environment of high school appears to have been perfect fuel for transmission.

Perhaps the most important takeaway is that tuberculosis is a contemporary threat, not a historical relic. In an era of rising TB rates, the ARHS outbreak is a warning. Its breathtaking escalation from a single case to hundreds of infections in just a few months underscores why the great white plague was once the most feared disease in the world. It's a reminder against complacency.

Tuberculosis was a death sentence just a century ago -- it would be arrogant to assume we've conquered it.

This perspective is the authors' alone and does not necessarily reflect that of any institutions or companies with which they are affiliated.

#5781. This Mid-90s Austrian Car Company Cobbled Together A Lineup With A Lightly Rebadged Ford, Mercury, Saturn And Dodge

Sauber isn't a strange way to say Saab, also a defunct auto brand. Nor is it in any way related to the Sauber racing team that finally closed shop in 2025, giving way for Audi to take a seat at the Formula 1 table. The Sauber we are talking about today was an extremely short-lived Austrian car brand that existed from 1993-1995, solely to import American cars to Austria to sell them under the Sauber name. Well, it was a little more complicated than that. Its relative obscurity sent YouTuber corsicar on one of the most amusing missions of discovering what exactly the brand was, and more importantly, "why?"

Prior to corsicar's deep dive into this mysterious car company, knowledge on Sauber had been little to none. It seemed to have made it into the curious car chasm in 2025 via TheTruthAboutCars, and an Autopost article done shortly after. One simply cannot internet search Google themselves into a hole for hours taking in information on Sauber otherwise. Coriscar, however, found a newspaper ad for a vehicle called a Sauber Villager. It looks strangely similar to Mercury's Villager. Almost identical, because it is the same vehicle. This gets the whole search rolling.

The Sauber brand was established by a married couple in Austria in 1993. After getting things situated in Austria, the owners founded another company in the U.S., in Florida, Sauber Automobiles USA, Inc. This was likely to get around import laws and accruing unwanted taxes.

According to a review Coriscar found of the Sauber Villager in Auto Revue magazine, the Florida office was used to purchase American vehicles that would then be registered in the U.S. From there, it could export those vehicles to Austria, where they'd get a light facelift to make changes to meet Austrian regulations, and with a little rebadging, they'd officially be "Sauber" cars, as demonstrated by the ads found and shared in the video.

The company essentially tried to make a complete lineup of in-demand or soon-to-be in-demand vehicles using different American market models. There was the family hauler, minivan or MPV Sauber Villager, which was the Mercury Villager, a Ford product, which was also a Nissan product. Sauber's mid-size sedan, coupe and or wagon, the Messager, was General Motors' Saturn S-class sedan, 2-door coupe, and wagon. The entry-level econo-car was the unfortunately named Sauber Teenager, or a Ford Aspire. And the sporty car was the Sauber S1, which was a Dodge Stealth or Mitsubishi 3000GT.

Sauber models went on sale in 1994 with 12 existing dealers. The hope was to expand to 30 by mid-year. At those dealers, interested buyers could consider the cheaper, poorly named Teenager at around $14,500 (in 1994), the Messager at $22,000, the base Villager at $41,600, its top-of-the-line First Class trim level cost around $54,700, and the S1 offered at $76,100. Just for kicks, to give you an idea of how much that costs today with inflation, the Teenager would start at $33,000 and the top of the line, sporty S1 would be just shy of $175,000.

To get the attention of potential buyers, Sauber really played with the Austrian sense of humor. One ad shown in the video reads (in Austrian) "In life you have to try everything at least once. A test drive in a Sauber doesn't hurt either." Pictured below the text was a Sauber Villager (or basically edited Mercury Villager), and above the text, a pair of boxing gloves, cigars, and a leather crotch harness for you know exactly what.

It seems the ads were not funny enough because in May 1995 documents show the Commercial Court of Vienna rejected the car company's intent to declare bankruptcy, and instead officially declared the company dissolved. Sauber was so broke, it had nothing to help pay off debtors in a bankruptcy. What ruined it isn't clear. Importing cars from another country is an expensive endeavor. Buying a car to then make costly adjustments to them to meet regulations likely didn't help either. The whole model doesn't feel very viable. It also happens that a new tax introduced in 1994 — the Austrian Value-Added Tax Act — would have subjected those imports to heavier taxation.

Also, spending $100,000 (today) on a minivan is outrageous. I can't imagine the pricing did them any favors when there were plenty of vehicles in Europe, as well as imported for a price that was much more palatable for European families.

The whole thing almost doesn't seem real, but coriscar prudently shared every bit of archived paperwork, magazines, and ads he finds to verify that Sauber was indeed real, including a 1994 review of the Villager in Austria's Auto Revue. He actually bought almost all of the Auto Revues he could find just to find this one real-life review.

Corsicar was also able to find out through extensive research that the brand had maybe sold 28 cars in that time. In reality, it's still more real than Tesla's lastest Roadster might ever be.

If you do have any bit of a soul, the last part of corsicar's video will tug at your heartstrings. The YouTuber looked into how many of these nearly extinct relics had stayed on the road by looking at Sauber registrations in Austria. The last one on the road was in 2018. By 2019, not a single Sauber remained in motion — at least in Austria. If one has survived, we'll only know if you post a photo of it in the comments.

#5779. Flock Won't Take No For An Answer, Keeps Cameras In Service After Communities Cancel Contracts

Cities across the country have been dropping their Flock camera contracts left and right as people object to the surveillance state they enable. Canceling these contracts isn't always a straightforward process, however. The Verge reports that Flock is not only delaying the removal of their equipment from communities that have requested it, but also reactivating it when officials take matters into their own hands.

One of these cities is Plymouth, Minnesota, where Joel Feder of The Drive was wrongfully accused of driving a stolen car based on a bad Flock hit. The city council voted to cancel its contract with Flock on September 22, and officially notified Flock the following day. From The Drive:

[Plymouth Police Chief Eric] Fadden said, "We did not hear any reply from Flock Safety Corporate or Legal, other than some communication with our local representative." Flock's silence and refusal to comply with the canceled contract forced the Police Chief to take matters into his own hands. "After hearing nothing for more than a week, I directed our staff to disconnect the power cords from the cameras in order to be sure that they are not functioning or recording plates," Fadden said.

It's rather ironic that the chief of police ended up instructing his officers to do exactly the same thing some vandals have done to disable the cameras. With Flock not responding to multiple attempts to cancel the service, this appeared to be the only way to be sure the cameras were off, as the city council's vote required.

Other cities have taken this process a step further, removing the cameras and storing them until Flock wants them back. From KARE 11:

"Once we made this decision, I personally went to the locations and removed the cameras and poles myself," Crystal police chief Pete Underthun told KARE 11 in a statement. "We are still working with the company to close out our contract and for them to pick the cameras up from our garage."

I guess what would otherwise qualify as vandalism is fine if the police do it themselves. Dayton, Minnesota, also physically removed its cameras, but even that didn't shut down the service. As the city explained in a Facebook post:

On September 17, 2026, the Police Department was made aware of a maintenance work order produced by Flock. The City notified Flock on September 18, 2026, that the program was on hold, and no work orders were to be completed. Unfortunately, the City's direction was not followed, and the camera was placed back into service without authorization. Following the report, City staff reviewed locations throughout the community to determine whether any additional cameras had been reinstalled, and one additional location was identified. The Police Department has been notified, and both cameras will be removed promptly.

Like so many things these days, Flock is a subscription service. Communities pay for the service, but Flock owns all the hardware and is responsible for installing and maintaining it, as well as removing it when requested. Technically, by the book, the police shouldn't be disabling or removing cameras, either. But we're not going to complain when they do, especially when Flock seems to be dragging its feet on the matter.

Other communities have resorted to covering cameras with trash bags while waiting for Flock to do its part. Even this strategy hasn't always been effective, though. The Verge also reports that Elgin Community College found the bags over its Flock cameras removed, presumably by Flock contractors sent out to "fix" the cameras they had covered while trying to cancel the service. This happened several times between December 2025 and April 2026. Only when the original contract expired did Flock arrange to remove the unwanted cameras.

Flock's only comment on this matter to KARE 11 was: "We are proud of the impact our technology had in Plymouth and Dayton. We respect the cities' decisions and are working with the customers to have the cameras removed." It gave no status of the cancellation requests or timeline for camera removal. Zach Doud, Dayton city administrator, told KARE 11 that Flock told him it would take 60 days to remove the equipment. It's hard to tell whether Flock is deliberately dragging this out, or simply overwhelmed by the large number of cancelation requests it's getting.

Either way, I wonder if whoever wrote Flock's cancellation policy was listening to "Hotel California" by the Eagles at the time. It seems like you can check out any time you like, but you can never leave.

#5778. Incretin Drug May Improve Menstrual Regularity

— Dual GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist tied to shorter cycles, less variability

BALTIMORE -- Use of a combined GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist was associated with improved menstrual regularity, an analysis of a prospective cohort showed.

Women taking the combination incretin drug had a reduction in cycle length of 2.5 days compared with a reduction of 0.4 days for those on a GLP-1 drug and 0.8 days for never-users, reported Shruthi Mahalingaiah, MD, MS, of the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health in Boston, and colleagues.

The combined GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist also was associated with a more pronounced decrease in mean individual cycle variability, at 6.93 days compared with 7.45 days for GLP-1 drugs and 7.46 days for never-users, they reported during a presentation at the American Society for Reproductive Medicine (ASRM) annual meeting.

Furthermore, a subgroup analysis of patients with polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome (PMOS; formerly polycystic ovary syndrome [PCOS]) showed even more marked effects. For this group, mean individual cycle variability was 5.80 days for combined GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist users, 7.34 days for GLP-1 receptor agonist users, and 9.45 days for never users, they reported.

"This more pronounced reduction among PMOS individuals might suggest a separate pathway that might focus on ovulatory health in addition to those metabolic parameters that support ovulation, but further research is necessary," Mahalingaiah said.

Rachel Weinerman, MD, an ob/gyn and reproductive endocrinologist at Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland who wasn't involved in the study, told MedPage Today that this study's findings about PMOS were particularly interesting.

"We know that because PMOS is a metabolic issue, weight loss can actually help patients achieve a more regular cycle," she said. Thus, when a PMOS patient is on a weight-loss medication, it makes sense that they would both lose weight and have more regular periods, she noted.

Weinerman added that irregular periods aren't only problematic for people trying to get pregnant; they can signal underlying health issues. This study is a good reminder that PMOS patients are a distinct group who may respond to medications differently than others with similar characteristics, she said.

More than 10 million women in the U.S. use either a GLP-1 or combined GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist, which work through different mechanisms of action (the only GLP-1/GIP drug approved by the FDA is tirzepatide [Zepbound]). These therapies may impact ovulatory health through systemic and metabolic health improvements or direct ovarian impacts, Mahalingaiah noted.

While some retrospective studies have suggested an association with improved menstrual regularity, no prospective studies have looked at it as a primary endpoint. So this research sought to determine if these agents were associated with changes in mean cycle length and cycle variability in tracked menstrual cycles.

"We wanted to show, with a little more granularity, the extent to which we might see impact," Mahalingaiah told MedPage Today.

Researchers utilized the Apple Women's Health Study (AWHS), which is a longitudinal digital cohort of about 147,000 U.S. women and their prospectively logged menstrual cycles. Patients are 18 and older, have an iPhone, and have menstruated at least once. Participants in this analysis were younger than 50, could not be using hormones or be pregnant or lactating, and had a cycle length between 10 and 90 days. They had to have logged at least 3 cycles.

Mahalingaiah and team ultimately analyzed 1,945 participants with 70,134 logged cycles; most (1,564) were never-users while 258 used a GLP-1 medication and 123 used a combined GLP-1/GIP medication in the past year.

This cohort responded to surveys with questions about weight-loss medications, demographics, and medical history. They also consented to share their logged menstrual information recorded on HealthKit, though authors did not use any sensor-based data.

Researchers stratified groups by those who indicated using a GLP-1 or combined GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist in the past year and those who hadn't, as well as those with and without PMOS. Baseline characteristics were similar between groups, though medication users veered older (age 38 to 39 vs 35) and had higher parity than never-users. They also had a higher proportion of PMOS, infertility, type 2 diabetes, and hypertension.

The primary reason for being prescribed a GLP-1 or GLP-1/GIP receptor agonist in the past year was weight loss for health, followed by weight loss for appearance and PMOS.

Mahalingaiah noted that future manuscripts will break down this data by particular agents.

"There is such little innovation in women's health pharmaceuticals that maybe data like this could help people in pharma think about the additional mechanisms that might promote ovulation," Mahalingaiah said.

#5777. Jeep Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept Is Your Inner-Child's Dream Jeep With A Hemi V8, Reservable Jump Seats And Independent Front Suspension

Jeep has just done something with the Wrangler that has never been done before: given it independent front suspension, and somehow, that's not even the wildest part of its latest concept vehicle. The automaker just pulled the covers off the Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept at the 2026 SEMA Show in Las Vegas, and right away you can tell this thing is no ordinary Jeep truck.

Out back, you'll find a Trophy Truck-style rear axle. All in all, it doesn't look too dissimilar from the Jeep Sandstorm Concept we saw back in 2018, but they're certainly different vehicles.

Developed with off-road racer Casey Currie, the new independent front suspension delivers 14 inches of travel up front and 15 inches out back. This is a Jeep aimed at desert running, not the rock-crawling crowd that usually flocks to Wranglers.

When paired with beefy 37-inch tires, it's clear that the Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is designed for off-road speed first and foremost. While I do love rockcrawling, there's nothing quite like prerunning to really get the heart pounding.

The Wrangler Scrambler SRT Concept is very much a concept, though I'll admit, I won't be too shocked if the Wrangler ends up getting independent front suspension at some point in the future. The Ford Bronco has it, and the Earth has yet to collapse in on itself despite that.

While this concept is still unmistakably a Jeep, Tim Kuniskis, head of American Brands, SRT Performance and Direct Connections at Stellantis North America, said the project was a dare to the brand's own playbook, which is probably where the use of an IFS comes in. Sure, it's going to tick some Jeep loyalists off, but some departures are good departures.
