#5708. ‘Three-parent IVF’ was supposed to prevent mitochondrial disease. Studies are raising doubts

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Megan covers the intersection of science and society. How is biomedical research funded? Who benefits? And how do new technologies reflect and shape our values? You can reach Megan on Signal at mmolteni.13.

The news out of the U.K. last year that eight healthy children had been born to mothers carrying disease-causing mutations in their mitochondria showed the promise of a pioneering reproductive technique known as “three-parent IVF.” The long-anticipated results seemingly showed the procedure, formally called mitochondrial replacement techniques, or MRT, could reduce the risk of babies inheriting sometimes fatal diseases, and raised hopes that other countries, such as the U.S. where MRT is banned, might soon permit it.

But even as regulators and researchers in Australia, the second country to explicitly legalize the specialized technique, prepare to launch their own national experiment with MRT, some scientists and ethicists are rethinking the potential risks and benefits of the technology, which combines genes from a mother and father with mutation-free DNA in the mitochondria of a donor egg. Emerging data from the U.K. as well as several small pilot studies from fertility clinics in other parts of the world are raising questions about whether trying to prevent mitochondrial disease is really the best first use of MRT.

“The general public may have the idea that it is very safe and low risk and that’s just not the case,” said Bert Smeets, a professor in clinical genomics who studies mitochondrial diseases at Maastricht University in the Netherlands.

Until now, pushback against MRT has mainly focused on its expanding use as a treatment for infertility. A STAT investigation published on Monday showed that IVF clinics globally are pitching it to older women desperate to have biologically related children despite scant evidence that it works for them. But some scientists are now saying that carefully run studies addressing severe forms of infertility may present the most ethical way to develop MRT safely.

Smeets serves on the oversight committee that reviews and approves applications for patients to receive MRT at Newcastle University, the only clinic that currently has a license in the U.K. to perform it. Newcastle is where one of the main methods of MRT, known as pronuclear transfer, was first developed in the early 2000s. It involves creating embryos from both the biological mother and the egg donor and then swapping out the nuclear DNA in one for the other.

Data published in 2010 by Newcastle scientists showed that in lab experiments, only a tiny amount of the mother’s mutation-bearing mitochondria — less than 2% — showed up in the reconstructed embryos. The technique looked safe and showed promise in preventing mitochondrial disease, they reported, though not very efficiently (meaning a lot of embryos didn’t survive the process).

Shortly after U.K. regulators began accepting applications from clinics to offer MRT, this picture grew more complicated. Shoukhrat Mitalipov, a developmental biologist at Oregon Health & Science University, had been developing his own method for MRT, called maternal spindle transfer. It involved putting a mother’s genetic material into a donor egg with healthy mitochondria prior to fertilization, when the egg’s chromosomes are lined up in a structure called the spindle.

In 2009, Mitalipov’s lab had reported the births of the world’s first monkeys following maternal spindle transfer. The animals had appeared healthy with no traces of mitochondrial DNA left over from the original eggs. But when his group tried the technique in the lab with human eggs, they noticed something odd.

Despite refining the spindle transfer to the point where his lab could swap up to 99% of defective mitochondria with healthy replacements, analyses run by one of his postdocs showed that the few problematic ones that had managed to cling to the spindle began to take over as the fertilized egg continued to divide. With each subsequent generation of cells, they saw fewer and fewer of the healthy mitochondria — the power plants of cells — and more and more of the mutated ones.

Before Mitalipov’s team fully understood why or how that happened, they rushed out a paper describing this problem, which they dubbed “reversion.” Their data, published in November 2016, suggested that in roughly 15% of cases, reversion could cause MRT to fail, allowing fatal defects to resurface or new health issues to arise. The revelation caused a stir but ultimately did not prevent the U.K. from moving forward with the Newcastle group’s plan to use pronuclear transfer. The group won a license for the work in 2017.

Mitalipov, stymied from pursuing his own clinical trial of spindle transfer in the U.S. by a 2015 congressional ban, began evaluating the technology as a potential fertility treatment. He and his collaborator Nuno Costa-Borges of the Spanish company Embryotools wanted to test the idea that young mitochondria might be able to help overcome poor egg quality — one of the reasons IVF fails. They recruited 25 women under 40 years old who’d had multiple IVF failures to a small study conducted in Greece. The results, published in 2023, showed that spindle transfer could produce pregnancies. But it also showed that reversion wasn’t just theoretical; it happened in the IVF clinic too. Two of the seven children born carried a mix of mitochondria from the biological mother — as high as 51% in one child and 35% in another — and the donor.

Two groups have now found that reversion can happen with pronuclear transfer, too.

When the Newcastle University team published papers last year about the births of the eight babies, the researchers noted that although the children showed no signs of disease, they found low levels of reversion, between 5% and 16%, in three of the infants.

A Ukrainian group from the Nadiya Clinic, led by its director Valery Zukin and embryologist Pavlo Mazur, has also found evidence of reversion. Out of six children whose parents allowed testing, two were found to have reversion — one with maternal mitochondrial levels up to 12% and the other with levels as high as 72% — according to unpublished data shared with STAT.

In the case of the Nadiya Clinic, pronuclear transfer was being tested as a fertility treatment, and the mothers’ mitochondria carried no apparent disease-causing mutations, so the finding of reversion is less of a concern, at least in terms of known risks, said Jacques Cohen, a New York-based embryologist who has reviewed the Ukrainian group’s data. But it adds to the growing evidence that even a tiny amount of maternal mitochondria carryover could compromise the efficacy of MRT, which would be a much bigger deal for people trying to avoid passing down mitochondrial diseases to any future children.

“To do it in a family affected by mitochondrial disease is to take a very big risk,” Cohen said. “The field is showing that it’s a bad idea.”

Cohen, who would like to see a moratorium on the use of MRT for preventing mitochondrial disease, is at one extreme of an ethical debate about what to do with this emerging information. He and others think that it’s most prudent to pause studies involving current iterations of the technology until scientists can figure out how to minimize the risks of reversion. That would allow scientists in the U.K. to continue to follow up on the children already born to see if the amount of faulty mitochondria continues to increase over time and to monitor for any resulting health complications.

Guido Pennings, a bioethicist at Ghent University in Belgium, has argued that because of the residual risk of serious disease to the offspring of carriers of mitochondrial mutations, MRT should be developed in carefully controlled trials only for infertile couples. That would enable researchers to sort out the mystery of reversion — insights that could lead to more refined methods of MRT — without exposing unborn children to known risks.

It would also allow scientists to study the unknown risks posed by the mismatch between the donor’s mitochondrial DNA and the mother’s nuclear DNA. (Mitochondrial DNA is typically inherited from the mother.) Some research in mice suggests this phenomenon could lead to immune issues or other unintended health complications. There have also been reports that mice carrying a mix of mitochondrial DNA from two animals had behavioral, cognitive, and other abnormalities.

Most ethicists and scientists who spoke to STAT wouldn’t go as far as Pennings. But there is an increasing recognition that prohibitions of trials of MRT in the context of infertility should be revisited.

In 2024, Esther Braun, of the Institute for Medical Ethics and History of Medicine at Ruhr University in Germany, laid out a case for changing the laws in the U.K. and Australia to allow for clinical trials for treating infertility, highlighting that previous ethical assessments may have underestimated both the risks of MRT for preventing mitochondrial disease and the suffering caused by involuntary childlessness. That shouldn’t be taken as an ethical green light for a burgeoning global MRT tourism industry, she emphasized.

“It seems evident that the routine clinical use of a novel medical procedure is impermissible until clinical trials have established that the procedure is effective,” Braun wrote. “However, this does not imply that conducting such clinical trials is itself impermissible.”

A spokesperson for the U.K.’s fertility regulator — the Human Fertilization and Embryology Authority — told STAT in an email that its scientific committee has considered research exploring the use of MRT for infertility, but that for now, only people who are at very high risk of passing a serious mitochondrial disease onto their children are eligible for this treatment.

Over the past year, a few research teams from around the world have made policy recommendations for how such clinical trials might responsibly proceed. In March, a group led by Smeets in the Netherlands proposed a staged approach to first identify and define types of infertility that MRT might plausibly address, then study its impact in the lab before moving on to small pilots to test its effectiveness only in patients exhibiting those specific infertility conditions. That would allow for the field to more critically evaluate which conditions MRT could safely tackle. The urgency has increased, Smeets said, as MRT is increasingly being adopted by commercial clinics as an all-purpose add-on, despite a lack of clear evidence.

“As a biologist, I always want to know that the intervention I’m doing targets the cause of something you want to solve,” Smeets said. “So this might be relevant to do this for certain subgroups of infertility where changing the mitochondria and the maternal factors in the oocyte is really allowing the embryo to develop. But that’s not the age-related cases.”

An example of what Smeets’ group has proposed is already underway in neighboring Belgium, at Ghent University. For the past few years, Dominic Stoop, a fertility specialist, and Björn Heindryckx, a reproductive geneticist, have been tracking down the molecular culprits behind the most difficult-to-treat infertility cases. They’ve helped define clinical criteria for diagnosing those kinds of cases, commonly grouped together under the term OZEMA — for oocyte/zygote/embryo maturation arrest. In a not-yet-published study spanning tens of thousands of IVF cycles at the Ghent University Hospital’s fertility clinic and a collaborating clinic in the U.S., Boston IVF, they found that OZEMA seems to occur across all ages more or less equally.

Stoop’s team has asked Belgian regulators for approval to study the effect of nuclear transfer technologies in three different patient populations — individuals with a history of mitochondrial disease, OZEMA patients, and women of advanced maternal age. The plan, he told STAT, is to treat seven patients in each group to start. So far, the government has given the green light for the first two, which Stoop hopes to be recruiting for this fall, with the first results out next year.

His team is still generating preclinical data to justify doing it for the advanced maternal age group.

“The patient population where the ethical committee finds the least problems is, in my opinion, the most risky group,” Stoop said, referring to the families with mitochondrial disease. “For the advanced maternal age and the OZEMA patients, it’s different. There may be a risk we don’t know. But if there’s a risk there, it will also be in the mitochondrial disease patients on top of the risk of these abnormal mitochondria. So these patients need very good counseling before doing it.”

Mary Herbert — a former leader of the Newcastle group who relocated to Monash University in Melbourne several years ago — said communicating both known and unknown risks to parents, and monitoring the long-term health of any resulting children, are essential for ethical use of MRT. “We have known for a decade that MRT may not work in all cases,” she told STAT.

Her own preclinical research, in addition to data from the Mitalipov group, suggested that MRT could reduce the risk of mitochondrial disease but could not guarantee prevention. That’s how it should be described to potential patients, not “as a means of preventing” mitochondrial disease, she said.

So far, clinical data from the Newcastle program have shown that MRT resulted in a 75% to 100% reduction in transmission of disease-causing mitochondrial mutations, she said. Even in the cases where reversion was observed, mutated mitochondrial levels were below the 50% threshold where disease symptoms are expected to arise. Herbert’s group at Monash has been training embryologists on MRT and is preparing to ask the Australian government for permission to begin a clinical trial in women carrying mitochondrial mutations. It would include follow-up studies of any carried-over mutated mitochondrial DNA “to ensure that levels remain stable over time and across different organ systems,” Herbert said.

#5707. Mayo Clinic discovers new ways to fight the “zombie” cells that drive aging

Seven studies from Mayo Clinic are revealing new details about senescent cells, often called "zombie" cells because they stop dividing but remain active in the body. These aging cells release inflammatory substances that can contribute to diseases associated with growing older.

The research, published in Nature journals, was conducted by scientists at Mayo Clinic's Robert and Arlene Kogod Center on Aging. Rather than simply confirming that senescent cells play a role in aging, the studies investigate how to recognize different types of these cells, why they produce harmful inflammation and how their effects might be reduced.

The findings also contribute to a nationwide effort to create detailed maps of senescent cells throughout the human body. Known as the Cellular Senescence Network (SenNet) Consortium, the project brings together researchers across the United States and receives funding from the National Institutes of Health Common Fund. Its goal is to document where senescent cells occur in different tissues and how they change throughout a person's lifetime.

"This body of work is moving the aging field forward to precisely identify, understand and target the specific senescent cells that contribute to age-related dysfunction, which is the necessary groundwork to develop new therapies that support healthy aging," says Marissa Schafer, Ph.D., a Mayo Clinic scientist whose laboratory directed several of the investigations.

Scientists Discover That Zombie Cells Are Not All Alike

Identifying senescent cells reliably has long been a major obstacle for scientists studying aging. The new research shows that these cells are much more varied than previously understood. Their characteristics differ depending on where they are located in the body and which biological processes caused them to become senescent.

To help address this challenge, researchers developed a tool called the SenMayo gene set. It uses patterns of gene activity to identify senescent cells more consistently across tissues and experimental systems.

Scientists tested the approach using bone biopsies from older adults. They also found that the gene signature became less prominent after senescent cells were removed in preclinical experiments. Since its development, SenMayo has become a widely used resource for researchers investigating aging and related diseases.

Mayo Clinic endocrinologist Sundeep Khosla, M.D., served as senior author of the study, "A new gene set identifies senescent cells and predicts senescence-associated pathways across tissues." Other Mayo Clinic researchers who contributed to the paper include Nathan LeBrasseur, Ph.D., Diana Jurk, Ph.D., João Passos, Ph.D., and LaTonya Hickson, M.D..

A Hidden Connection Between Mitochondria and Chronic Inflammation

Other studies explored one of the most damaging features of zombie cells: their tendency to generate ongoing inflammation.

The researchers discovered additional biological processes that explain why senescent cells continue producing inflammatory signals. Several of these processes involve malfunctioning mitochondria, the tiny structures responsible for producing much of a cell's energy.

In one pathway, DNA and RNA originating from mitochondria activate immune responses that contribute to inflammation. Another involves changes in mitochondrial metabolism that influence inflammatory gene activity through epigenetic mechanisms. These mechanisms affect how genes are switched on or off without changing the underlying DNA sequence.

The discoveries suggest that researchers may eventually be able to interfere with the processes responsible for chronic inflammation while leaving the senescent cells themselves intact. This would offer another approach to treatment beyond attempting to destroy every harmful aging cell.

Dr. Passos served as senior author of three papers examining these mechanisms and the diversity of senescent cells:

Experimental Treatments Show Promise Against Aging Cells

The Mayo Clinic team also investigated possible ways to reduce the number of senescent cells or limit the damage they cause.

The approaches included senolytic medications, which are designed to eliminate senescent cells, a natural compound present in tomatoes, and genetic techniques intended to target particular populations of aging cells.

When tested in older mice, these interventions produced encouraging results. Depending on the approach, researchers observed reductions in inflammatory measures and improvements in several aging-related outcomes, including physical frailty, inflammation in the brain and performance on cognitive tasks.

Another investigation uncovered a possible way to measure aspects of biological aging through blood testing. Researchers identified IL-23R as a potential biomarker that might eventually help scientists evaluate aging-related changes and determine whether future treatments are working.

These results remain preliminary in terms of medical applications. More research will be necessary to establish whether the approaches are safe and effective in people. Nevertheless, the experiments provide valuable clues for developing treatments that more precisely address the cellular processes involved in age-related diseases.

Dr. Schafer was the lead author of two studies examining biomarkers and possible interventions:

A New Direction for Healthy Aging Research

Together, the seven studies represent an important shift in how researchers approach cellular aging. Scientists are moving beyond the broad observation that senescent cells contribute to age-related decline and toward identifying which populations cause the greatest problems, what makes them harmful and how those specific effects could be controlled.

The findings also challenge the idea that eliminating senescent cells must always be the primary treatment strategy. By understanding the molecular pathways that trigger persistent inflammation, researchers may be able to develop therapies that block damaging signals without removing the cells responsible for producing them.

Mayo Clinic researcher Darren Baker, Ph.D., served as senior author of the paper "Senotypes define the diverse landscape of senescent cells," which examines the varied characteristics of these aging cell populations.

The work also supports Mayo Clinic's broader Precure Research initiative. This program aims to equip physicians with better ways to identify and intervene in harmful biological changes before they develop into disease or advance into conditions that are difficult to treat.

By revealing how zombie cells differ, why they promote inflammation and which processes might be targeted, the research offers a more detailed roadmap for future treatments designed to support healthier aging.

#5706. Opinion: How meditation helped me become a better doctor overnight

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

Kinast is an ophthalmologist at Legacy Devers Eye Institute, a clinical scientist at Legacy Research Institute, and a clinical professor at OHSU Casey Eye Institute.

Last fall I attended a meditation retreat in the Santa Cruz Mountains. I had hoped for a respite from a busy ophthalmology practice in Portland, Ore. Instead, I returned to the most difficult challenges I have faced in practice.

One night, we were asked to remain awake in meditation through dawn. The teachers explained that this “all-nighter” would be quite different from those in our past, such as late nights studying in college or socializing with friends.

For me, however, the term “all-nighter” did not evoke memories from a library or party. Instead, I recollected the most devastating injuries I have ever witnessed as an ophthalmologist: a patient who survived an execution-style gunshot and required brain surgery and an enucleation; a serene woman waiting in her car near a street festival, struck by stray gang violence; and eyes ruptured by knives, fireworks, bungee cords, windshields, beer bottles, sticks, rocks, and fish hooks. Many of them “just minding my own business.” Each story life-changing and traumatizing.

Ophthalmologists are called in — often in the middle of the night — to help these individuals. With limited hope for preserving sight, we try to reconstruct their ruptured globes. An all-nighter in this context requires moving efficiently, precise care, and endurance. We must provide the best surgical care possible to help these wounded souls while leading an equally exhausted operating-room team, everyone aware of the day’s work still ahead.

Staying up all night in the meditation hall, I realized that I had never fully digested the trauma of these devastating injuries. I had never taken the time and space to sit with the losses — the eyes, the lives, the damage.

As dawn approached, an anticipatory excitement filled the hall and most joined in a rejoiceful meditative chant. I sat in the back of the hall and grieved.

Mourning into the morning led to a tremendous gratitude and respect for physicians who treat trauma, including my fellow ophthalmologists and myself. Patients may think of ophthalmologists as doctors who perform friendly examinations with “Star Trek”-like equipment and brief surgeries to help with sight, and that is true. We also perform vital work alongside emergency physicians and trauma surgeons, managing injuries so severe they can be difficult to even witness. In these worst moments, times of dire need, we come in and help. Sometimes, we stay up all night.

These “all-nighters” are a service of the heart that benefit our fellow human beings, even when our lionhearts are too closed to grieve in the moment. Across medicine, physicians need support to carry the profound emotional burdens of helping patients and families through tragedy. What feels like a weight of helplessness and sorrow on our shoulders may, with enough space, also reflect our remarkable capacities for strength, steadfastness, and compassion.

That night taught me how the inner work of meditation and self-inquiry can support the outer work of patient care. The stoic rigidity that held back my tears and helped me appear strong had also kept patients, and their distress, at a distance. Within that rigidity lay a fear of becoming overwhelmed by patients’ suffering and then unsettled just before operating. With a tonic of awareness, space, and time, the physical tension and fear released. In its place emerged a true strength: to be open to another’s suffering, present with their experience. Without a rigid barrier, I can better attune to my patients whether they are facing trauma, the loss of a loved one, or simply a bad day.

Since the retreat, I have tried to be more present with my patients in clinic. Each time I enter an examination room and sit on my swivel chair, I ritualistically sense my feet on the ground as a reminder to be mindful. Meditation is often described as a returning to the present moment after each successive drift. The returning itself is the practice. Each patient now offers an opportunity for both clinical and meditative practice. Forget my feet and then remember them; become overwhelmed by long wait times, then ground myself; slip into autopilot, then return. Clinic itself becomes a meditation. Returning again and again helps keep the heart open.

Trauma call remains my least favorite part of medicine and often the most meaningful. I see traumatic eye injuries only a few times each year; many physicians in other fields treat this type of suffering daily. Thank you to the trauma physicians and surgeons who care for unimaginable injuries, each a devastating story. May we mourn with open hearts the tragedies that find their way into our hands.

Robert M. Kinast, M.D., is an ophthalmologist at Legacy Devers Eye Institute, a clinical scientist at Legacy Research Institute, and a clinical professor at OHSU Casey Eye Institute in Portland, Oregon. He invented the GentleDrop eye drop guide and the CleverDrop eye drop monitor.

#5705. Samaritan Health Services, MultiCare Health System close merger

Samaritan Health Services, MultiCare Health System close merger" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

After months of securing the necessary regulatory approvals, Samaritan Health Services officially joined up with MultiCare Health System at the top of November to create an 18-hospital, $7.5 billion nonprofit health system.

The Northwestern organizations' deal, announced last year, directs $700 million from MultiCare into care services, workforce development, facility improvements and technology investments across Samaritan facilities over the coming decade. Those investments and other "longer-term" decisions will be informed by local community needs and perspectives, with decisions headed by "a locally led regional strategic planning process," they said in this week's announcement.

“MultiCare brings expertise and resources that will help us meet the changing healthcare needs of our region and support our clinicians and employees in their work every day," Marty Cahill, Samaritan's president and CEO, who has also taken on the roles of senior vice president and chief executive of MultiCare's Oregon Coast to Cascades Region, said in the announcement.

Samaritan comprises five hospitals in western Oregon, and will also remain locally led under its new parent organization, officials have said throughout the merger process. Its addition represented a geographic market expansion for the 13-hospital MultiCare.

Samaritan Health Services and MultiCare Health System have cleared all the regulatory bars necessary to complete their merger, which will cross the finish line on Nov. 1.

The nonprofits' affiliation would create an 18-hospital system with more than $7.5 billion in revenue—and give MultiCare an acute-care foothold in Oregon. Announced in 2025, it also includes a $700 million, 10-year commitment from MultiCare to invest in Samaritan's facilities, workforce and care access points.

On Monday, the pair said that all public agencies that were reviewing their deal "have either approved the transaction or announced their intent to do so." Some of these, such as the approval from the Oregon Health Authority (see below), would bring additional conditions on areas such as the reinvestment of operating margins into local care.

“We look forward to investing in the future of healthcare across Samaritan’s service area and advancing our vision to be the Pacific Northwest’s highest-value system of health,” Bill Robertson, CEO of MultiCare, said in a statement. “Together, we can build on the strengths of both organizations and invest in the future of healthcare for the people who depend on us.”

A phased integration process will begin on Nov. 1, with the organizations reassuring patients and health plan members that the process wouldn't interrupt services or coverage. Samaritan is also slated to retain its name, local leadership and community-based governance, they reaffirmed.

The Oregon Health Authority (OHA) approved a deal on Monday that would merge the nonprofits MultiCare Health System and Samaritan Health Services.

State regulators said the OHA's Health Care Market Oversight (HCMO) program reviewed how the proposed merger would affect Samaritan's facilities and its impact on Oregon citizens' access to affordable and equitable healthcare.

HCMO approved the deal provided it meets established conditions (PDF), including requiring MultiCare to follow its financial commitment of investing $700 million towards Samaritan and posting a public-facing version of the commitment on Samaritan's website. Other conditions involve reinvestment of Samaritan's operating margins into local communities and a requirement to maintain existing services.

The proposal to form a $7.5 billion, 18-hospital system still has to face review from other state programs prior to moving forward.

OHA's Coordinated Care Organization (CCO) Form A review is analyzing the deal's potential impact on InterCommunity Health Network's financial stability and ability to serve state Medicaid recipients. Moreover, the state Department of Consumer and Business Services (DCBS) is reviewing the financial and overall impact of changing control of Samaritan commercial health plans.

Samaritan President and CEO Marty Cahill said in a statement that the approval is "an important step forward for the communities we serve."

"Our affiliation with MultiCare will provide additional resources to invest in our workforce, facilities, technology and services—and help make it easier for people to receive high-quality care close to home," Cahill said.

The nonprofits will continue to operate as independent organizations until the transaction closes, and executives say they are working toward an Oct. 1 closing.

The boards of nonprofits MultiCare Health System and Samaritan Health Services have approved an affiliation they expect to consummate in mid-2026.

The arrangement would bring Samaritan, which runs five community hospitals as well as health plans and clinics in Oregon’s Benton, Lincoln and Linn counties, under the 13-hospital MultiCare—a new geographic foothold for the Tacoma, Washington-based organization.

“MultiCare and Samaritan are closely aligned in our mission, vision and values, making us ideal partners as we strengthen our networks across our service regions,” MultiCare CEO Bill Robertson said in the announcement. “It will be our privilege to be a part of the communities Samaritan serves, and we look forward to working together to support and advance health care in Oregon.”

The systems said there are no immediate changes for Samaritans’ patients, plan members or employees as the two sides move through the affiliation process.

Once the deal is finalized, Samaritan will remain “locally governed and community-based” but receive new resources from MultiCare that will expand services, update its operations and ensure sustainable care in its Oregon communities, according to the announcement.

More specifically, the deal includes a 10-year investment commitment focused on modernizing Samaritan’s facilities, expanding the flagship Good Samaritan Regional Medical Center’s inpatient capacity, adopting new technologies including telehealth capabilities and growing primary and specialty care. MultiCare’s behavioral health will also expand into Samaritan’s service area along the mid-Willamette Valley and central coast.

These changes will together increase care quality and access while helping to lower the cost of care, the organizations said.

“This affiliation represents an important step in securing the future of nonprofit health care in our region,” Marty Cahill, president and CEO of Samaritan, said in the announcement. “Our commitment has always been to remain a community-based, mission-driven organization, and this partnership strengthens that promise for decades to come. […] We are excited and honored to become MultiCare’s first health system in Oregon and to bring the benefits of MultiCare’s expertise home to the communities we serve.”

The parties said they will sign a formal affiliation agreement “in the coming weeks.”

MultiCare Health System employs more than 28,000 people across its 13 hospitals. It has 300-plus care locations in Washington, Idaho and Oregon, though no hospitals in the latter. The system reported $5.9 billion of total operating revenue but a $116.5 million operating loss (-2% operating margin) in 2024, a nearly $70 million improvement over the prior year.

Samaritan Health Services operates more than 80 physician clinics and multiple health insurance plans, serving 110,000 people, as well as its five community hospitals. In 2024, the nonprofit reported more than $1.7 billion of revenue but a $93.6 million operating loss (-0.5% operating loss).

#5704. Opinion: What the 2024 electoral map reveals about America’s mortality divide

Test your knowledge with our new weekday mini crossword

By Brandon Yan, Maddie Feldmeier, and Renee Y. Hsia

Yan is a physician and public health researcher affiliated with the University of California San Francisco Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies. Feldmeier is a medical student at the UCSF School of Medicine. Hsia is professor and vice chair of health services research of the UCSF Department of Emergency Medicine.

In this 2026 midterm election season, health care ranks third on voters’ minds. That’s no surprise: U.S. life expectancy persistently lags those in comparable countries despite substantially greater spending on health care. As health and health care become increasingly political, we asked whether the leading drivers of mortality looked different by political geography in the United States.

In 2024, the mortality rate, adjusted for differences in age composition, was 19.2% higher in states that voted for Donald Trump than in states that voted for Kamala Harris. As the Make America Healthy Again (MAHA) agenda continues to shape U.S. health policy, the causes for these differences deserve close attention.

The political mortality divide in the U.S. is a relatively new phenomenon. In 2001, mortality rates adjusted for age were just 2% higher in counties where the plurality voted for a Republican presidential candidate versus a Democratic candidate.

By 2019, that relative difference had widened to 16.1%. The widening gap followed slower declines in mortality rates in Republican versus Democratic plurality counties (-11.1% versus -21.9% from 2001 to 2019, respectively).

To better understand this divergence and its more recent evolution, we compared publicly available mortality rates (measured in deaths per 100,000 people in the population and adjusted for age) between states that by plurality voted for Trump and those that voted for Harris in the 2024 presidential election over the period 2016 to 2024.

Stark differences in mortality rates between states that went for Trump and those that went for Harris have persisted and widened. When Trump won his first presidential election in 2016, mortality from all causes was 17% higher (776 versus 664 per 100,000) in the states that eventually went for him in 2024 compared with those that went for Harris. By 2024, that difference had widened to 19.2% (774 versus 649 deaths per 100,000).

This reality in 2024 reflects modest improvement from when the gap was even wider in 2021, largely because of. Covid-19. Covid-19 mortality peaked in 2020 at 86 per 100,000 people for states that went for Harris, while Covid-19 mortality in states that went for Trump continued climbing to 122 per 100,000 in 2021.

Yet Covid-19 played just one part in a more widespread phenomenon. We also examined deaths from the leading causes in the U.S.: heart disease and cancer. Whereas heart disease mortality decreased 9.1% in states that went for Harris from 2016 to 2024, it decreased only 2.9% in states that went for Trump.

Similarly, cancer mortality decreased 12.9% in states that went for Harris but only 9.1% in states that went for Trump. The persistence of these differences beyond the pandemic points to chronic disease, not Covid-19 alone, as a key component of the political mortality divide.

Drug overdose mortality tells a different story. In 2016, drug overdose mortality was 18% (or 3.4 per 100,000) higher in states that went for Trump; in 2024, it was estimated to be 2% (0.4 per 100,000) higher in states that went for Harris. Beginning in 2023, estimated drug overdose mortality rates in states that went for Trump fell below those in states that went for Harris, following an earlier peak in 2021 for Trump states (35 per 100,000) compared with 2022 for Harris states (32.5 per 100,000).

In the nine years leading up to the second Trump administration, trends in mortality portray two increasingly disparate mortal Americas — one with persistently higher mortality from heart disease and cancer independent of higher Covid-19 mortality burden and another with a widening lead in overall mortality but slower to bend the curve in drug overdose deaths.

Politics play an influential role in health policy and access to health care likely play a part. Medicaid expansion under the Affordable Care Act has been associated with lower mortality, yet 10 states have not adopted expansion. All 10 of these states went for Trump in 2024.

Coverage losses have also been greater in non-expansion states during Medicaid unwinding, and policy changes related to Medicaid work requirements and reverification could further affect continuity of coverage.

Beyond insurance coverage, access to care is increasingly challenging in rural communities, which have historically voted Republican, with disproportionate hospital closures as just one example.

Policy responses to health events can shape mortality. Differences in political priorities could explain some of the higher Covid-19 mortality rates in states that went for Trump, recognizing that policies meant to save lives also bring collateral effects.

With the drug overdose epidemic, mortality rates from drug overdose between states that went for Trump over Harris have converged. An epidemic once thought to predominantly affect distressed rural and de-industrializing communities has spread to and persisted in coastal and urban communities, where political debates continue regarding harm reduction policies versus enforcement.

Beyond health care policy, social factors shape the environment in which health is determined. Education — a predictor of health risk factors including smoking, obesity, cardiovascular risk, and preventive screening rates — has become increasingly aligned with political geography. Differences in economic opportunity, access to necessities such as healthy food and internet access, and exposure to media and popular culture can also shape health behaviors, with downstream effects on mortality.

Finally, differences in mortality from Covid-19 raise concern about an increasingly troubling phenomenon: the stark polarization of trust in health care and public health institutions across political lines. Marked differences in vaccination rates between states that went for Trump and those that went for Harris serve as a salient marker of its health effects.

“Making America healthy again” requires confronting the realities of disproportionate chronic disease-related mortality in states that went for Trump, an evolving opioid epidemic with shifting burden toward states that went for Harris, and communities vulnerable to novel infectious disease along with growing mistrust in science.

Addressing these challenges will entail sustained investment in the conditions that shape health, such as expanding access to affordable health care, closing educational gaps, strengthening rural and behavioral health infrastructure, and rebuilding trust in public health.

Policymakers ought not treat “red” and “blue” states as fixed categories of health risk but instead tackle the drivers of preventable deaths across these diverse communities. Doing so involves communities and their elected leaders bringing lived and technical expertise together to find solutions rooted in truth, evidence, and a shared conviction that while death may be more certain than taxes, disparities in when and why Americans die are not.

Brandon Yan, M.D., M.P.H., is a physician and public health researcher affiliated with the University of California San Francisco Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies. Maddie Feldmeier, B.S., is a medical student at the UCSF School of Medicine. Renee Y. Hsia, M.D., M.Sc., is professor and vice chair of health services research of the UCSF Department of Emergency Medicine. She is also a core faculty member of the Philip R. Lee Institute for Health Policy Studies.

#5703. Pinch Hitting for the Geriatricians

— As the population ages without enough elder specialists, we all need to help out

America is growing older, like it or not. And as this happens, we need to find ways to take better care of our older and oldest patients.

Many elderly patients will live out those years with health and vitality, the path we all wish for.

But many of them will become infirm, challenged by the devastating effects of chronic diseases and the development and discovery of life-altering terminal illnesses. We need to be able to take better care of people at the end of life, as well as in the years leading up to that point.

What this country certainly needs, in addition to tens of thousands more primary care doctors, is a huge number of new geriatricians.

The "sexier" (higher paying) specialties like cardiology and gastroenterology have people flocking to them, but there is certainly no dramatic growth in the number of people choosing to enter geriatrics. Until that happens, we all need to do a much better job of taking care of people in their twilight years.

In outpatient medicine, we've always tried to ensure patient's wishes for end of life were known and clear to them, their family members, and loved ones, and all others caring for them.

Not having these discussions before it's too late leads to nothing but trouble down the road. Family members disagree about what their loved one wanted, and it often doesn't end well.

When we see young patients, healthy folks with no major medical issues, and we suggest they assign a healthcare proxy, sign an organ donor card, or complete a form outlining what they would want done in the event of catastrophic illness, they often look at us like we're crazy.

Usually at the point when it finally starts (needs) to come up, it's too late, or close to too late.

Whenever patients come see us, they have a barrage of forms thrown upon them by the administrative team at our practice. They need to complete so many screening questions, surveys about social determinants of health, food insecurity, housing insecurity, tobacco use, depression, domestic violence screening, substance use disorders screening, and more.

It's not until we finally get to the Medicare Annual Wellness Visit Annual Health Review that a question about advanced directives even comes up. And at that point, the templated questions just ask if they have healthcare proxy or if they've filled out any form of advanced directives.

Wouldn't it be great if at every opportunity when a patient was seen and taken care of in our healthcare system, this gap was closed, or at least an effort to fill in the blanks was made?

Whenever I get my driver's license renewed, they ask me if I want to be an organ donor.

In the same vein, when someone comes into a new provider's practice, we should really get to know the patient up front by getting to know what they would want should things take a turn, a terrible turn, for the worse.

If they say yes, they have an advanced directive, we should give them an immediate opportunity to upload it to the system, make that an expectation of getting care in the practice.

We won't see them without scanning a copy of their insurance card at every visit; why should we allow someone to be under our care without this crucial information?

If they don't have any of this, then push the blank forms to them, shower them with useful educational materials, help them understand how important this is, give them a Medical Order for Life-Sustaining Treatment (MOLST) form and a Living Will and a Medical Power of Attorney form -- whatever our patients need to let us know what they should really want us to know.

But how to get the conversation going between the patient and their providers?

Smart systems should be able to do this pretty easily, and the time to do it is not when a catastrophic illness has been diagnosed or at the point where critical timely decisions need to be made.

Sure, there will be situations where people want to update these things, change their minds, special circumstances, something in their situation has changed that makes them want to do a little more or a little less.

But the comfort that comes from knowing and being ready to respect a patient's choices should be something we could build into the system and make foolproof, or nearly so.

Right now, filling out a MOLST form, enrolling a patient in a hospice program, even getting someone started in the new Medical Aid in Dying program in New York State, seems much more complicated than need be.

Getting a patient the care they need to spend their last days in comfort, surrounded by their loved ones, free from pain and anxiety and minimizing suffering, should be paramount to the interests of society and any civilized healthcare system. We should be able to overcome whatever bureaucratic nonsense exists that make these processes so onerous.

Fewer rules, fewer checklists, less co-signing, less witnessing, less notarizing, less lawyering.

When the time comes for each of us, we all want things to go smoothly, no one wants to see another person, especially someone they love, suffer.

Geriatricians are masters of this stuff, but until a time where we have thousands more who can help take care of patients during these challenging moments as they approach the end of their lives, we should build up stronger, better, and more respectful systems that don't make this all so complicated.

Having the discussions we need with every patient is the hard part; the paperwork need not be that burdensome.

#5702. Scientists solve a 30-year mystery behind inflammatory bowel disease

Scientists from the University of Oxford, Newcastle University, and Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust have uncovered a previously unexplained cause of inflammatory bowel disease (IBD). The discovery could change how doctors understand, diagnose, and treat certain forms of the condition.

The findings indicate that IBD is not simply one disease. Instead, it appears to include several biologically distinct conditions that develop through different processes in the body. Identifying these differences could make it possible to provide treatments tailored to the specific cause of each patient's illness.

In a study published in the New England Journal of Medicine, researchers examined more than 4,900 people with IBD and identified two important findings. First, some patients produce antibodies that interfere with interleukin-10 (IL-10), an essential protein that helps prevent excessive inflammation. Second, this autoimmune reaction explains how one of the strongest known genetic risk factors for IBD contributes to the disease.

Under normal circumstances, IL-10 acts as a chemical messenger between cells, helping the immune system regulate inflammation. However, certain antibodies can block its activity, effectively disabling one of the body's built-in safeguards against excessive immune responses. Without this protection, inflammation can persist and become difficult to control.

Hidden Antibodies Reveal a Cause of Inflammatory Bowel Disease

Inflammatory bowel disease includes Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, two chronic conditions that affect approximately 500,000 people in the UK and millions more around the world.

Symptoms often first appear during adolescence or early adulthood, and patients may face lifelong medical challenges. Managing the disease can involve repeated hospital visits, medications that suppress immune activity, and sometimes surgery. Although treatments have improved, many people must try several different therapies without achieving lasting relief. This places a substantial burden on patients and creates significant costs for healthcare systems.

The researchers discovered that approximately 3.5% of patients with IBD had elevated levels of antibodies that neutralize IL-10. These antibodies were detected in people with both Crohn's disease and ulcerative colitis, but not in healthy individuals.

Based on the prevalence of IBD in the UK, the researchers estimate that 15,000 to 20,000 patients nationwide could carry these harmful antibodies.

Scientists Solve a 30-Year Genetic Mystery

The investigation also revealed a strong association between the IL-10-blocking antibodies and a genetic variant called HLA-DRB1*01:03.

Scientists at Oxford first connected this genetic variant to a severe form of inflammatory bowel disease 30 years ago. However, the biological process linking the gene to the condition had remained unclear.

The new results help resolve that longstanding mystery. People who carry HLA-DRB1*01:03 are substantially more likely to develop antibodies that interfere with IL-10, providing an explanation for how this genetic risk factor can contribute to severe intestinal inflammation.

Professor Holm Uhlig, a pediatric gastroenterologist and Director of the Centre for Human Genetics at the University of Oxford's Nuffield Department of Medicine, was a senior author of the study.

"We've suspected an important role of interleukin 10 in patients with inflammatory bowel disease for decades. The study now provides clear evidence and contributes the missing link between a well-known genetic variant that had been linked to severe inflammatory bowel disease in the past and the very recently discovered autoimmunity to interleukin 10."

"Understanding what drives the inflammation, provides a clear explanation for disease in this group of people and opens the door to new treatments that target the autoantibodies themselves or cells that produce those autoantibodies."

How Earlier Discoveries Helped Explain Severe IBD

The findings build on more than a decade of research into rare inherited disorders that disrupt the body's ability to control inflammation.

Sophie Hambleton, Professor of Pediatrics and Immunology at Newcastle University, explained that studying these uncommon conditions provided important clues about the mechanisms involved in more widespread forms of IBD.

"This discovery shows how the study of rare, inherited disorders can shed new light on common conditions. The groundwork was laid over 10 years ago when genetic defects in IL-10 or its receptor were found in young children with severe IBD. Later, we realized that neutralizing autoantibodies against IL-10 were mimicking this effect in 2 little girls with colitis."

These earlier observations helped researchers recognize that antibodies blocking IL-10 could produce effects similar to inherited defects involving the same protein or its receptor. The latest study now establishes the importance of this mechanism in a larger group of patients with inflammatory bowel disease.

A Blood Test Could Lead to More Targeted IBD Treatments

Beyond explaining a previously mysterious cause of intestinal inflammation, the discovery could have important implications for patient care.

Researchers believe the results provide a foundation for developing a blood test that identifies people whose disease is associated with antibodies against IL-10. Such a test could help doctors recognize these patients earlier and select treatments that address the underlying immune malfunction.

Dr. Rainer Doffinger, a clinical immunologist at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust, highlighted the potential benefits for both patients and healthcare systems.

"By identifying patients early and giving them targeted treatment, we could reduce reliance on expensive ongoing therapy and prevent complications. Even modest reductions in biologic treatment, admissions and surgery could translate into savings of many millions of pounds annually for the NHS, alongside the major benefits for patients through fewer interventions, improved quality of life or even durable remission."

Targeting the antibodies themselves, or the immune cells responsible for producing them, could offer a new treatment strategy for this particular group of patients. The approach could potentially reduce the need for repeated therapies, hospital admissions, and surgery while improving the chances of sustained disease control.

Professor Simon Travis, Professor of Clinical Gastroenterology at the University of Oxford and the Kennedy Institute of Rheumatology, emphasized the significance of identifying a specific biological cause of IBD.

"This is the most exciting discovery in a lifetime specialising in IBD. It means that we can now identify a group where we know what is causing the disease and that creates a real opportunity to change how we manage this disease."

The research marks an important advance toward personalized treatment for inflammatory bowel disease. Rather than relying primarily on symptoms to guide medical decisions, doctors may eventually be able to use biological testing to determine what is driving inflammation in individual patients and choose more appropriate therapies.

The study involved researchers from the Nuffield Department of Medicine at the University of Oxford, Newcastle University's Translational and Clinical Research Institute, and the Department of Immunology at Cambridge University Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust.

Funding was provided through the National Institute for Health and Care Research (NIHR) Biomedical Research Centres in Oxford, Cambridge, and Newcastle.
