#5696. Hinge Health revenue jumps 52% in Q3 as it expands beyond MSK, eyes hardware acquisitions

Hinge Health revenue jumps 52% in Q3 as it expands beyond MSK, eyes hardware acquisitions" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Hinge Health is seeing early traction with its migraine and gastrointestinal care programs as it pushes beyond musculoskeletal care and builds a broader, multi-condition platform.

But the company's core MSK business remains the engine fueling its robust growth.

"Our vision has always been to automate the delivery of care using technology to close the gap between the care people need and the care they actually receive. We're now applying that same approach and the same trusted relationships with employers and partners in neurology and gastrointestinal care," Daniel Perez, Hinge Health co-founder and CEO, told analysts and investors on the third-quarter earnings call Monday. "We're not starting from scratch in each new category. We're extending a platform that's already proven into conditions that are often connected to the ones we already treat. We believe that's a fundamentally different and more powerful way to expand than what other companies in our space are attempting."

During a Q&A with analysts and investors on the earnings call, Perez asserted, "We’re not taking our eye off the ball in MSK. I think we’re actually widening our lead on MSK… But it’s allowing us to expand into other areas as well."

In the third quarter, the company posted $235 million in revenue, up 52% from $154 million a year ago, and above its guidance range of $223 million to $225 million. The company posted third-quarter adjusted earnings of 66 cents per share, exceeding Wall Street analysts' estimates of 60 cents per share. Hinge Health's non-GAAP income from operations increased 154% to $77.2 million in the third quarter.

Hinge Health, which launched in late 2014 and went public in May 2025, developed software combined with AI to automate physical therapy services for joint and muscle health. The company has designed its platform to address a broad spectrum of MSK care, including acute injury, chronic pain and post-surgical rehabilitation. To address the automation of care, Hinge has developed AI-powered motion tracking technology, a proprietary FDA-cleared wearable device called Enso and an AI-supported care team to deliver scalable and personalized MSK care.

The company reported strong client growth, with 3,270 clients as of September 30, up 28% from a year ago. Last twelve months (LTM) calculated billings increased 54% year-over-year to $960 million as of September 30, compared to $624 million during Q3 2025.

The company also benefited from strong operational efficiency as it reported gross margin of 87% in Q3, compared to 82% during the same quarter a year ago.

Free cash flow for the quarter was $113 million, representing a 51% free cash flow margin. The company ended the September quarter with total cash and equivalents of $359 million.

Based on strong Q3 and year-to-date results, Hinge Health boosted its 2026 outlook, now expecting full-year revenue to reach between $879 million and $881 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 50% at the midpoint. That compares to the prior revenue target of $856 million to $860 million. The company now projects non-GAAP income from operations to be between $266 million and $268 million, reflecting year-over-year growth of 123% and non-GAAP operating margin of 30% at the midpoint.

Core MSK is still the company's largest revenue contributor by a wide margin, Perez noted, and that business is growing robustly. "We expect it to remain that way for years to come; the opportunity at MSK remains massively underpenetrated," Perez said.

"The MSK opportunity is still enormous. Musculoskeletal conditions are among the leading drivers of disability and healthcare spend in the United States, and the vast majority of people in America still don't have access to a digital MSK solution," Perez said during the call.

"We built something that works clinically, commercially, and economically, and we're still in the early innings of penetrating that market. We are the undisputed leader in this space, and we estimate 88% of lives within our markets are yet to be won, leaving a long runway for growth. That alone is a multi-year growth opportunity," he said.

The company is building on top of that MSK care foundation as it expands into migraine care and gastrointestinal care. Hinge acquired GI startup Cylinder Health in August for $105 million in cash.

The company's client base is up almost 30% year-over-year for its MSK care program and roughly 40% for its new GI Care Program since the acquisition announcement of Cylinder Health in August, Perez noted.

The company expects to make more acquisitions and is even looking at hardware acquisitions, Perez said. "I think too many technology companies, especially in healthcare, focus exclusively on software, but I absolutely firmly believe you will not automate care delivery without also investing in hardware. And, we've shown we're pretty good at hardware," he said, as the company internally developed its Enso wearable device.

Perez told Bloomberg last month that the company was interested in hardware that can augment virtual care.

"We will build organically first and use M&A when it accelerates our timeline. And our acquisitions, particularly in hardware, have historically been small tuck-ins of technology in a team, and then you build it out into something much larger," he added.

Looking at the company's new care programs, Perez called out notable early results from Hinge's migraine program, which is still in early access: 23% reduction in monthly migraine days, 28% reduction in migraine duration, equivalent to roughly five hours and just over half of surveyed members achieved a clinically meaningful improvement.

"We're also seeing a meaningful reduction in monthly prescription use days, which matters both for members and for the clients paying for their care," Perez said.

More than 800 clients, representing 9 million lives, now have access to the migraine program, approximately double the previous quarter, according to management. The migraine program was announced in May.

For the GI care business, Hinge Health is taking Cylinder's existing program and building it into the same app and care infrastructure it uses for MSK and migraine. The company is targeting summer 2027 for the fully integrated product. Meaningful revenue contribution should emerge particularly in 2028, after Hinge gets a fuller sales cycle with the integrated product, Perez noted.

Hinge Health sees an opportunity to offer health plans and employers one integrated care platform that covers multiple health conditions rather than separate point solutions.

Nearly one in two people with GI conditions also have MSK pain, and 70% of people withmigraine also have a GI condition, Perez noted.

"GI cost has been a growing pain point for employers and health plans, especially with the growth of GLP-1s, given GI side effects are so common, and our employer clients are very grateful for taking this on," he said during the call.

Hinge Health had a strong selling season in Q3, according to Aaryn Pure, Hinge Health's chief commercial officer, with three new Fortune 15 clients. "We've already received verbal agreements on more lives this year than we closed in all of last year, and last year was a record-breaking sales year for adding eligible lives," Pure noted.

More than 10 million lives across more than 800 clients have access to multiple Hinge products, he said.

Small and midsize businesses are becoming an important growth channel for the company, even though Hinge began investing in that market just a year ago. Through Q3, Hinge Health closed nearly 1 million SMB lives, "demonstrating we're not just winning at the top of the market, we're adding clients across every size tier," Pure said on the call.

He also noted that some health plan and third-party administrator (TPA) partners are implementing or considering arrangements where Hinge Health is automatically embedded or offered on an opt-out basis in their SMB book of business.

"Being the first-mover preferred partner is allowing us to capture that market," Pure said.

The company also announced Monday that Jim Pursley will step down as president, effective January 1, and will join Hinge Health's board of directors. Following this transition, Pure will lead the commercial organization, the company said.

In an analyst note, Ryan Daniels, group head of healthcare technology and services at William Blair, wrote that Hinge Health demonstrates "market leadership with significant advantages both on the product and go-to-market fronts."

"With a nearly 150% increase in shares YTD, HNGE now trades at approximately 11 times our 2027 adjusted gross profit, a premium to mature, high-margin, growth-oriented healthcare IT peers. Still, at these levels, we believe the stock presents a compelling long-term risk/reward and see continued growth momentum and upside to operating income and free cash flow estimates," Daniels wrote.

#5693. The secret to slower aging may be hiding in your gut

Scientists have uncovered a surprising connection between the bacteria living in the human gut and the speed at which the body ages. Researchers at the University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa found that certain gut microbes are associated with slower biological aging, while others are linked to faster aging.

The study, published in Scientific Reports, found that differences in gut bacterial communities accounted for approximately 15% of the variation in participants' biological aging rates. The results suggest that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive system, may provide valuable clues about aging at the molecular level.

"This study advances our understanding of the relationship between the gut microbiome and biological aging," said senior author Alika K. Maunakea of the UH Mānoa John A. Burns School of Medicine. "We found that microbial patterns in the gut were significantly associated with molecular measures of aging, even independent of chronological age. These findings open important new directions for understanding how modifiable biological systems influence long-term health trajectories and longevity."

Scientists Identify Gut Bacteria Linked to Faster and Slower Aging

To investigate the relationship between gut bacteria and aging, researchers examined stool and blood samples collected from 123 adults across a wide range of ages. They identified the bacteria present in each participant's gut and compared those findings with blood-based molecular markers used to estimate the body's rate of aging.

These biological measurements differ from chronological age, which simply reflects how many years someone has been alive. Instead, they are designed to assess how quickly aging-related changes are occurring within the body.

The researchers found a notable association between the composition of the gut microbiome and DunedinPACE, an advanced biomarker that measures the pace of biological aging.

Some bacterial species stood out for their particularly strong relationships with aging. Bifidobacterium adolescentis was among the microbes most strongly associated with slower biological aging. In contrast, Succinivibrio dextrinosolvens showed one of the strongest associations with faster aging.

These differences suggest that particular patterns of gut bacteria may offer important information about how rapidly the body is aging.

How Diet, Lifestyle, and Environment May Influence Gut Health

Lead author Braden P. Kunihiro said the discovery adds to growing evidence that the gut microbiome could play an important role in precision health research, which aims to better understand individual differences in health and disease.

Unlike chronological age, the composition of the gut microbiome can change in response to everyday influences, including diet, lifestyle, and environmental conditions. This makes it a particularly interesting area of investigation for scientists studying healthy aging.

"The gut microbiome is highly responsive to lifestyle, diet, environment and other everyday exposures," Kunihiro said. "Our findings suggest that the microbiome may reflect important aspects of biological resilience and aging in ways that could eventually help inform future wellness and healthy aging strategies."

The research also included Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander participants, groups that have historically received limited representation in studies of aging and gut microorganisms.

Co-author Ruben Juarez explained that including these populations could help scientists investigate how social circumstances and environmental conditions leave lasting biological effects over the course of a person's life.

"The microbiome exists at the intersection of behavior, environment and human biology," Juarez said. "Studies like this help illuminate potential pathways through which lived experiences and social factors influence long-term health outcomes."

Could Changing Gut Bacteria Influence How We Age?

Although the findings reveal a meaningful relationship between gut bacteria and biological aging, researchers stress that the study does not establish cause and effect. In other words, finding certain microbes in people who age more slowly does not necessarily mean those bacteria are responsible for slowing the aging process.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether deliberately changing the gut microbiome can influence biological aging or improve long-term health.

Still, the findings offer a promising starting point for exploring how the microorganisms living inside us relate to the aging process and whether they could eventually help guide more personalized approaches to healthy aging.

"This is an important early step toward understanding the gut microbiome's relationship with healthy aging," Maunakea said. "Future research will help clarify the mechanisms involved and whether these microbial signatures may eventually contribute to precision approaches for promoting long-term health and wellness."

#5692. Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases

Measles update: New York reports first measles-associated death; US nears 5,000 confirmed cases" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The New York State Department of Health on Monday afternoon reported its first measles-associated death in 30 years.

The state has counted 210 total cases this year as of Nov. 3. The reported death was a child in the northern Lewis County, according to the department. No information was given about the child's specific illness or the role measles infection may have played in their death.

Sixteen confirmed cases of measles have been reported in Lewis County as of Tuesday, the department said. Many of New York's cases are located among upstate counties, and just eight are in New York City, according to the department.

In a statement, New York Governor Kathy Hochul—who on Oct. 5 declared a Disaster Emergency in response to rising measles case rates—expressed her sympathies to the child's family and told residents that "vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease."

"This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," the statement reads, echoing criticisms of federal health leadership voiced by Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro regarding measles-associated deaths in his own state.

As of Oct. 29, the Centers for Disease Control reports 4,852 confirmed cases of measles this year across the country, far outpacing 2025's total of 2,289. Of these, 511 have been hospitalized (versus 244 in 2025) and three deaths have been recognized—though health officials in Pennsylvania alone said they have confirmed five measles-associated deaths. The CDC has said its death count may change after it completes work to develop a new standardized case definition for "deaths due to measles."

The U.S. is in the midst of its worst measles outbreak in decades, with more than 4,000 cases reported to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention as of early October and a sixth measles-associated death disclosed by local Pennsylvania officials on Monday.

The vaccine-preventable disease was declared eliminated in the U.S. back in 2000—meaning that there was no endemic spread of the disease—but has resurfaced in force during recent years as declining childhood vaccination rates have pushed most states below the 95% coverage bar for school-age herd immunity.

The CDC had counted 2,289 cases across the entirety of 2025, which had been the country’s highest total since 1990, and several public health officials have warned for months that number would likely be surpassed based on the scale and frequency of early-year cases.

Measles-associated deaths have also accompanied the higher case counts, though just how many is a subject of dispute. While three deaths were confirmed in all of 2025, this year logged its first in late August with Pennsylvania, which hosts more than a quarter of the total cases, now reporting six measles-associated deaths as of Oct. 13. The CDC, however, lists two deaths alongside a note that its count is subject to change, and has promised more broadly to develop a new, standardized case definition to be used across all reporting states.

That discrepancy is an example of friction between federal health leadership and the broader public health community that experts say has contributed to this year’s outbreaks.

Pennsylvania’s initial death announcements in August were contested by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who accused Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro of withholding sufficient information for the CDC to confirm the deaths and using his press conference announcing them as “gaslighting the public” for political purposes.

During an ensuing social media feud, the governor and the secretary described a heated phone call in which Shapiro (at the time) rejected federal assistance and accused Kennedy of fueling the outbreaks with only lukewarm endorsement of the MMR vaccine and a broader concurrent campaign to scale back other routine childhood vaccinations.

Numerous state public health officials and experts have lobbed similar criticisms of Kennedy, who is affiliated with anti-vaccine groups, and federal health agencies under his purview.

The CDC, for its part, has reportedly infused at least $100 million of extra public health funding to states for immunization programs and surveillance, and leading officials including Kennedy and new CDC Director Erica Schwartz, M.D., have described the MMR vaccine as safe and effective when asked directly. Still, the agency has not launched the type of broader vaccine messaging and awareness campaigns that it would have in years past, critics are quick to note.

Pennsylvania isn’t alone in raising alarms over rising measles cases. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in early October, the first such declaration in recent years.

Before you make the move, check out these 5 packing tips.

A common mistake people make when moving is to pack all of their belongings and move them, only to realize upon unpacking that many of the items should have been donated, sold, or thrown out. Before you pack, ruthlessly declutter your home. Packing things only to get rid of them at the new house is a waste of your time and money.

Some questions to ask yourself as you declutter before packing are:

As you pack and move, things are bound to get misplaced. To avoid the stress of a missing document or essential information, keep a folder (either physical, digital, or both) where you won't misplace it that is filled with essential paperwork. This might include:

Greg Dallaire - Green Bay Real Estate Expert says, "Be sure to set up any utilities in the new place to be turned on and ready when you arrive. Even if it means paying for utilities at two places for a brief overlap, it is often worth the convenience. In addition to basics like water and power, call ahead to make sure you will have internet, TV, and any other services you need."

This is also a great time to move additional services to the new address, like security, pest control, or house cleaning.

Even if you are moving all in one day from one Calgary home to another, don't count on being able to unpack everything you need on night one. One of the easiest ways to do this is by color coding. Assign a color to each room and label accordingly. For example, let's say the kitchen is blue. #5688. Low testosterone may make sugar far more harmful to your liver

Low testosterone can contribute to several health problems, and an unhealthy diet may make some of those risks even worse. One major concern is metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), a condition that affects approximately 40% of adult men worldwide and has become a significant global health issue.

Fatty liver, the earliest stage of MASLD, occurs when excess fat builds up in the liver. Several factors are associated with the condition, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, low testosterone levels, and excessive fructose consumption from sugary drinks and processed foods. However, scientists have not fully understood how these factors interact or whether their combined effects are more harmful than each one individually.

How Low Testosterone and Fructose Affect the Liver

To investigate this connection, a research team from the Graduate School of Agriculture, led by graduate student Hiroki Takahashi and Associate Professor Naoki Harada, examined how reduced testosterone and high fructose intake influence liver health.

The researchers used eight-week-old male mice and divided them into six experimental groups. Some underwent castration to lower testosterone levels, while others received a sham operation. The groups included Sham/Control, Sham/Fructose, Sham/Fructose + Antibiotics, Castration/Control, Castration/Fructose, and Castration/Fructose + Antibiotics.

To determine how these conditions affected the animals, the team analyzed liver cells and tissues, blood plasma, organic acids from the cecum, and samples of gut bacteria.

The results revealed that mice with reduced testosterone levels developed heavier livers when they consumed fructose. However, this increase in liver weight was smaller in mice that also received antibiotics.

When examined separately, low testosterone and fructose intake produced only modest changes in liver triglyceride levels. When combined, however, the two factors had a much stronger effect, significantly increasing fat accumulation and worsening fatty liver.

The researchers also identified changes in the composition of gut bacteria, altered liver gene activity, and elevated levels of pyruvate in the cecum among mice exposed to both reduced testosterone and fructose.

These findings suggested that the gut microbiome could play an important role in explaining why the combination was particularly harmful.

Further experiments helped the researchers identify a possible biological explanation for the increased liver fat.

"Upon examining this mechanism, we found that changes in the gut microbiota led to increased levels of pyruvate within the intestine. Furthermore, experiments using mouse-derived primary hepatocytes revealed that pyruvate acts synergistically with fructose to promote neutral lipid accumulation in hepatocytes," explained Takahashi.

In other words, changes in gut bacteria appeared to increase intestinal pyruvate, a compound involved in energy metabolism. Laboratory experiments with liver cells isolated from mice showed that pyruvate and fructose worked together to increase fat storage in those cells.

The discovery suggests that interactions among testosterone levels, dietary fructose, and gut bacteria may help explain how fatty liver develops and worsens.

Potential New Ways to Prevent Fatty Liver Disease

Understanding this relationship could eventually help researchers identify new approaches to preventing or treating fatty liver disease. In particular, targeting the processes through which pyruvate contributes to fat accumulation may offer promising possibilities.

"Going forward, we hope to clarify the mechanism by which pyruvate promotes triglyceride accumulation to pioneer the development of therapeutic drugs and establishment of preventive methods through dietary interventions," added Professor Harada.

Although the findings come from experiments in mice and isolated mouse liver cells, they provide new insight into how hormonal changes and diet may interact to influence liver health.

The study was published in American Journal of Physiology-Endocrinology and Metabolism.

Materials provided by Osaka Metropolitan University. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Humana, athenahealth collaborate on expanded electronic prior authorizations nationwide" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Humana and athenahealth are expanding electronic prior authorizations nationwide in a newly announced collaboration.

Through athenaPayer, Humana is able to connect with more than 180,000 providers across the athenaOne network, which the partners said will create a more connected experience between the health plan and clinicians.

“Every phone call, fax and portal log-in adds work for a practice trying to get a patient the care they need,” said Paul Brient, athenahealth chief product and operations officer, in a statement. “Prior authorization shouldn’t require care teams to navigate a different process for every health plan. By connecting health plans and practices through one solution with a common workflow, we’re creating a more scalable way to exchange information, reducing work for both providers and payers while, most importantly, helping patients access care faster.”

Athenahealth internal data show more than 6,000 providers processed nearly 35,000 electronic prior authorizations with Humana in September, with more than 70% completed without requiring additional information from staff.

The collaboration reflects Humana’s broader strategy to improve care access through requiring less prior authorizations and making the process simpler when needed, executives said.

“Our goal is straightforward: help people get the right care at the right time while reducing unnecessary burden on the physicians and care teams who serve them,” said Traci Granston, M.D., Humana vice president of clinical innovation and trend, in a statement. “… This collaboration with athenahealth is another step forward, ensuring that providers spend less time navigating administrative processes and more time focused on patient care.”

In June 2025, insurers nationwide—including Humana—agreed to take steps to reform prior authorization, including supporting electronic prior authorizations.

A decade later, the eight-time NBA All-Star is hoping to score a sizable profit on the property, with his latest asking price coming in $5.7 million above what he originally paid for the spread.

The home, which is represented by Maninga Capehart of HomeSmart, sits on approximately 14 acres and offers 12 bedrooms, 12 full bathrooms, and nine half-bathrooms.

Built in 2010, the European-inspired residence boasts approximately 26,233 square feet of living space, providing no shortage of room for both overnight guests and lavish entertaining.

Indeed, the listing touts the property as one of Georgia's "most distinguished private estates," pointing to its impressive scale, elaborate architecture, and lengthy list of resort-worthy amenities.

The main-level primary suite is equally extravagant, with a private executive office and enormous dressing areas lined with custom cabinetry. Its spa-worthy bathroom adds a sunken soaking tub, steam shower, and dedicated makeup vanity.

A separate multiroom residential suite also comes with its own kitchen and two bathrooms, providing a self-contained living space for family members or overnight visitors.

There's even a salon and barber area, sauna, and additional bedroom suite on the same level.

Howard won't need to leave the grounds to squeeze in a workout either. A separate two-story fitness and recreation pavilion has its own kitchen and bathroom, allowing the building to double as another space for gatherings.

The sprawling outdoor areas are equally geared toward leisure, with a saltwater swimming pool overlooked by a fully equipped outdoor kitchen.

The 14-acre grounds also include landscaped gardens and an orchard growing blueberries, blackberries, peaches, apples, and figs, while a private drive winds toward the property's lake.

Car enthusiasts, meanwhile, have an enormous amount of space to house their collections.

Perhaps one of the estate's more unexpected features is an underground passage connecting different portions of the property, while an elevator inside the main house provides access to every level.

The listing describes the sprawling compound as a "private legacy estate"—one outfitted to accommodate far more than the day-to-day needs of a single owner.

#5684. Scientists discover a hidden reason why muscles weaken with age

Muscles naturally become weaker as we get older, but scientists have discovered that some of the changes associated with aging may actually help protect muscle cells from damage. New research reveals why aging muscles shift toward a different type of muscle fiber and identifies a crucial molecule that could offer a new approach to treating muscle loss.

Muscle tissue contains bundles of fibers with different functions. Fast-twitch fibers produce powerful, rapid movements but fatigue relatively quickly. Slow-twitch fibers, by contrast, support sustained activity and contain higher concentrations of mitochondria, the cellular structures responsible for producing much of the energy muscles need.

As people age, muscle strength declines and mitochondria become less efficient. Surprisingly, aging muscles also develop a greater proportion of slow-twitch fibers, even though these fibers depend heavily on the very mitochondria that are losing their ability to function. Researchers have observed similar changes in several conditions that cause muscle wasting.

This raises an important question: Why would muscles increasingly rely on an energy-producing system that is becoming less effective?

A Crucial Molecule Linked to Muscle Aging

To investigate this puzzle, scientists focused on cardiolipin, a specialized fat molecule located almost exclusively within the inner membrane of mitochondria. Cardiolipin helps maintain the membrane's distinctive folded architecture, which is essential for proper mitochondrial activity.

When cardiolipin is lacking, mitochondria struggle to generate sufficient energy. They also become less capable of producing the chemical signals and essential materials that cells require to function.

The researchers discovered that cardiolipin levels decrease in muscle mitochondria from both mice and humans as they age or experience disease. This decline was accompanied by structural abnormalities in the mitochondria and a loss of normal function.

To determine whether reduced cardiolipin directly contributes to these changes, rather than simply occurring alongside them, the team experimentally lowered cardiolipin levels in young mice.

The results closely resembled what happens during natural aging. Muscle fibers shifted away from the fast-twitch type toward slow-twitch fibers, matching the pattern previously observed in older mice and humans.

Even more strikingly, restoring cardiolipin to approximately two-thirds of its normal concentration began reversing muscle wasting and completely prevented the premature deaths seen in the affected animals.

Why Aging Muscles Sacrifice Strength for Protection

Further experiments revealed an unexpected explanation for the transformation. Rather than representing only a breakdown in muscle function, the shift toward slow-twitch fibers appears to be a protective response.

When cardiolipin concentrations fall, damaged mitochondria produce much larger quantities of reactive oxygen species (ROS). These highly reactive molecules can harm cellular structures, but they also play an important role in signaling that something is wrong.

The researchers found that ROS help initiate the transition from fast-twitch to slow-twitch muscle fibers. When they treated muscle cells lacking cardiolipin with an antioxidant to reduce ROS, the transformation became less pronounced.

A protein known as ERRγ plays a central role in coordinating this response. It directs cells to reorganize their mitochondria and change their muscle fiber characteristics. When scientists inhibited ERRγ in muscle cells grown in the laboratory, the transition between fiber types stopped entirely.

The team also discovered how the newly remodeled fibers help defend themselves.

Mice with insufficient cardiolipin absorbed considerably more glucose from their bloodstreams. However, their muscles were not primarily using this additional sugar to produce energy.

Instead, experiments that tracked specially labeled glucose showed that muscle cells redirected the sugar toward manufacturing their own antioxidants. This helped protect them against the damaging effects of excess ROS.

"The fiber switch is not the muscle failing, but the muscle trading power for protection. That's also why interfering with it can backfire: when we gave the mice antioxidants to mop up the ROS, their muscles fared worse, not better," says Assistant Professor Fabian Finger, first and co-corresponding author, from the University of Copenhagen.

A Potential New Approach to Treating Muscle Wasting

Although the findings point toward possible treatments for age-related muscle decline, the experiments demonstrating the protective mechanism and reversal of muscle wasting were conducted in mice. Human muscle samples were used only to establish that cardiolipin levels also decrease with age in people.

Nevertheless, researchers already have some ways to influence cardiolipin.

The FDA recently granted accelerated approval to elamipretide, a medication designed to help stabilize cardiolipin, for Barth syndrome, a rare inherited disorder. This suggests that targeting the molecule is medically feasible, although its effectiveness against ordinary age-related muscle loss remains unknown.

Another potential treatment target is ERRγ, the protein responsible for helping muscles adapt to mitochondrial stress.

ERRγ belongs to a family of proteins called nuclear receptors. These proteins are already established targets for approximately 10 to 15 percent of FDA-approved medications made from small molecules. Drugs that activate ERRγ are also being investigated in preclinical research for other medical applications.

The findings suggest that future therapies might work by restoring cardiolipin levels or by influencing the protective adaptations controlled by ERRγ.

"What encourages me most is that even a partial recovery of cardiolipin was enough to bring the muscle back. The question now is whether we can increase cardiolipin in aging muscle or target ERRγ to promote healthy adaptations. This is where the therapeutic potential lies," says senior author Zachary Gerhart-Hines, Associate Professor at the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research, University of Copenhagen.

The research involved scientists from more than 20 institutions. It was led by the NNF Center for Basic Metabolic Research at the University of Copenhagen in collaboration with the Center for Adipocyte Signaling at the University of Southern Denmark.

Financial support came from the Novo Nordisk Foundation, European Research Council, Lundbeck Foundation, US National Institutes of Health, and additional funding organizations.

#5683. A simple daily fiber supplement reduced arthritis pain and improved strength

A simple daily fiber supplement may offer a surprising new way to relieve knee arthritis pain while improving muscle strength. In a clinical trial led by researchers at the University of Nottingham, people with knee osteoarthritis (OA) who took a prebiotic fiber called inulin experienced significant reductions in pain, improved grip strength, and decreased sensitivity to pain.

The supplement also appeared to be considerably easier for participants to stick with than a digital physical therapy program. Only 3.6% of those assigned to inulin alone dropped out of the study, compared with 21% of those assigned to physical therapy alone.

Published in the journal Nutrients, the findings suggest that improving gut health could become an additional strategy for managing arthritis. They also reveal an intriguing connection between the bacteria living in our digestive system, the way our bodies process pain, and muscle function.

A Simple Dietary Change Could Help Relieve Arthritis Pain

Knee osteoarthritis affects hundreds of millions of people worldwide and is a major cause of chronic pain and disability, especially among older adults. The condition develops as the tissues within the knee joint, including the cartilage that cushions the ends of bones, gradually deteriorate. This can lead to pain, stiffness, swelling, and difficulty with everyday activities such as walking or climbing stairs.

Treatment typically focuses on reducing symptoms and maintaining mobility. Pain medications can provide relief but may cause unwanted side effects, while physical therapy and regular exercise can help improve joint function. However, keeping up with an exercise program can be difficult, particularly for people already struggling with persistent pain.

The new research raises the possibility that a simple dietary supplement could provide another way to manage symptoms.

"This study raises the exciting possibility that a simple dietary change -- adding a fiber supplement to your breakfast or yogurt -- could meaningfully reduce pain and improve physical function," said Dr. Afroditi Kouraki, lead author of the study from the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham.

The supplement tested in the study was inulin, a naturally occurring fiber found in foods such as chicory root, Jerusalem artichokes, and certain other vegetables. Unlike many nutrients, inulin is not broken down by digestive enzymes in the small intestine. Instead, it passes into the large intestine, where beneficial bacteria can use it as food.

How Gut Bacteria May Influence Arthritis Pain

Researchers are increasingly discovering that the gut microbiome, the vast community of microorganisms living in the digestive tract, influences much more than digestion. These microbes interact with the immune system, produce biologically active compounds, and may even affect how the nervous system responds to pain.

Inulin is classified as a prebiotic because it nourishes certain beneficial gut bacteria rather than directly supplying living microorganisms, as probiotics do.

When bacteria ferment inulin, they produce substances known as short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs). One of the most important is butyrate, a compound that helps support the intestinal lining and can influence inflammation and biological pathways involved in pain.

The researchers found that participants taking inulin had increased levels of butyrate, suggesting that the supplement was influencing activity within the gut microbiome.

They also observed higher levels of glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), a hormone released by the gut that helps regulate blood sugar and appetite and has also been linked to pain regulation and muscle health.

GLP-1 has attracted widespread attention because it is the hormone targeted by medications such as Ozempic and Wegovy. However, the inulin supplement used in this trial was not a GLP-1 medication. Instead, researchers examined whether supporting beneficial gut bacteria could influence the body's own production of the hormone.

One particularly interesting finding was that higher GLP-1 levels were associated with better grip strength. Although this does not establish that GLP-1 caused the improvement, it suggests that changes originating in the digestive system may be connected to muscle function as well as pain.

To investigate these effects, the researchers conducted the INSPIRE trial, a six-week randomized controlled study involving 117 adults with knee osteoarthritis.

Participants were assigned to one of four treatment groups: a daily inulin supplement alone, digitally supported physical therapy exercises (PSE) alone, a combination of inulin and physical therapy, or a placebo.

This design allowed researchers to examine the effects of the supplement and exercise separately, as well as investigate whether combining them offered additional benefits.

Both inulin and physical therapy independently reduced knee pain, indicating that each approach provided meaningful symptom relief.

However, the supplement produced additional improvements that were not observed with physical therapy alone. Participants taking inulin demonstrated better grip strength and reduced pain sensitivity.

Pain sensitivity reflects how strongly the nervous system responds to potentially painful stimulation. Reducing that sensitivity could be particularly valuable for people with osteoarthritis, because persistent pain is not always explained by the amount of visible damage within a joint. Changes in how the nervous system processes pain can also contribute to discomfort.

The improved grip strength was another unexpected result, suggesting that the supplement's effects might extend beyond the knee itself.

The researchers also found a substantial difference in how many participants completed their assigned treatments. Only 3.6% of the inulin-only group dropped out, compared with 21% of the physical therapy-only group.

This difference suggests that taking a daily fiber supplement may be easier to incorporate into a regular routine than following a structured exercise program.

A Surprising Connection Between Gut Health, Muscles, and Pain

Dr. Kouraki said: "Our findings suggest that targeting gut health with a prebiotic supplement is a safe, well-tolerated, and effective way to reduce pain in people with knee osteoarthritis. The very low dropout rate compared to the exercise group is also encouraging from a public health perspective -- people were able to fit this supplement easily into their daily lives."

Beyond the reduction in arthritis pain, the researchers are particularly interested in what the findings reveal about interactions between the digestive system, muscles, and nervous system.

The association between GLP-1 and grip strength raises the possibility of a broader biological relationship connecting gut health with physical performance and resilience as people age.

Senior author Professor Ana Valdes from the School of Medicine added: "The link we observed between GLP-1 and grip strength is particularly intriguing and points to a broader gut-muscle-pain axis that warrants further investigation. This could have implications not just for osteoarthritis, but for understanding how gut health influences aging and physical resilience more broadly."

The findings are promising, but the trial was relatively small and lasted only six weeks. Larger studies with longer follow-up periods will be needed to establish whether the benefits persist, identify which patients are most likely to respond, and clarify the biological mechanisms responsible.

The results also do not suggest that fiber supplements should replace exercise or other established arthritis treatments. Instead, they point toward a potentially useful additional approach that could complement existing care.

The potential importance of this research becomes clearer when considering how many people live with persistent arthritis pain.

Professor Lucy Donaldson, Director of Research at Arthritis UK, said: "The pain of arthritis can severely impact quality of life. Our recent lived experience survey showed that six in ten people are living in pain most or all of the time due to their arthritis.

"Researchers are starting to explore the role of the gut microbiome in our experience of pain. This exciting preliminary research highlights how diet and physiotherapy can act in different ways to have benefits for people with arthritis. We know a variety and balance of healthy foods, including fiber, and regular physical activity matter, and we're glad to be supporting research that explores how they work to help people with arthritis."

For people living with knee osteoarthritis, the findings offer an encouraging possibility: a relatively simple change in daily nutrition may help reduce pain while supporting other aspects of physical health.

Perhaps most intriguingly, the research suggests that treating arthritis may involve looking beyond the joints themselves. #5679. A single sauna session sends immune cells surging through your body

A single sauna session may trigger a surprising response in the immune system. Researchers in Finland have discovered that spending just 30 minutes in a sauna, with a brief cold shower halfway through, causes white blood cells to surge into the bloodstream. These cells are essential to the body's defenses, helping identify and fight infections and other potential threats.

The findings suggest that sauna bathing may temporarily mobilize immune cells that normally remain in tissues, allowing them to circulate more widely throughout the body. This increased movement could help the immune system monitor for harmful pathogens, including bacteria and viruses.

During the study, researchers observed an increase in every type of circulating white blood cell they measured. Among them were neutrophils and lymphocytes, two important groups of immune cells. Neutrophils are often among the first defenders to respond to an infection, while lymphocytes include cells that recognize specific threats, produce antibodies, and help coordinate immune responses.

The increase was temporary. Within 30 minutes after the sauna session, neutrophil and lymphocyte counts had returned to their original levels.

How Sauna Bathing May Activate Immune Defenses

"This may indicate that sauna bathing mobilizes additional white blood cells into the bloodstream from tissues, where they are then redeposited after the session. This kind of periodic release of white blood cells into the bloodstream is beneficial, as once they leave their storage sites, they are better able to patrol the body and respond to pathogens," says Ilkka Heinonen, an Academy Research Fellow at the University of Turku.

This process is known as immune surveillance. Rather than remaining in one location, immune cells travel through the bloodstream and tissues, searching for signs of infection or other abnormalities. By temporarily increasing the number of white blood cells in circulation, the body may improve their ability to detect potential threats.

Interestingly, a similar response occurs during physical exercise. Exercise can temporarily increase the number of immune cells moving through the bloodstream, helping distribute them throughout the body. The new findings suggest that sauna bathing may produce a comparable short-term response, although this does not mean the two activities provide identical immune benefits.

Sauna Heat Also Affects Immune Signaling Molecules

The researchers also investigated whether sauna bathing influenced cytokines, small proteins that help immune cells communicate with one another. Cytokines play important roles in regulating inflammation, coordinating immune defenses, and directing the body's response to infections.

Overall, the sauna session produced little change in average cytokine levels in the bloodstream. However, a closer examination revealed an interesting connection between certain cytokines and changes in body temperature.

"Interestingly, however, the levels of several cytokines changed in relation to how much body temperature rose during sauna bathing. No similar association was observed between white blood cell counts and changes in body temperature," says Professor Jari Laukkanen, who led the study at the University of Eastern Finland.

In other words, some immune signaling molecules responded differently depending on how much a person's body temperature increased. White blood cell counts, however, did not show the same relationship with rising body temperature.

This distinction suggests that sauna bathing may influence different parts of the immune system through different physiological processes.

What This Discovery Means for Sauna Health Benefits

Previous research has linked regular sauna bathing with several potential health benefits. The latest findings offer another clue about what may be happening inside the body during these sessions, particularly how heat exposure and the sauna routine affect immune cell circulation.

However, the researchers caution that the results do not establish whether sauna bathing produces lasting improvements in immune function or reduces the risk of illness. The study examined only the immediate effects of one sauna session, and the observed changes in white blood cells were short-lived.

Because the session also included a brief cold shower, the findings reflect the combined sauna and cooling routine rather than the isolated effects of heat alone.

The research involved 51 adults with an average age of 50. The findings were published in the scientific journal Temperature, which specializes in research on body temperature regulation and its effects on human physiology.

Although more research is needed to understand the long-term implications, the study reveals that even a single sauna session can rapidly change how immune cells circulate through the body, potentially offering new insight into the biological effects of this popular relaxation practice.

Materials provided by University of Eastern Finland. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#5677. Philadelphia Renters Win Record Settlement Over Unsafe Conditions and Illegal Rent Collection

A group of Philadelphia renters has reached a settlement in one of the largest per-tenant recovery class action suits in the city’s rental law history.

A preliminary approval of the settlement, which requires Odin Properties LLC to provide the tenants at Bentley Manor apartments with rent forgiveness and refunds for wrongly collected rent, was finalized by a Philadelphia judge last week.

The aggregate settlement amount exceeds $140,000, and individual renters will receive varying amounts based on their payment history, with the average refund estimated at about $1,200.

Three residents of Bentley Manor, located in West Oak Lane, filed a class action suit in March 2025 against Odin Properties and related companies for allegedly illegally collecting rent after the building was designated “unsafe” by the Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections (L&I), according to The Public Interest Law Center.

Philadelphia law prohibits a landlord from collecting rent if a serious L&I violation if not corrected within 30 days. However, the plaintiffs alleged that Odin Properties continued to charge, demand, and collect rent each month, even as the building remained in unsafe status.

Odin Properties will now be required to forgive all unpaid rent and associated fees, estimated to be $66,891, and provide $75,000 in cash refunds for any rent collected, for a total of $141,891 in relief.

“This case sends a simple message: Landlords cannot collect rent while ignoring serious safety violations,” Madison Gray, the staff attorney at the Public Interest Law Center, tells Realtor.com®. “We hope it becomes clear that collecting rent while ignoring serious safety violations is a losing business model in Philadelphia, and we hope it encourages every landlord in the city to fix dangerous conditions promptly and comply with the law before tenants are forced to go to court.”

Realtor.com reached out to Odin Properties for a statement, but received no response.

Bentley Manor, which has approximately 71 sets of renters, was constructed in 1962. Between November 2021 and February 2024, L&I issued several violations related to fire safety, electrical hazards, and nonlatching building doors, all of which were resolved, according to the complaint.

On Nov. 14, 2024, L&I issued another notice of violation declaring the building an “unsafe structure,” citing “loose and missing bricks” and a “leaning parapet” as dangerous conditions. At the same time, multiple previous violations continued to resurface.

When the class-action complaint was filed four months later, in March, Odin Properties had allegedly still not made the building safe to the satisfaction of L&I, which made it ineligible to collect rent.

“Nevertheless, the Odin Defendants charged and collected rent from Plaintiffs and other tenants in December 2024, and in January, February, and March, 2025,” the complaint reads.

Three tenants were named as plaintiffs in the complaint: SEPTA transit operator Porter Grant, who paid $1,274 in monthly rent; Philadelphia police officer Casey Allison, who paid $1,352 in monthly rent; and a grandmother with mobility impairments, Dawn Colbourne, who paid $317 in monthly rent with the Philadelphia Housing Authority paying a monthly $968 subsidy.

“Without admitting or conceding any wrongdoing, liability, or damages, the Defendants have agreed to settle the Action to avoid the substantial expense, inconvenience, burden, and disruption of continued litigation,” the settlement document reads.

In between the lawsuit being filed in March 2025 and the settlement, the defendants made the necessary repairs to Bentley Manor.

Tenants will receive individualized amounts of the $75,000 settlement pool based on how much they paid during the non-compliance time period. On average, tenants will receive more than $1,200 per refund check, according to Gray.

“We also hope this sends a message to tenants. Philadelphia's housing laws only matter if they're enforced, and they don't enforce themselves,” says Gray. “This settlement shows that when landlords break the rules, tenants can fight back and win. Ultimately, we hope this settlement shows that tenants can hold even large landlords accountable when those laws are broken.”

#5676. How Making Daylight Saving Time Permanent Affects Homeowners

Most homeowners change their clocks twice a year: forward by one hour on the second Sunday in March and back by one hour on the first Sunday in November.

However, this longstanding ritual may come to an end, thanks to the Sunshine Protection Act, which was passed by the U.S. House earlier this year and aims to make daylight saving time permanent year-round.

If passed by the Senate and signed into law, the act would lead to lighter evenings and darker mornings. And whether it’ll work in your favor depends on where you live.

Homeowners in Alabama, Florida, and Texas, for example, would enjoy more usable daylight while those in Maine, Michigan, and Wisconsin could see much later sunrises and limited daylight hours.

However, at the moment, the bill has stalled, and during a recent campaign rally in Mississippi, President Donald Trump weighed in, calling the twice-yearly clock change "stupid" and urging the Senate to pass the measure.

Regardless of where you live, it’s important to understand how permanent daylight saving time might affect your home and lifestyle. That way you can prepare for the changes if the legislation becomes law.

With more daylight in the evening, you’ll be less reliant on artificial indoor lighting when you’re awake and active. And this could slightly reduce your electricity use.

However, any savings may be offset by increased heating and cooling demands.

“The dark, cold winter mornings that stem from permanent daylight savings would mean that your furnace will need to work harder before sunrise,” says Brandon Young, CEO of Payless Power in Fort Worth, TX.

In the summer, the additional sunlight can keep your house warmer later into the evening, forcing your air conditioner to run when energy use is the highest.

“As for the landscaping, additional sunlight can allow you to take care of your lawn in the evening rather than wait for the weekend. You might also have to adjust when you water and maintain your lawn,” Young explains.

More sunlight can also improve the security of your home as most perpetrators commit their crimes at night when it’s dark outside.

Lastly, if you plan to list your home in the future, the extra daylight could help you out.

“Since most buyers look at homes in the evenings, you’ll have more opportunities to show your home in the winter months,” Young says.

Plus, the natural lighting can provide a better view of your home’s exterior, landscape, and overall curb appeal.

There are several ways you can prepare for the darker winter mornings you’ll face if permanent daylight saving time becomes law.

“Allow it to preheat your house 30 to 45 minutes prior to your alarm clock going off—not all night long,” explains Young.

Marcus Griswold, founder of Little Green Myths in Vallejo, CA, suggests closing the doors and turning off the heat in rooms you’re not using.

“Some smart systems also help you isolate unused rooms by sensing when someone is present. This is known as zoned heating,” Griswold explains.

Also, take advantage of smart shades that can stay open during the day to heat your home and close with the sunset to hold in the warmth in the winter.

Additionally, use the gradual sunrise option on your smart bulbs, which will mimic the increase in brightness. Place the smart bulbs in bedrooms, bathrooms, and hallways to help enhance alertness as you wake up and ease into your routine.

Don’t forget to be patient with yourself as it might take some time for your body to get used to the change.

“In our survey, 84% of Americans claim it takes at least one day to adjust to a new time after the time change, while 29% say it takes at least one week. Setting your smart home devices like thermostats and lighting to automatically adjust can make the transition easier,” Young explains.

And if you use time-of-use pricing from your utility company, schedule the dishwasher and the laundry to work outside of peak hours. Doing so can lead to cheaper rates and potentially save you some serious cash.

Adjusted net income and adjusted EBITDA were both down slightly from last quarter to $419M and $748M, respectively.

But looking at Rocket’s year-over-year earnings shows a total top-line turnaround. Its GAAP total net revenue increased over 94% from $1.69B; adjusted revenue up 37% from $1.87B; adjusted net income up 165% from $158M; adjusted EBITDA up 114% from $349M and most notably, a net income increase from a $124M loss swinging to that $709M profit.

In a release, Rocket Companies CEO and Director Varun Krishna attributed the numbers coming in against a backdrop of mortgage rates at three-year highs, to gains in both purchase and refinance.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter-over-quarter and year-over-year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” said Krishna. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.”

In an investor call following the release of the data, Krishna attributed Rocket’s turnaround to a company rebuild three years ago that’s “built for any cycle,” which today is experiencing historic housing market hardships—from the 10-year Treasury rising to its highest point in 24 years to mortgage rates rising to their highest point in three years, to declines in existing-home sales and refinance applications.

“Here’s the truth about tough markets: they don’t lie,” he said. “They strip everything down to what’s real—who has the capital to keep investing, whose model works in any cycle, who can win their clients back, and who can move fast when it counts. This quarter did all of this. This was our highest margin in nearly five years and our fourth straight quarter of expansion since we closed the Mr. Cooper transaction. Adjusted net income of $419 million; $0.15 of adjusted EPS.

“So why does Rocket win?” he continued. “It’s no accident. Three years ago we made a decision: Rebuild this company at every single level. An ecosystem that serves clients from home search through servicing. A technology platform built for scale, speed and efficiency. Distribution that reaches homebuyers and homeowners everywhere. And a fortress balance sheet, now over $11 billion in liquidity, so we can keep investing while others pull back.”

On the investor call, Rocket Companies’ Chief Financial Officer Brian Brown walked through the Q3 numbers in more detail.

“We expanded adjusted EBITDA margin to its highest level in nearly five years, and we ended the quarter with record liquidity,” he said, noting that the $2.6B adjusted revenue was near the midpoint of its guidance range (an estimate of the company’s future financial performance). He said the company generated $40.4 billion in net rate lock volume and $43.6 billion in closed loan volume and that based on its estimates, purchase market share approached 6.5% and refinance market share was 15.5%. That’s compared to the 6.2% and 14.3% reported in the second quarter, he added.

Brown also commented that Rocket Local, its team of in-market loan officers who work directly with real estate agents, also grew volume more than 30% year-over-year, and now includes 400 loan officers across several major metro areas. He said the company’s partnership with Redfin and Compass extends that reach, with one in five of its purchase clients represented by a Redfin or Compass agent.

On the wholesale and partner lending side, he said over the last few months, the company has added around 200 new Rocket Pro partners to its platform, representing $12 billion in potential annual volume. Refinance volume set a record, Brown noted, saying cash-out refinance volume remained healthy, supported by another step up in recapture.

“Recapture rates on the combined portfolio reached an all-time high, the fourth consecutive quarter of improvement. Gain on sale margin, excluding correspondent, was 333 basis points, up from 311 basis points last quarter,” he said.

Krishna said that more than 70% of the company’s revenue this year is coming from recurring or less rate-sensitive sources, such as servicing fees, subscriptions, purchase, cash-out refinance and home equity. He said because of the firm’s integration with Redfin, mortgage buyers are brought into their ecosystem early, creating a path to Rocket from the beginning of their home-search journey. He said as of this earnings report, visitors who click through to start a purchase mortgage transaction are up 50% year-over-year.

“Redfin’s contribution to our refinance leads also more than doubled this quarter from a year ago,” Krishna said. “Compass simply extends that same playbook and delivers what buyers want most—homes and the agents who sell them. Cumulative unique listings are now nearly 40,000, up from roughly 25,000 last quarter. Homes you cannot find anywhere else. Rocket Pro net rate lock volume through Compass has passed $3 billion since February, up 50% from last quarter. Then there’s servicing—our ballast. More than $1 billion a quarter in servicing fees. More than $4 billion a year. That’s triple where we were three years ago. That’s recurring cash flow in any rate environment, revenue that shows up whether rates are 4% or 8%. And here’s what makes it compound: Because we know these clients; we’re first in line when they’re ready for their next loan. In Q3, recapture across the combined portfolio hit the highest level in our history.”

Rocket has a three-year agreement with Compass to provide national exposure to its private and coming-soon listings via Redfin.

Krishna said advances in AI in mortgage lending are a game-changer for Rocket, citing four segments of the process: Credit pulls, digital refinance, voice agents and the future of agentic AI.

On nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer volume, AI completed the credit pull step on digital purchase and refinance leads before the client spoke to a loan officer, he said.

On refinance loans, he said clients can choose to pull their credit, see their loan options and lock their rate without having to speak to a loan officer. In Q3, he said digital was more than 40% of all direct-to-consumer refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of every other channel.

Rocket’s AI voice agents now handle 65% of inbound servicing calls and resolve more than half of them on their own, Krishna added. On the future of agentic AI, he said consumers are starting to shop with their own AI agents to compare price, speed and ratings across lenders. Over the past 18 months, Rocket has built the APIs and protocols those agents need to complete the mortgage process with Rocket end to end, he noted.

Looking ahead, Brown said he expects the economic headwinds that have hammered the better part of this year to continue in Q4 and beyond, especially in the refinance sector.

“The MBA Purchase Application Index is down nearly 20% year-over-year, and refinance applications are down more than 50%,” he said. “The fourth quarter is seasonally low for our industry, and this year that slowdown comes at a time where mortgage rates are reaching highs we haven’t seen in two decades.”

Brown added that Rocket expects the refinance market to decline by almost half from the third quarter, “which would leave the overall mortgage activity near multi-decade lows.”

With that context, in the fourth quarter, Brown said they expect adjusted revenue to be between $2.1B and $2.3B with their guidance reflecting continued share gains. For expenses, they expect total expenses of $2.05B, including $110M of intangible amortization, $80M of stock-based compensation and $10M of one-time integration costs. Excluding these items, Brown said they expect expenses of $1.85B, a decline of $165M from the third quarter.

“Tough markets drive separation,” Brown said in his closing remarks. “This quarter, rates rose, volumes fell, and the industry felt it. Rocket Companies grew share, expanded margin, delivered synergies ahead of plan and ended the quarter with record liquidity. The fourth quarter will be harder still. We’re ready for it.”

Beth McGuire is RISMedia’s vice president of online editorial.
