#5674. These State and Local Elections Will Hinge on Housing Policy—What Voters Need To Know

In this year's midterm elections, housing affordability has emerged as a central flashpoint in three high-profile races: the California gubernatorial contest and the mayoral races in Los Angeles and Washington, DC.

At both the state and municipal levels, voters face major structural and economic constraints, from scarce buildable land and a sluggish pace of new construction to restrictive zoning, drawn-out permitting timelines, high inflation, and mortgage rates topping 7%.

On this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California was among six states to earn an F grade because of a dismal housing affordability score. Washington, DC, fared only marginally better, earning a D+.

Meanwhile, Los Angeles ranked dead last on the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards among the 100 largest U.S. cities, posting the lowest combined score measuring both affordability and homebuilding metrics.

Statewide and local candidates appearing on the Nov. 3 ballot have spent months pitching their proposed solutions to the housing crisis.

On the eve of the vote, here is where each of the contenders for these key gubernatorial and mayoral races stands on housing.

Former Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Fox News contributor Steve Hilton, a Republican, are the front-runners vying to replace termed-out California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

If elected governor, Becerra pledges to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his first day in office and appoint senior staffers across state agencies to tackle the crisis.

His agenda also includes implementing "shot clocks" to clearly communicate permit wait times to developers, overhauling and lowering impact fees statewide, standardizing and streamlining reviews for modular construction, and simplifying affordable housing financing.

"California should be a place where the carpenter who builds a home can afford to buy one," he said in a speech this summer.

According to a new Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and American Community Survey data, the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to finance a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state in the nation behind Montana.

Becerra has voiced support for building "missing-middle" multifamily housing, especially near transit hubs, and expanding first-time homebuyer down payment assistance programs to put homeownership within reach of more renters.

On the issue of homelessness and homeless encampments, which has become a lightning rod for political candidates in California this election cycle, Becerra is laser-focused on prevention.

At an event in the East Bay last week, Becerra argued that keeping at-risk people housed after a medical emergency or a sudden job loss is far less costly to the state than rehousing them from the street, reported ABC 7 News (KGO).

"We have to do everything we can to prevent them from falling into homelessness," Becerra said.

His strategy includes bolstering tenant protections, expanding funding to organizations that have proven effective in addressing the homelessness crisis, and holding accountable those who have failed to act.

The Donald Trump-endorsed GOP hopeful for governor of California has been aggressively pushing for the clearing of homeless encampments, vowing to rid the state of every single one by Dec. 31, 2027.

Similarly to his Democratic rival, Hilton has highlighted the need to cut through red tape constraining residential construction, though his approach hinges on capping fees, permits, and regulation costs at $50,000 per new home to make it cheaper for developers to build.

"We have to get rid of the regulations that make it two or three times as expensive to build the exact same home in California as in neighboring states," said Hilton during a televised debate in May.

His housing platform also includes utilizing over a million vacant lots to build starter homes, and creating 10 new municipalities across California to expand housing supply instead of trying to shoehorn multifamily developments into single-family communities.

“We have to stop trying to force housing into suburban neighborhoods where people don't want it," he proclaimed during the debate.

Despite their contrasting platforms, Hilton and Becerra are united in their fierce opposition to the California Billionaire Tax, officially known as Proposition 40, which Gov. Newsom had unsuccessfully tried to keep off the ballot.

Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the measure would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the worldwide assets of more than 200 Californians with a net worth of $1 billion or more who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Opponents of the initiative across the political spectrum have warned that it will accelerate an exodus of high-net-worth residents and tech innovators from California, diminishing the state's tax base.

Speaking on "The Steve Hilton Show" in January, Hilton criticized Proposition 40 as the epitome of what he called the "stupidity and the failure of 16 years of one-party rule" in California that, if adopted, will "drive business out of state."

On his part, Becerra dismissed the proposal as a "sketchy policy" and instead threw his support behind an alternative measure that would extend temporary tax rate increases on the ultrawealthy to reliably fund healthcare and public schools.

At the municipal level, incumbent Mayor Karen Bass, a Democrat, is seeking reelection for a second term. She is being challenged by L.A. City Councilmember Nithya Raman, a member of the Democratic Socialists of America.

Since taking office in 2022, Bass has made fast-tracking affordable housing construction and tackling homelessness the twin pillars of her agenda.

One of Bass' signature initiatives was Executive Directive 1, which streamlined approval for roughly 50,000 units of fully affordable housing. About 6,000 of those units are currently under construction.

In an email to Realtor.com last month, the mayor's office said that under Bass' leadership, the city has carried out a historic rezoning program to create the capacity for half a million new homes and bring more housing to transit corridors and commerical centers.

"After decades of inaction, Mayor Bass has been laser-focused on slashing red tape and accelerating the building of affordable housing in Los Angeles," a mayor's representative said.

Beyond construction permitting, Bass used her executive power to update the Rent Stabilization Ordinance for the first time in 40 years to lower the maximum allowable annual rent hike from 10% to 1%–4% for rent-controlled units, expanded the Adaptive Reuse Ordinance to convert vacant office buildings and parking lots into housing, and streamlined the building application process.

That last action, according to Bass' camp, was in direct response "to the barriers that applicants, developers, and contractors have identified as impediments to building in L.A."

Bass' plan to solve homelessness is anchored by her Inside Safe program, which clears encampments and moves unhoused people into motels and hotels on a voluntary basis with the goal of helping them secure permanent housing.

Councilmember Raman, who is seeking to unseat Bass, has been sharply critical of her record on housing, arguing in a statement to Realtor.com last month that her administration has not done enough to address L.A.’s housing crisis, leaving tens of thousands of residents "struggling to afford rent."

Responding to the Realtor.com Metro Report Cards' findings, that named L.A. the nation’s least affordable large city, Raman said she was not surprised.

"We’ve made it too difficult, time consuming, and costly to build homes in Los Angeles," said the candidate.

To lower costs, Rama’s platform outlines a plan to triple annual housing production by accelerating permitting through strict "shot clocks" for approvals, overhauling inspections, updating codes, and eliminating additional fees to create more starter homes for working families, and pressuring state lawmakers to pass reforms that wold incentivize developers to build more for-sale homes.

Citing results in 4th District, where her office recorded a 49% drop in street homelessness, Raman has made a campaign promise to cut the citywide population of unhoused people in half by the 2028 Summer Olympics through rental subsidies and the expansion of low-cost housing.

Raman and Bass share common ground on the issue of L.A.'s controversial Measure ULA, colloquially known as a Mansion Tax, which they both want to see reformed.

Enacted in April 2023, the measure imposes a 4% tax on property sales of $5.4 million to $10.9 million, and a 5.5% tax on sales exceeding $10.9 million. These rates apply on top of Los Angeles' standard 0.45% base real estate transfer tax.

Contrary to its nickname, the tax applies not only to luxury homes but to all real estate priced at over $5.4 million, including apartment buildings.

A recent report from the nonpartisan global policy think tank RAND Corporation found that the tax cost the city over 9,000 new housing units, 16,500 construction jobs, and $452 million in lost revenue.

Earlier this year, Raman unsuccsefully proposed a ballot measure to exempt newly built multifamily, commercial, and mixed-use buildings from Measure ULA for 15 years, arguing that it was suppressing much-needed housing production.

In Washington, DC, three candidates are striving to succeed three-term Mayor Muriel Bowser: Janeese Lewis George, a Democratic Socialist and member of the Council of the District of Columbia; Rhonda Hamilton, a veteran and community advocate running as an independent; and Robert L. Gross, representing the DC Statehood Green Party.

The cornerstone of Lewis George’s platform is the "Homes for All" plan, which includes provisions for rent stabilization, a coordinated affordable housing development system, stricter code enforcement, and expanded down-payment assistance.

Additional planks in her platform include amending the city’s zoning restrictions to add more homes and mixed-income housing, especially closer to transit lines.

"Increasing supply, paired with policies to protect residents, really is critical to stopping further displacement and making housing more affordable for all," she wrote in an op-ed.

The latest ACS numbers from the Census Bureau reflect the urgent need for change. Buyers in DC have to contend with a 25% gap between earned income and the minimum required income to afford a home.

Her long-term goal is to add 72,000 new housing units throughout DC within five years.

Lewis George has secured the backing of several pro-housing development groups, but President Trump does not count himself among her supporters.

Trump said in June that he "wouldn’t like" having Lewis George as mayor and floated the prospect of overseeing a federal takeover of DC.

"Maybe we’ll take back Washington, run it on a federal basis," he said. "We won’t put up with it. We’re not going to lose our businesses."

Rhonda Hamilton, who grew up in DC, is focused on building deeply affordable housing and requiring all new residential development to include this type of units. Her other major project aims to audit underperforming agencies, including the Housing Production Trust Fund and the District of Columbia Housing Authority (DCHA) waitlist.

"We’ve got to do something about the high rents," said Hamilton, per DC News Now. "We’ve got to make sure that our citizens are not being pushed out of the city."

Like L.A., the nation's capital is dealing with high levels of homelessness. Hamilton's agenda looks to put an end to street encampment clear-outs and partner with local churches to temporarily shelter unhoused residents.

Robert Gross, an information technology engineer by trade, wants to harness the power of artificial intelligence to speed up housing approvals and streamline zoning permits as part of his broader agenda to modernize city government.

Gross’ platform hinges on his "Human Life Standard" framework, which has as its goal to establish green infrastructure standards and reform the housing voucher structure by creating two distinct tracks for families with children and for single, unhoused individuals.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5673. Mastering the Art: How Real Estate Agents Should Write Facebook Ad Copy

In the digital age, social media platforms have become powerful tools for real estate agents to market their listings and attract potential clients. Among the various platforms available, Facebook remains a dominant force with its massive user base and advertising capabilities. To stand out in the competitive real estate market, agents must not only create compelling visual content but also craft persuasive ad copy that engages and captivates their target audience. In this article, we will delve into the key elements and strategies for writing effective Facebook ad copy, equipping real estate agents with the knowledge to maximize their advertising efforts and generate leads.

The first step to writing compelling Facebook ad copy is gaining a deep understanding of your target audience. By knowing their demographics, preferences, and pain points, you can tailor your copy to resonate with their needs and desires. Conduct thorough market research, utilize Facebook's audience insights, and analyze data from previous campaigns to gather valuable information about your target audience.

The headline is the first element of your Facebook ad copy that users will see. It needs to be attention-grabbing and compelling enough to entice people to read further. Use action-oriented words, emphasize unique selling propositions, and create a sense of urgency to pique the audience's curiosity and encourage them to click on your ad.

When writing Facebook ad copy, it's crucial to highlight the benefits of the property or service you're promoting, rather than merely listing its features. Benefits explain how the property or service can improve the lives of potential buyers or renters. By emphasizing the value and advantages, you can create an emotional connection with your audience and motivate them to take action.

Storytelling is a powerful tool for capturing the attention of your audience and making your Facebook ad copy more relatable. Craft a compelling narrative that showcases the unique aspects of the property or the positive experiences of previous clients. Engaging stories can evoke emotions, create a sense of authenticity, and build trust with potential clients.

In the fast-paced world of social media, attention spans are limited. To ensure your Facebook ad copy is effective, keep it concise and clear. Use short sentences and paragraphs, bullet points, and subheadings to enhance readability. Avoid jargon and technical terms that may confuse or alienate your audience.

Social proof, such as testimonials, reviews, or success stories, can significantly influence potential clients' decision-making process. Incorporate social proof into your Facebook ad copy to build credibility and trust. Highlight positive feedback from satisfied clients or showcase awards and recognition you've received in the real estate industry.

To encourage immediate action from your audience, create a sense of urgency in your Facebook ad copy. Limited-time offers exclusive deals, or a countdown timer can instill a fear of missing out (FOMO) and prompt potential clients to take the desired action promptly.

An effective call-to-action (CTA) is vital to prompt users to take the desired action, whether it's contacting you, visiting a landing page, or scheduling a property viewing. Use action verbs, provide clear instructions, and create a sense of urgency to motivate users to click on your CTA button.

Continuous testing and optimization are essential for improving the performance of your Facebook ad copy. Create multiple variations of your ad copy, test them against each other, and analyze the results. Fine-tune your copy based on metrics such as click-through rates (CTR), conversion rates, and engagement levels to identify what resonates best with your audience.

Writing compelling Facebook ad copy is a crucial skill for real estate agents looking to excel in their digital marketing efforts. By understanding their target audience, crafting attention-grabbing headlines, focusing on benefits, incorporating storytelling techniques, and utilizing social proof, agents can create persuasive and engaging copy that captivates potential clients. Remember to keep your copy concise and clear, create a sense of urgency, and use compelling calls to action. Through A/B testing and continuous optimization, agents can refine their ad copy to maximize its effectiveness. By mastering the art of writing Facebook ad copy, real estate agents can unlock the full potential of social media advertising and boost their success in the competitive real estate market.

#5672. Jenny McCarthy Is Living in a Tent and Considering a Move to Las Vegas After ‘Serious’ Mold Problem

Jenny McCarthy is opening up about her unusual living situation as she’s moved into a tent in her yard while she deals with the effects of a “mold and mycotoxin poisoning” diagnosis.

During the Oct. 28 episode of “The Jenny McCarthy Wahlberg Show,” the actress explained the health-related challenges she’s faced over the last two years, which have included multiple surgeries and rounds of antibiotics.

Eventually, medical professionals tested “The Masked Singer” judge for mold, and she was diagnosed with mycotoxin poisoning.

McCarthy, 54, believes she was initially exposed to mold at her “very, very old” dressing room that “had a dampness to it,” as the makeup artist who exclusively works with her “in that dressing room also wound up getting mold poisoning.”

After the diagnosis, McCarthy embarked on a “mold protocol” in January 2025, following a routine of taking vitamins and undergoing treatments. She also took on the costly experience of remediating her home—which she said can cost anywhere from tens of thousands of dollars to “a hundred grand.”

“Remediation costs are so high because it takes a specialist to be able to move the mold without ruining your entire house,” she said, noting that the process was not covered by her insurance.

After remediation, McCarthy explained she had to hire contractors to “come in and rebuild” the home.

“You have to get rid of all your furniture. You have to get rid of all your clothes. I’m like, ‘Oh my god, that’s crazy!’” she said of the advice she received. “So, we remediated and because I am paranoid now about basically sleeping anywhere, I live in a tent. And I’m not even joking.”

McCarthy shared a look at the tent she’s been living out of, noting that it has a rain-proof cover for safety.

“I don’t have to worry about rain in California, but I do worry about chemtrails. And sprinklers,” she said.

She also added that she “won’t even go into an RV” because she is concerned about “chemicals.”

The podcast host went on to explain that she feels “a little bit crazy sometimes,” noting a “paranoid” state of mind, “like the walls are caving in.” She called the situation “really, really hard,” and confirmed that her husband, Donnie Wahlberg, 57, is not living in the tent with her.

“Donnie is working in Canada, and he is safe inside of a building,” McCarthy said. “Does he think I’m crazy? Yes. But he completely understands it.”

McCarthy also said that in the wake of the ordeal, she’s considering a relocation.

“I am so paranoid that I’ve even talked to Donny about moving out of the Midwest, where it’s humid, and going to a dry location like Vegas or Arizona or something, because my body just can’t detox mold very well,” she said.

While it appears that the tent McCarthy is residing in is located in California, it’s unclear whether the home she had remediated is the St. Charles, IL, residence she and Wahlberg listed for $2.799 million in September of this year.

In a recent Instagram comment, McCarthy indicated that the couple was “Going to Vegas. Not Cali.” following the listing of their longtime home.

The couple have owned the property for over a decade, and purchased it for $1.1 million in 2015.

“This isn’t an extravagant home, but there’s no greater symbol of our love for each other than this house and how much love has gone into it,” Wahlberg told People magazine of the dwelling in 2019.

The four-bedroom, 5.5-bathroom home was built in 1996. Spanning 7,236 square feet, the abode sits on 1.26 acres. Based on the contingent status on the property’s listing, it appears the couple has found a buyer.

#5671. Houston’s Historic Kirby Mansion Is Demolished To Make Way for Convenience Store

Preservationists in Houston are up in arms after a historic mansion dating back to 1894 was demolished to erect a convenience store.

On Friday, demolition on Kirby Mansion began but was quickly halted by Houston Public Works after it was discovered that a demolition permit had been applied for but not approved.

Dozens of locals held a candlelight vigil on Sunday to protest the demolition, but the permit was approved over the weekend. Demolition resumed and was completed on Monday morning.

The Kirby Mansion was named after lumber baron and industrialist John Henry Kirby who purchased the small home that was originally on the site in 1896 and expanded it into a 36-room Tudor Revival mansion.

Among the many unique features of the home was a library with hidden panels and a “thunder room”—a sound-insulated room built because Kirby's wife, Lelia, had a severe fear of thunderstorms.

The Kirby family sold the property in 1947, and the mansion served as the headquarters for the Houston-Harris County Red Cross for 30 years, though it had not been occupied in recent years.

Over its 132-year history, the mansion hosted presidents Franklin D. Roosevelt, Herbert Hoover, and George H.W. Bush, as well as British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher.

This past September, OB Texas Properties LLC, a company owned by Omair Bashir, purchased the property for more than $9.3 million. Bashir and his brother, Usman, are the owners of Brake Time Corner Market, a fast-growing convenience store and gas station chain.

In September 2025, Brake Time announced it would be opening 35 new convenience stores across Texas, Arizona, Arkansas, Colorado, and Kansas through the end of 2026, with three planned for Houston.

This past June, OB Texas Properties filed a plan for a 13,254-square-foot, one-story commercial building at an address within the mansion’s property boundaries. The filings included a hemp registration—indicating consumable hemp products would also be sold at the location.

Local preservationists had rallied to save the mansion, but because it lacked local, state, or federal historic designation, there was little they could do.

Over the weekend, Preservation Houston tried to contact Bashir’s company about removing some of the historic details from the site, including the mansion’s hand-carved oak staircase and imported tiles, but received no response.

“We wish the owner had been transparent and honest about the plans for this property and willing to discuss preservation options,” Jennifer Kapral, the executive director of Preservation Houston told Realtor.com in a statement. “We offered to explore ways to give this building a future. We also asked for the opportunity to document it and discuss salvaging irreplaceable materials if demolition went ahead. We received no response. Houston deserves better than this.”

“What’s so sad is the people that did buy this, and again, it’s their private property they can do with it as they choose. It just seems like not the best place for a vape store and gas station when there are numerous gas stations within a three-mile radius,” local resident Jason Fuller told the Houston Chronicle.

This isn’t the first time the Kirby Mansion was scheduled for demolition. In 2018 Central Houston Auto Properties LLC purchased the property, with the intention of turning it into a car dealership, though those plans never came to fruition.

Realtor.com has reached out to Brake Time for comment.

She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5670. How To Deal With Noisy Upstairs Neighbors: 8 Clever Tricks To Keep The Peace

Shortly after they were married, Brittany H. and her husband moved into an apartment in Chicago’s Irving Park neighborhood. With Victorian houses and vintage flats dotting the tree-lined streets, they assumed their new home would be a peaceful spot to build their life together.

But the couple got more than they bargained for. At all hours of the night, they heard strange, loud sounds coming from the neighbors upstairs.

“It was midnight, and the loud upstairs neighbors sounded like they were dropping bricks on the floor," Brittany says, vividly recalling her first night in the unit. "Our ceiling light fixture rattled from the loud, noisy pounding.”

When their lease was up, the couple promptly moved to the top floor of a different apartment building. Brittany was so scarred by her experience with noisy neighbors, she says she'll never live anywhere but a top floor again.

As a renter, you have to be ready for some day-to-day noise—that's just part of living in close quarters with other people. So, how can you reduce noise from upstairs neighbors?

If you've lived below noisy upstairs neighbors like Brittany has, you know the sound: the relentless stomping, dropped objects that seem to ricochet off every surface, the mysterious midnight furniture rearranging. Beyond frustrating, it can feel inescapable.

In many apartments, especially older buildings, this kind of noise is more than a nuisance: It's a feature.

Many vintage units were built before modern soundproofing standards were a thing. That means there might be little to no insulation between floors, allowing every footstep, conversation, or clattering object to echo directly into your living space.

While some level of noise is part of communal living, chronic disruptions can wear on your nerves and your sleep cycle.

But you're not powerless to deal with it. Whether you have noisy upstairs neighbors stomping around at odd hours or sudden loud thuds overhead, these renter-friendly tips can help restore your peace and quiet.

Say what now? Ceiling clouds are acoustic panels that hang from the ceiling and can reduce noise and echoes. (Science!) Take that, noisy upstairs neighbors.

You've probably seen them before in auditoriums, atriums, and restaurants. They can do wonders for cutting down noise in your home, too.

Just make sure to check with your landlord before installing them since they need to be securely mounted to the ceiling.

If your landlord isn't on board, there are other less invasive approaches to dissipate sound, including acoustic light fixtures that claim to absorb sound.

Have you ever lived next to a neighbor who plays the piano (or worse, an amped-up electric guitar) well past bedtime?

If the neighbor won't knock it off, you don't have to move (or file a complaint with the landlord or police). Just put some stuff between you and the pandemonium next door.

Start by placing bookcases or other heavy furniture against the dividing wall, covering as much of the wall as possible.

"The more mass between you and the neighbor, the less sound that will come through,” says Zach Ziskin, a recording engineer in Fort Lauderdale, FL.

Then, rearrange fabric-covered sofas or chairs so that they're close to windows and doors. And for more quiet, use lots of decorative pillows and throws.

“The heavier and denser the textile, the greater the absorption,” says Heather Humphrey, owner of the interior design firm Alder & Tweed, in Park City, UT.

If you can hear your neighbors flush the toilet, they can probably hear you, right? That’s because open spaces with tile and hard surfaces, such as a bathroom, amplify sound.

Short on space? Fill the bathroom with wall coverings and soft goods such as rugs and towels, which is a pretty easy way of dealing with noisy upstairs neighbors and their sounds.

“The same principle goes," she says. "The more you cover your walls, the greater the barrier to sound created."

Sometimes, the outside noise you hear in your apartment can be just as irritating as noise from your neighbors. And closing your windows isn't always a cure-all—those sounds can trickle in regardless.

One way to dial it down? Make sure the window casings and frames are fully caulked and sealed. (You'll want to call your landlord about this one.) Or use a window insert to make the seal more airtight, Ziskin says.

Even easier? Just hang some heavy curtains, which will help muffle any noise from outside.

You'd be surprised by how much noise can seep in through the cracks around your door and ruin your quiet. Your best soundproofing efforts will be futile unless you address them.

Make sure there's high-quality weatherstripping between the door and door frame to create a seal when closed, Ziskin says.

Likewise, if there's an air gap between the bottom of the door and the floor, attach a heavy-duty door sweep or draft blocker to create a seal.

Because wall hangings and tapestries are porous, they can absorb sound and excessive noise.

If you're conjuring up images of your college dorm room, don't worry—there are tons of options these days that are beautifully on trend.

For instance, the heavy knotting in macramé makes it perfect for buffering noise and giving your place stylish flair.

Canvas wall art can also help absorb sound; consider adding a layer of foam to the hollow inside for an extra buffer. Or try sound-absorbing felt panels—you can even use one to make a DIY bulletin board.

"It will add a decorative touch and keep you organized, while reducing noise levels," says Dayna Hairston, interior designer at Dayziner in Cary, NC.

If you have wood floors, do yourself and your neighbors a favor and throw down some area rugs. (Heck, if you have carpet, go ahead and do this, too—the more padding, the better.)

When buying a rug, seek out thick-pile material or something with a rubber backing to muffle sound, Humphrey suggests.

Of course, it just isn't always possible to completely soundproof your apartment. If you're still fighting the urge to grab a broom and bang on the ceiling, it's probably time to talk to the neighbors.

"If all else fails, invest in high-quality earplugs or a white noise machine,” Ziskin says.

Sometimes, your noisy upstairs neighbors aren’t just annoying—they’re violating local laws. Most cities have noise ordinances, which define quiet hours, typically between 10 p.m. and 7 a.m. (These can vary by location.) If your neighbors are consistently blasting music late into the night or stomping around at 2 a.m., you might have legal grounds to act.

Start by documenting the disturbances. Note the time, duration, and type of noise. Audio recordings and written logs can help if you need to escalate the issue down the line.

Next, try to resolve the problem directly. Politely let your neighbor know the noise is disruptive. If that doesn't work, reach out to your landlord or property manager.

Still no improvement? Then it's time to contact your local nonemergency number. Don’t dial 911 unless it’s an emergency—for everything else, most municipalities have a nonemergency line for noise complaints.

If you're unsure about your city’s laws, search “[your city] noise violation hours” or visit your city’s website to understand when and how to file a formal legal noise complaint.

It might be tempting to fight noise with noise by blasting your own music, banging on the ceiling with a broom, or leaving a snarky note taped to their door. But while getting back at your neighbors might sound like a dream, these passive-aggressive tactics rarely work—and often make things worse.

Instead, aim for constructive solutions. Communicate clearly, keep things civil, and involve your landlord or building management when needed. If all else fails, rely on renter-friendly soundproofing upgrades and consider investing in a white noise machine or noise-canceling headphones.

Allaire Conte contributed to this report.

Jenny Lelwica Buttaccio is a writer living in Chicago. Her work has appeared in HuffPost, Prevention Magazine, Reader's Digest, and more.

#5668. Confused by Home Price Headlines? Here’s Why.

Whether you own a house already or you’re looking to buy one, you probably care about home prices. But it’s not always easy to figure out what’s really happening right now, especially if you look at the headlines.

One says home prices are falling. The next says they’re still climbing.

So, which one’s right? It comes down to where you live.

Part of the confusion out there may be based on what’s happening to asking prices and how the media is talking about it. They’re calling attention to how asking prices are falling, but don’t give the full context or say that seasonality is at play. So here it is.

Right now, there are more homes on the market than at any other time since November 2019. And with mortgage rates rising since the spring, those homes are taking a little longer to sell. One way to help a home sell quickly in that environment is to have a lower asking price.

According to HousingWire Data, the median asking price is down from $449k in early August to $435k just 2 months later (see graph below):

That’s a dip of about 3%, and a lot of it is normal for this time of year.

Asking prices cool off every fall once the busy summer season wraps up. With fewer buyers this time of year, sellers price a bit more competitively. Today’s rates play a role too, since sellers are pricing to match what buyers can afford right now. And that’s a good thing. Smart pricing helps homes sell.

Just keep in mind, that’s a national list price. It doesn’t show what homes near you are actually selling for. So before you react to a headline, ask a local agent what’s really happening in your area.

“While national headlines might suggest a buyer’s market is taking hold, the reality on the ground depends heavily on where and what you’re trying to buy. Local trends can diverge sharply from national averages, especially when you factor in price range, property type, and post-pandemic market dynamics.”

The latest numbers from S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index show how true that is. Over the past year, sales prices in Chicago rose almost 7%. In Seattle, they dipped about 1.6%. That’s a gap of nearly 9 percentage points between two major cities (see graph below):

That gap changes your game plan. Selling in New York, where prices are up almost 6%? You may not need to cut your price. Buying in Denver or Las Vegas? You may have more room to negotiate.

Just in case you’re seeing those slight declines in some markets and worried it means a bigger crash is coming, here’s what you need to remember. Even in the major metros where prices are down, the declines are 2% or less. That’s a long way from a crash like 2008. And if you look back at the graph above, there are more cities in the green than in the red.

And over time, home values have a strong track record. The Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) says national prices have grown year-over-year every quarter since 2012. Go back further, and a $100k home bought in 1991 would be worth about $436k today, even with the 2008 crash factored in (see graph below):

So, this short-term dip probably won’t stick around. The small declines we’re seeing now are in markets that overheated during the pandemic. As a whole, the market is headed back to normal – and normal means prices should rise over time.

National headlines can’t tell you what your home is worth or how much room you have to negotiate. Local data can. If you’re thinking about buying or selling, connect with a local real estate agent to look at how prices are moving in your area, so you can set your price or make your offer with confidence.

#5666. To Sell or Rent? How To Choose the Best Path for Your House.

Selling your house is a big step, and you want it to go smoothly. And with houses taking a little longer to sell these days, renting it out might start to sound like a nice backup plan.

But the reality is, while renting can work well for some people, it’s also a big commitment. So before you decide, it helps to see the whole picture first.

Lately, some sellers are choosing to hang on to their houses and rent them out instead. According to Parcl, around 9% of homes for rent right now were previously up for sale.

Some homeowners put their houses on the market expecting a faster process than they got or a certain price buyers didn’t respond to. And when things didn’t go exactly as planned, they decided to rent instead. As Kara Ng, Senior Economist at Zillow, explains:

“Bargaining power is tilting toward buyers and homes are taking longer to sell, making renting out a property one way to buy time rather than compete aggressively on price.”

But here’s the important distinction. Just because some sellers are choosing to rent doesn’t mean selling isn’t working. In many cases, the difference comes down to how well a house is priced, prepared, and marketed for today’s buyers.

Parcl data shows where these “accidental landlords” – owners who planned to sell but decided to rent instead – are most common (see graph below):

They make up around 17% of homes for rent in places like Sherman and Houston, TX, but less than 4% in markets like Des Moines, IA and Bloomington, IN.

That’s a pretty big difference. And it shows why you have to know what’s happening in your neighborhood. Your market, your asking price, and your strategy all play a role in how your sale goes.

A local agent can show you how houses like yours are selling, what strategies work best, and help you weigh your options – not to push you to sell, but so you at least have the full picture based on today’s market. And part of making an informed decision is understanding what renting your house would actually take.

While renting might sound like easy passive income on paper, in practice, it’s a hands-on job with rules to follow. As Invest West Management puts it:

“Even if you never intended to become a landlord, the law still sees you as one — and you must meet all legal obligations that come with that role. This often includes registering the tenancy, providing tenants with certain disclosures, and ensuring the property meets safety standards.”

You’d also be the one chasing missed rent payments, fixing damage between tenants, and covering unexpected repairs. Not to mention fielding weekend calls about leaky dishwashers or broken AC units.

There are expenses beyond regular maintenance and repairs, too. According to Bankrate, these are a few of the biggest:

Insurance premiums (landlord insurance typically costs about 25% more than a standard homeowners policy)

Management fees (if you hire a property manager, they usually charge around 10% of the rent)

Gaps between tenants, when you pay the mortgage without rental income

If you want to be a landlord and you’re prepared for the responsibility, renting may be a great fit. But if you’d really rather sell, don’t let today’s market convince you that you can’t.

A great agent can make it happen. The key is having an open conversation up front with your agent about pricing and how to market your house. Nailing those details from day 1 helps your house make a great first impression, so renting doesn’t have to be your fallback.

Renting can be a good fit for the right person with the right house, but it isn’t the only option. A smart sales strategy can help your house stand out to buyers from day one.So, if you’re on the fence, a local real estate agent can help you compare what selling and renting would each look like for you.

#5664. Why More Buyers Are Turning To Adjustable-Rate Mortgages Today

When mortgage rates climb, buying a home can start to feel like trying to hit a moving target. Every jump in rates makes monthly payments bigger, and that pushes a lot of buyers to look for another way in.

More and more of them are finding it in the adjustable-rate mortgage, or ARM.

Here’s how an ARM differs from a more traditional mortgage. With a regular fixed-rate mortgage, your rate stays the same for your whole loan. But with an ARM, your rate is locked for the first few years, then it can move up or down based on market conditions.

Some people don’t like that level of uncertainty – and that’s okay. But others are drawn to this option specifically because there’s usually a lower rate to start when you opt for an ARM. And in an affordability-strapped market, that’s going to gain popularity.

Bankrate recently found that, in September, rates for ARM products were over a full percentage point lower than a regular fixed-rate loan. Depending on the ARM product, that can make a difference of $150-300 in the monthly payment on a median-priced home.

And for some buyers, that’s enough to turn “not right now” into “let’s do this.” You can see it in the numbers. Data from the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA) shows that, in October, roughly 1 in 10 people applying for a mortgage chose an ARM (see graph below):

If you think you may want to consider this yourself, here’s what you need to know about how it works.

An ARM is like a phone or cable plan that has an introductory deal for new customers. You start out at a lower price, and then it adjusts after a specified amount of time. A popular loan is the 5/1 ARM.

The “5” means your introductory rate is locked for the first five years, and the “1” means that the rate can change every year after that. The rate change is called the “reset.” And here’s the really important part.

When your rate resets, your mortgage payment could go up or down. The good news is that most ARMs have caps, which are limits on how much your rate can rise each year and over the life of the loan. But either way, you have to be ready.

To see if this type of loan may be right for you, here are some things to think about and discuss with your loan officer:

Before you decide, ask your lender to work up the numbers and walk you through the different potential scenarios you could run into with an ARM. That way, you go in with your eyes open.

And, if you do go with an adjustable-rate mortgage, just know that you’ll have choices when the reset time arrives. You could:

Do nothing and keep your loan in place if the new payment still fits your budget.

Refinance into a fixed-rate loan with a payment that never changes.

Refinance into another ARM with a new lower rate locked for a specified timeframe.

Talk to the loan servicer about assistance or modification.

Remember, a refinance is a brand-new loan that you’ll have to qualify for – even if it’s on a home you already own. So, keep tabs on your credit and debt levels and ask your loan officer how major financial moves like job changes and major purchases will affect your mortgage readiness. It’s important to keep your credit and finances in “mortgage shape.”

One more quick note. ARMs got a bad name after the financial crisis of 2008. Back then, there were some risky loans with small starting payments that later shot way up. Others let people borrow without proving how much money they earned.

But now, there are new laws to protect both borrowers and lenders. The biggest change is the Ability-to-Repay Rule, which says that before a lender makes a home loan, it has to check real paperwork (like pay stubs, W-2 forms, and tax returns) to make sure you can afford it. The lender also has to look at what your payment could be after the reset, not just the low starting payment.

So, you don’t have to worry that today’s ARMs are the same as the ones we saw back during the crash.

Today's market has more options than many people realize. Finding the right one could be as simple as getting more information about tools like ARMs. A trusted lender can run the numbers with you, walk you through the what-ifs, and help you explore the possibilities.Is an ARM a good option for you? #5662. Why Builders May Be More Motivated To Sell Than Homeowners

Here’s something most homebuyers don’t think about. When the housing market slows down, homeowners and builders don’t always respond the same way.

Think about it. If you’re selling your house and aren’t getting the offers you want, you could make the choice to take it off the market and stay put, and wait for things to improve.

But builders? They may be more motivated to stay the course.

They’ve already invested money in building those houses. And every completed home that sits unsold means money tied up in a property, plus ongoing costs that can add up.

That’s why some builders may be more motivated to negotiate right now. And that could work in your favor.

You’ve probably seen the headlines. According to the latest report from the National Association of Realtors (NAR), pending home sales – homes that have gone under contract but haven’t closed yet – fell 7.3% in September and 11.3% compared to last year.

Why? Higher mortgage rates are making it harder for buyers to make the numbers work. Now, that report tracks existing homes, not new construction. But we’re seeing signs of the same slowdown on the builder side, too.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), builder confidence dropped to 29 in October, its lowest level since June 2012. Traffic from prospective buyers also dropped to its lowest level in more than a decade, excluding the start of the pandemic.

As Robert Dietz, Chief Economist at NAHB, explains:

“Demand persists, but higher mortgage rates, elevated construction costs and weaker consumer confidence are keeping more buyers on the sidelines.”

A homeowner may be able to wait for the right offer. But a builder with several finished houses sitting unsold may have more reason to get those homes sold sooner rather than later.

And that means they may be more willing to work with you than you think.

If you’ve always assumed builders don’t negotiate, take a look at what they’re actually doing. According to the latest survey from NAHB, in October:

65% of builders are offering sales incentives.

43% are cutting prices, the highest share recorded between 2020 and 2026.

And 6% is what they’re typically taking off the price.

So, yes. Builders absolutely do negotiate. And with demand slowing, there’s good reason to explore just how flexible they may be right now.

That could mean asking for a lower price. But it could also mean asking for a mortgage-rate buydown, help with closing costs, or upgrades that would otherwise cost you extra.

And here’s a tip that could make a real difference.

Don’t just look at the newest communities or the prettiest model homes. Look for builders with completed houses that haven’t sold yet.

Those are sometimes called quick move-in homes or spec homes. And the longer one of those move-in ready homes sits unsold, the more reason a builder may have to consider an offer that helps get it off their books.

Don’t assume the advertised price or incentive package is the best they’ll do.

This is where having your own agent can really pay off. An agent who knows the local market can help you compare what builders are offering, identify communities with more available homes, and understand where there’s room to negotiate.

Of course, not every builder will offer the same incentives. And some may be more flexible on closing costs or mortgage rates than on the price itself.

The trick is knowing where to look, what to ask for, and how much room there may be to negotiate. And that’s where having your own agent is key.

A homeowner who isn't ready to accept a lower offer may be able to wait. But a builder with finished houses to sell has a different set of priorities. #5660. Who’s Buying Homes with Cash Right Now?

Ryan Serhant, CEO of SERHANT, says there isn’t just 1 housing market right now. There are really 4: cash buyers, buyers who need a mortgage, homeowners with low mortgage rates, and builders.

Today, let’s zoom in on the 1st group – cash buyers.

According to the National Association of Realtors (NAR), 27% of homes sold in September were bought with all cash. That’s more than 1 in 4 buyers. And that’s a pretty big number, especially when so many people are struggling with affordability.

So where is all that cash coming from? When you hear a number like that, it’s easy to picture wealthy investors buying up houses left and right. But that’s not necessarily the case. Some of those cash buyers are actually homeowners who’ve built up enough equity to buy their next home outright.

Here’s what you should know about who’s paying cash and what that really means for the market.

Cash buyers tend to fall into a few groups, according to NAR:

Homeowners who sold a house and are using that money to buy their next one

So, it’s not all those big investors social media talks about. That 1st group may include people a lot more like you. Here’s how. According to Cotality, the average homeowner with a mortgage has about $310,000 in equity.

That’s a big deal right now. Many homeowners feel stuck because they don’t want to give up the low mortgage rate they have today. But once they learn they may have enough equity to move and pay cash for their next home, today’s rates don’t matter nearly as much. Because buying in all cash means…

No need to borrow at today’s mortgage rates

No loan approval process, so you may be able to close faster

And even if the equity won’t cover the whole purchase, putting more of it toward the next home means borrowing less. That can mean a smaller monthly payment, too.

But cash buyers like this are more common in some places than others. And how big of a segment of your local market this is, is going to depend on where you live.

For example, Realtor.com data shows cash buyers made up almost 47% of sales in Mississippi and 46% in Montana earlier this year (see map below).

According to Realtor.com, the states with the most cash buyers reflect “a mix of affordability, wealth and buyer demographics.” Think places with lower home prices, or lots of retirees and 2nd-home buyers.

So, depending on where you live, you may see a lot more (or a lot fewer) cash buyers than the national number suggests. An agent who knows your area can tell you who’s actually buying near you.

And if all of this has you thinking everyone’s paying cash, they’re not. If you’re planning to buy and need a mortgage, you’re actually in the majority.

Based on NAR’s numbers, nearly 3 out of 4 home purchases still involve financing. And for homes priced between $200,000 and $750,000, only about 1 in 5 sold for cash, according to Realtor.com (see graph below):

That means most people buying in that price range are financing their purchase, too. So, there’s no need to assume you’re at a disadvantage just because you’re using a loan.

So, what does all this mean for you? Maybe more than you think.

If you already own a house, you may have enough equity to make your next move more affordable than you realize. And if you’re buying with a mortgage, remember, you’re in good company. Most buyers are financing their purchases, too.

The takeaway? Don’t make assumptions about what’s possible based on how other people are buying homes. What really matters is your equity, your budget, and what’s happening in your local market.

#5659. Tax-Assessed Value vs. Market Value: What’s the Difference?

Home prices aren’t set in stone. A property’s value can shift depending on who’s doing the calculation—and why. That’s why you’ll often hear two different numbers thrown around during a home sale: assessed value and market value.

So what’s the difference between tax-assessed value versus market value? And how should buyers and sellers use each when negotiating a home sale?

The technical definition of market value is "the most probable price that a given property will bring in an open market transaction," says Casey Fleming, a former real estate appraiser and author of “The Loan Guide: How To Get the Best Possible Mortgage.”

Put simply, “It’s the price that a buyer is willing to pay for a home, and that a seller is willing to accept.”

Real estate agents are trained to pinpoint a home's value in the real estate market, which is done by looking at a variety of factors, including the following:

External characteristics like curb appeal, exterior condition of the home, lot size, home style, and availability of public utilities.

Internal characteristics like the size and number of rooms, construction and appliance quality and condition, heating systems, and energy efficiency.

Comps, or comparable homes in the same area that have sold recently.

Supply and demand, or the number of buyers and the number of sellers in your area.

Location and desirability of the neighborhood.

A home's market value is often a good starting point for determining all kinds of concerns that homebuyers might have.

For one, listing agents use this value to help sellers come up with a fair asking price for their home. And, since buyers shouldn't just trust what sellers say their place is worth, their own agents can also determine the home's approximate value and come up with a different price that they think their clients should offer.

No number is right or wrong. The ultimate deciding factor is what price a buyer and seller determine they are willing to shake hands on to close the deal.

Assessed value is calculated by your local government—usually a county tax assessor—to determine your property tax liability.

To assess a home’s taxable value, assessors consider the following:

Recent sales of similar homes in the area.

The home’s condition and any recent improvements.

Potential income the property could generate (e.g., from rentals).

Replacement cost in case of damage (e.g., from fire or natural disaster).

Once this value is established, the assessor may subtract any tax exemptions (like a homestead exemption) and multiply the remaining amount by the local assessment ratio—a uniform percentage that each tax jurisdiction sets (typically 80% to 90%), to arrive at the taxable value of your property.

For example: If your home has a market value of $500,000 and your local assessment ratio is 80%, your taxable value would be $400,000. That number is then used to calculate your annual property tax bill.

To determine your home's assessed value, you can contacting your local tax assessor or use the Realtor.com® property tax tool, which allows homeowners to compare their assessed value to similar homes. It even pulls comparable properties that homeowners can use as evidence if they choose to appeal their property taxes.

Some states, like Oregon, prohibit the assessment from being increased by more than 3% a year, “even if the market value goes up more,” says Nathan Miller, founder of Rentec Direct, a software company that educates property managers and landlords.

That means your home’s taxable value might lag behind its market value, especially in hot real estate markets.

Don't be upset as a property owner if your assessment is calculated at a lower amount than you'd figured. It doesn't mean your property value is less. In fact, this could be great news for you.

Assessed value is used mostly for property tax purposes. A lower assessment means a lower tax bill—that's all. Homebuyers and home sellers, on the other hand, look more to marketplace value than to property tax data.

However, assessed value can come up when you buy or sell a home, because this number, unlike the loosey-goosey market value, is public knowledge contained in property records. So, rising assessed values bode well when home sellers try to justify their sales price to a buyer: “Hey, the assessed value is $310,000, and I’m only asking $320,000.”

Likewise, buyers can use assessed value to justify a lower price: "Hey, the assessed value is $260,000, and you're asking for $300,000. What gives?"

However, negotiating based on assessed value is highly unlikely in today's inventory-constrained market. Even though home prices have cooled after record appreciation in the early 2020s, there is still steep competition for homes, pushing the market value well out of range of assessed values.

At the end of the day, the price of a home is the amount at which a seller is willing to sell, and a buyer is ready to buy. The only number that matters is the price that a buyer and a seller agree on.

Lisa Kaplan Gordon is an award-winning writer who's covered real estate and home improvement for realtor.com, Yahoo, AOL, and many others.

#5658. Don't Let the Fear of a Buyer Backing Out Scare You Away from Selling

There’s nothing quite like the excitement of getting an offer on your house. You’re one step closer to moving on to what’s next. But what happens if that buyer backs out or ghosts you before closing?

If you’ve been seeing headlines about more home sales falling through lately, that possibility may be keeping you up at night. And it’s true. According to Redfin and Cotality, canceled contracts have been on the rise.

But here’s what those headlines don’t always tell you…

Most sales still go through. Only 10-15% hit this snag. And even so, there are things you can do to help keep your sale from becoming one of them.

The key is knowing what tends to scare buyers away and getting ahead of those issues before they have a chance to derail your move.

Today’s buyers are being more cautious. Mortgage rates are stretching budgets, and with more homes to choose from, buyers have more freedom to walk away if something doesn’t feel right. As Redfin explains:

“That gives house hunters more options and makes them more likely to walk away if an inspection uncovers problems, an appraisal comes in low or the seller doesn’t agree to concessions.”

That’s why an accepted offer isn’t always a guaranteed sale. But it doesn’t mean you should be afraid to put your house on the market, either.

It just means getting ahead of potential problems matters more than ever.

A Redfin survey asked real estate agents why some buyers are backing out. And their answers give you a short of cheatsheet into what could go sideways and how you can get ahead of those headaches (see graph below):

This is the big one. And the good news? It’s also one of the areas where you can be the most proactive.

One simple way to head this off is by getting a pre-listing inspection before your house goes on the market. That way, if something needs attention, you can decide whether to fix it upfront (before you sell), adjust your price, or disclose it and come in already prepared for what’s likely to pop up in negotiations. It’s a lot better to find the skeletons in the closet before a buyer does.

Even buyers who are pre-approved can run into financing issues before closing. And with mortgage rates putting extra pressure on affordability, some buyers are finding it harder to make the numbers work.

While you can’t control whether a buyer’s loan goes through, you can work with your agent to look closely at their financing before accepting an offer. And if affordability is the concern, your agent can help you explore whether incentives like closing cost credits or a mortgage-rate buydown could make a difference.

Sometimes, your buyer needs to sell their house before they can buy yours. And if their sale falls through, yours could be affected too.

That’s why it’s important to understand any home-sale contingencies before accepting an offer. Your agent can help you look at where the buyer is in their own selling process and what protections you may want in place.

The goal isn’t to eliminate every possible risk. It’s to avoid being caught off guard by the ones you can plan for.

Just remember when you read headlines about canceled deals, they don’t give you the full picture. Most home sales still make it to closing.

And if a sale does fall through, that doesn’t automatically mean your house won’t sell. Sometimes a buyer’s circumstances change. Sometimes an issue comes up that can be addressed before the next offer.

What matters is having an agent who knows how to spot potential problems early, help you navigate negotiations, and keep your sale moving forward.

Because while you can’t control every twist and turn, you can control how prepared you are.

There's no need to let the fear of a buyer backing out hold you back. #5657. Credit Scoring Is Changing: 3 Things Homebuyers Should Know

Quick, what credit score do you need to buy a home? If a number pops into your head, there’s a pretty good chance it’s wrong. And the right answer is getting harder to pin down, because the way credit scores are determined and delivered is changing – for the better.

Here’s what you need to know in today’s changing credit climate.

Fannie Mae has been tracking consumer perceptions about mortgage requirements since 2015 and found that consumers consistently overestimated the minimum credit score lenders required to qualify for a mortgage. As recently as 2023, the average guess was 652.

In reality, the long-standing benchmark for loans backed by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac is lower, at 620, and today even that isn’t a hard rule for every mortgage they back.

Like the Fannie Mae research, a recent survey from Veterans United found consumers continue to overestimate what it takes to qualify for a home loan:

The takeaway? Guessing wrong can cost you.

A renter who assumes their score is too low and they can’t qualify for a mortgage may never take steps to find out for sure.

For decades, the mortgage industry relied on one set of scores – Classic FICO. Thanks to a push to promote competition, make credit scoring more inclusive, and help more Americans become homeowners, the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA) has approved the use of new credit score models such as FICO 10T and VantageScore 4.0.

A different model can mean a different number for the same person. VantageScore says its model can score about 33 million adults that the Classic FICO’s model can’t. So the score you saw on an app last month may not be the one your lender pulls.

Remember: the models may be new, but the basics haven’t changed.

Your credit score is important – no matter how it’s measured. Following the same basic rules will benefit your profile in the old and new score models:

Because while credit models may change, the general advice for you to improve your score doesn’t. Financial awareness and consistency mixed with a little willpower can go a long way.

Don't make credit or homebuying decisions from a chart, an app, or a friend's advice. With the rules shifting and so many misconceptions out there, it's never too early to talk to a professional loan officer for advice on credit, budgeting, and what it would take to qualify for a mortgage.You may be closer to owning a home than you think.

#5656. California Candidates for Governor Offer Different Visions on Housing

The midterm elections are now just hours away, and California voters prepare to head to the polls to elect their next governor, with the state's housing shortage taking center stage.

The contest is among the highest-profile of the 36 gubernatorial races taking place across the U.S. this cycle.

Former Secretary of Health and Human Services Xavier Becerra, a Democrat, and Fox News contributor Steve Hilton, a Republican, are the front-runners vying to replace termed-out California Gov. Gavin Newsom.

The Golden State's 41st governor will inherit an acute housing affordability crisis alongside a roster of state-specific challenges: a controversial billionaire tax proposal, persistent homelessness, an insurance market undermined by wildfire risk, and escalating policy battles surrounding artificial intelligence.

Everyday Californians' purchasing power continues to be severely squeezed by scarce buildable land, restrictive zoning rules, and slow permitting pace holding back new construction, exacerbated by high inflation and mortgage rates exceeding 7%.

On this year's Realtor.com® State-by-State Housing Report Card, part of the Let America Build campaign, California was among six states to earn an F grade due to its disastrous housing affordability score.

Local voter frustration is evident: A new survey by the Public Policy Institute of California found that roughly 6 out of 10 participants say the state is headed in the wrong direction.

Becerra, 68, is heavily favored to win the governor's seat in the largely Democratic state, leading his GOP opponent by 27 points in the latest UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies poll.

If elected governor, Becerra pledges to declare a housing-shortage state of emergency on his first day in office and appoint senior staff across state agencies to tackle the crisis.

His agenda also includes implementing "shot clocks" to clearly communicate permit wait times to developers, overhauling and lowering impact fees statewide, standardizing and streamlining reviews for modular construction, and simplifying affordable housing financing.

"California should be a place where the carpenter who builds a home can afford to buy one," he said in a speech this summer.

According to a new Realtor.com analysis of the latest available housing and American Community Survey data, the typical household in California earns 49% less than the income needed to finance a median-priced home—a shortfall of $98,292—making it the second-most unaffordable state in the nation behind Montana.

Becerra has voiced support for building "missing-middle" multifamily housing, especially near transit hubs, and expanding first-time homebuyer down payment assistance programs to put homeownership within reach of more renters.

On the issue of homelessness and homeless encampments, which has become a lightning rod for political candidates in California this election cycle, Becerra is laser-focused on prevention.

At an event in the East Bay last week, Becerra argued that keeping at-risk people housed after a medical emergency or a sudden job loss is far less costly to the state than rehousing them from the street, reported ABC 7 News (KGO).

"We have to do everything we can to prevent them from falling into homelessness," Becerra said.

His strategy includes bolstering tenant protections, expanding funding to organizations that have proven effective in addressing the homelessness crisis, and holding accountable those that have failed to act.

Hilton, 57, the Donald Trump–endorsed GOP hopeful for governor, has been aggressively pushing for the clearing of homeless encampments, vowing to rid the state of every single one by Dec. 31, 2027.

Like his Democratic rival, Hilton has highlighted the need to cut through red tape constraining residential construction. However, his approach hinges on capping fees, permits, and regulation costs at $50,000 per new home to make it cheaper for developers to build.

"We have to get rid of the regulations that make it two or three times as expensive to build the exact same home in California as in neighboring states," said Hilton during a televised debate in May.

His housing platform also includes using over a million vacant lots to build starter homes and creating 10 new municipalities across California to expand housing supply instead of trying to shoehorn multifamily developments into single-family communities.

“We have to stop trying to force housing into suburban neighborhoods where people don't want it," he proclaimed during the debate.

Despite their contrasting platforms, Hilton and Becerra are united in their fierce opposition to the California Billionaire Tax, officially known as Proposition 40, which Newsom had unsuccessfully tried to keep off the ballot.

Championed by a coalition of labor unions, the measure would impose a one-time tax of up to 5% on the worldwide assets of more than 200 Californians with a net worth of at least $1 billion who resided in the state as of Jan. 1, 2026.

Opponents of the initiative across the political spectrum have warned that it will accelerate an exodus of high net worth residents and tech innovators from California, diminishing the state's tax base.

Speaking on "The Steve Hilton Show" in January, Hilton criticized Proposition 40 as the epitome of what he called the "stupidity and the failure of 16 years of one-party rule" in California that, if adopted, will "drive business out of state."

For his part, Becerra dismissed the proposal as a "sketchy policy" and instead threw his support behind an alternative measure that would extend temporary tax rate increases on the ultrawealthy to reliably fund healthcare and public schools.

Voting has been underway in California since early October, and hundreds of thousands of mail-in ballots have been processed ahead of Nov. 3.

#5654. The Home Insurance Move That Could Save You $440 a Year

When you’re planning a move, every monthly cost counts. That’s why it can be frustrating to see home insurance keep creeping up. According to Intercontinental Exchange, it now makes up 9.6% of the average monthly mortgage payment.

But the latest numbers show some progress on that front – as the increases start to slow down. Here’s what you need to know and what you can do about it.

A look at the past two years shows how much things have cooled down. In mid-2024, home insurance premiums rose 4.3% in a single quarter. By the second quarter of this year, that was down to 1.8%. That’s the smallest quarterly growth in almost 3 years – and that’s a good thing (see graph below):

As Andy Walden, Head of Mortgage and Housing Market Research at Intercontinental Exchange, explains:

“Property insurance has been a fast-growing component of the monthly mortgage payment, but this quarter’s data shows the pace of increase is finally slowing.”

While your premium will likely still go up over time, it may not climb as quickly as it did a couple of years ago. And that’s, at the very least, a step in the right direction.

Here’s where you have some say in what you pay. Let’s take current homeowners as an example. Intercontinental Exchange found that when homeowners shopped around and switched insurance companies, their premiums went down 6.6% on average. Those who stayed with their current company saw an increase of 10.4% (see graph below):

Think about that. That’s a big difference and it goes to show that looking for a new provider can literally pay off.

That works out to about $440 a year in savings for the people who switched. And they didn’t have to give up coverage to get it. Their deductibles dipped 1.4%, and their coverage limits actually rose 7.3%.

While this example is current homeowners, the same general idea applies for first-time buyers too. Shop around and get multiple quotes before you pick your insurance provider. Then, once you’re settled in, review your policy each year when it comes up for renewal. You’re not locked into the first price you get.

The home itself plays a role as well. According to John Burns Research and Consulting (JBREC), newly built homes are 10% to 15% less expensive to insure than older ones nationally.

And while a brand-new home won’t necessarily be the right fit for every buyer, if you’re open to one, it could be one more way to keep your monthly insurance costs down.

Home insurance is certainly a bigger part of the monthly costs than it used to be, and that can feel like just one more thing to juggle when you’re buying a home or moving. But knowing you have ways to keep it in check can take some of the pressure off. Compare a few options before you buy, revisit your policy each year, and lean on trusted local professionals as you plan for your next move.

#5653. Miami Cash4Keys Execs Accused of Stealing Vulnerable Senior’s Home in Brazen Scheme

A Florida man's $300,000 home was allegedly stolen in a real estate scheme dubbed “Operation Dirty Deed,” which investigators say involved fraudulent documents and the exploitation of the homeowner's dementia.

The case took a disturbing turn when the 71-year-old man, identified in court records as Thomas P. Hegarty, was allegedly kidnapped from his longtime Hollywood home and discarded at a "dilapidated rooming house" several miles away, according to the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office.

Now, two executives for Cash4Keys, a South Florida real estate investment company, each face six criminal charges in connection with the alleged plot. A notary and real estate agent also face charges in connection with the alleged scheme.

“His home was taken from him,” Hollywood Police Department Detective Theo Defreze said at a news conference last week. “He lost all of his possessions―belongings, cars. I mean, he lost everything."

Investigators allege that Brandon Lee Miguel and Jordy Luis Perez obtained Hegarty's signature on a power of attorney document and a warranty deed, which were then used to transfer ownership of the property to their company, Cash4Keys.

Monica Elizabeth Castelli, 56, a real estate agent with United Realty Group, is accused of kidnapping Hegarty, while Derek Enrique, 43, allegedly notarized the documents used in the transfer.

Hegarty’s property on Mayo Street was valued at approximately $300,000 but was allegedly transferred to the company for just $191,000.

Broward County property appraiser Marty Kiar said at the news conference that there is no evidence Hegarty received any of the money and that the suspects used the man's severe case of dementia to take advantage of him and take over his home.

The investigation was launched after Hegarty's family raised concerns about his declining health and became suspicious about the recent transfer of his home.

His sister-in-law, Peggy Hegarty, who was contacted by the rooming house where he had allegedly been taken, told CBS News that he believed he was signing paperwork to refinance his home, not sell it.

“It's shocking. Absolutely shocking," she said.

When she traveled from her home in Georgia to Florida after learning what had happened, she found Hegarty depressed, in shock, and not eating, according to the report. He is now living in an assisted-living facility in Jacksonville.

“Investigators allege that due to documented dementia and significant cognitive impairment, the victim was incapable of understanding the documents he was signing and appreciating their consequences,” the Broward County Property Appraiser's Office said in the news release.

After the alleged transfer, Miguel and Perez arranged for Castelli, of Margate, to remove Hegarty from his home, authorities said.

Castelli allegedly drove Hegarty to a “dilapidated rooming house” in Miami Gardens and left him there, according to investigators. Hegarty was distraught and crying, which then led to Castelli driving him to Memorial Regional Hospital in Hollywood.

Once Hegarty was gone from his house, Miguel and Perez allegedly went inside and removed his personal belongings, including three vehicles, according to the property appraiser's office.

Miguel and Perez each face six charges, including organized scheme to defraud $50,000 or more, grand theft exceeding $100,000, unlawful filing of false documents affecting real property, mortgage fraud, exploitation of an elderly person, and money laundering.

Castelli faces charges of kidnapping with intent to facilitate the commission of a felony and exploitation of an elderly person. Enrique faces one count of false or fraudulent acknowledgments.

Kiar said Cash4Keys still controls the property, but added that Hegarty's family has hired an attorney in an effort to get the home back.

Investigators believe the scheme could extend beyond Hegarty’s home, suspecting there may be additional victims and properties involved.

Realtor.com reached out to Cash4Keys South Florida for comment but did not receive an immediate response.

The case has also prompted warnings from local officials about the vulnerability of older homeowners to real estate fraud.

Kiar urged South Florida residents with elderly relatives to monitor their family members' finances and consider enrolling in the free Owner Alert program, which notifies property owners when a deed transaction occurs.

“It’s very upsetting, very sad, and what really bothers me is the person they picked on was about as vulnerable as they come and that really is what makes this case a case that’s very sad,” Kiar said. “I’m very glad that people have been arrested, and they will have their day in court.”

Greensboro has already surpassed 40% of its “Road to 10,000” housing goal, with 4,071 homes completed or under construction roughly 18 months after the initiative launched. City leaders say the program is ahead of schedule toward its goal of adding 10,000 housing units by 2030, an effort that has taken on greater importance as major employers expand across the region.

The housing need extends well beyond the initiative. Greensboro officials estimate the city will require at least 33,000 additional housing units to serve current and future residents across a range of incomes and housing types.

That demand outlook is being reinforced by large employment investments, including Toyota Battery Manufacturing NC, JetZero, and Boom Supersonic. JetZero alone has broken ground on a campus at Piedmont Triad International Airport and plans a $4.7 billion investment that could eventually create up to 14,500 jobs by 2037.

The near-term sales backdrop offers another encouraging signal. As of August, the broader Greensboro market recorded 1,344 new-home sales over the prior 12 months, up 24.9% year over year. Attached sales were especially strong, rising 67.8% to 515, compared with a 7.8% increase in detached sales to 829.

The stronger sales picture comes despite a slower labor market. Greensboro’s non-farm employment increased just 0.6% year over year in July, representing an addition of 1,000 jobs. While still positive, that pace has moderated from earlier periods. The metro’s unemployment rate stood at 3.8%, and Zonda forecasts annual employment growth of 0.6% for 2026 before improving to 0.9% in both 2027 and 2028.

Greensboro is adding housing fast, attached product is contributing meaningfully to sales growth, and major economic development projects could support future household formation. Yet slower near-term job growth and increasing lot and finished inventory reinforce the need for disciplined product selection, pricing, and submarket strategy.
