#5650. Immigration Slowdown To Sharply Reduce Renter Household Growth, Study Says

The clampdown on immigration has slowed the nation's population growth. Now, Harvard estimates it is also slowing the formation of new households in the United States.

Harvard's Joint Center for Housing Studies estimates that immigration policy means 500,000 fewer households formed in the country each year from 2024 to 2027. Those 2 million households are mainly renters, but over time become homebuyers, Harvard said.

President Donald Trump's immigration crackdown has broad implications for the national housing market. People coming into the country on work and student visas are a major contributor to rental demand. Homebuilders rely on a significant immigrant workforce, and crackdowns have contributed to worsening builder sentiment.

Harvard researcher Daniel McCue said this marks a sharp turn from the 571,000 net new-renter households formed by immigrants who entered the country from 2022 to 2024 under President Joe Biden. At least one Fed study indicated illegal immigration may have driven up housing costs during the Biden administration.

Instead, McCue projected immigrants would account for just 132,000 new household formations by 2027.

This is based on the U.S. Census Bureau's most recent housing vacancy survey, which showed a marked increase in rental vacancy and a slowdown in new household formation overall. The national rental vacancy rate bumped from 7.1% in the third quarter of 2025 to 7.6% in the same time this year.

"This may be a sign that the sharp curtailment of immigration has begun to lower demand for rental units in a significant way," McCue said.

Jiayi Xu, senior economist at Realtor.com®, says such a slowdown could spell trouble for the housing market over the long term.

"A significant slowdown in immigration growth would cause household growth to slow over the next decade, dragging down economic growth in the long term," Xu says.

Eric Finnigan, vice president of demographics research for John Burns Research and Consulting, says the shifting immigration policies of Biden and Trump have led to disruptions in the housing market. Immigration has been a central pillar of the nation's population growth, and falling birthrates haven't kept up.

"We knew at the beginning of the decade, given our demographic trends, that immigration would be important to economic growth," Finnigan says. "That includes housing demand, labor supply, and homebuyers and renters. We didn't plan for this sharp surge in immigration nor a sharp decline."

In the past, immigrant populations have been an important contributor to the housing market. Students and workers on visas routinely generate demand for new rental properties. In time, some of those renters eventually become buyers. But, Finnigan says, the whiplash of the policies of recent years could chill demand at a time when the housing market is seeing fewer buyers.

"The rules about their own visa could change overnight without any warning," Finnigan adds. "The last thing they want to do is plunk down a down payment on a home or be on the hook for an asset they want to leave at some point. They don't want to be with an asset they might have to leave without warning."

Tristan Navera is a senior reporter on housing policy, covering trends and solutions in the housing market from Washington, DC. He was previously a senior reporter at Bloomberg Law, and before that covered real estate for the Washington Business Journal. Earlier in his career, he spent a decade reporting on business and real estate in Dayton and Columbus, OH. A Cincinnati native, he holds a journalism degree from Ohio University.

#5648. Higher Rates, Affordability Pressure D.R. Horton Orders and Closings

Rising mortgage rates and persistent affordability constraints weighed on D.R. Horton’s home sales during its fiscal fourth quarter, contributing to year-over-year declines in both closings and new orders.

The Arlington, Texas-based builder closed 22,915 homes during the quarter, down 2% from the prior year period. Home sales revenue declined 2% to $8.4 billion.

Net sales orders fell 7% to 18,619 homes, with the value of those orders declining 9% to $6.6 billion. The cancellation rate was 23%, compared with 20% a year earlier.

On the earnings call, D.R. Horton reported an average sales price on net orders of approximately $357,000, down 2% both sequentially and year over year.

“Housing market conditions became more challenging during the fourth quarter as rising mortgage rates, affordability constraints, and cautious consumer sentiment continued to pressure new-home demand,” executive chairman David Auld said.

Home sales gross margin was 19.5% in the quarter, down 120 basis points sequentially. Management attributed 80 basis points of the sequential decline to above-normal litigation costs.

Home building pre-tax income declined 11% to $891 million, while its pre-tax profit margin was 10.6%. Auld said incentives are expected to remain an important affordability tool heading into the new fiscal year.

“We expect incentives to remain elevated in fiscal 2027, the extent of which will depend on market conditions throughout the year,” he said.

D.R. Horton also pulled back sharply on starts as it worked to align inventory with the slower sales environment. The builder started approximately 13,100 homes during the September quarter, down 45% sequentially, according to the earnings call.

The builder ended Sept. 30 with approximately 28,200 homes in inventory, including 17,700 unsold homes. Of those unsold homes, 8,800 were completed.

Despite the challenging end to the year, D.R. Horton closed 84,202 homes during fiscal 2026, generating $30.6 billion in home sales revenue. Consolidated revenue for the full year totaled $33 billion, with net income attributable to the company of $2.9 billion, or $10.11 per diluted share.

D.R. Horton enters fiscal 2027 expecting affordability constraints and elevated mortgage rates to continue influencing buyer demand.

The company expects to close between 79,000 and 84,000 homes in fiscal 2027 and generate consolidated revenue of approximately $30 billion to $32 billion.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5645. Inside Legacy Hills’ Strategy for Reaching a Broad Range of Buyers

Developed by Centurion American, the Legacy Hills master-planned community (MPC) spans over 3,000 acres in Celina, Texas, and is planned for up to 7,000 homes at full buildout. The community opened in April 2024 and includes a diverse mix of builders, lot sizes, and floor plans. Pricing generally ranges from the $300,000s into the mid-$500,000s.

Importantly, Legacy Hills is not relying on a single buyer profile. Its product strategy creates multiple entry points into the community, with housing choices that can appeal to buyers at different price points and stages of life.

That product diversity is paired with a layered amenity program. Plans call for seven amenity centers throughout Legacy Hills, along with a 27-acre sports park and a 3-mile walking and biking trail. The planned 1876 Country Club adds a destination component with an 18-hole championship golf course, clubhouse, driving range, putting green, and short game facilities.

For families moving to Legacy Hills, children in the broader community attend Celina ISD, while future school sites are planned within the development. The community also broadens its reach further through Del Webb’s dedicated 55+ neighborhood, which adds to Legacy Hills’ family-oriented offerings with age-targeted homes and amenities.

The strategy is unfolding against a strong demographic backdrop. Celina’s population and household base are projected to more than double between 2020 and 2029, expanding the potential pool of buyers around the community.

At the same time, the broader housing environment remains competitive. The Zonda Market Ranking for MPCs characterized Dallas as slightly underperforming per August data, yet Legacy Hills stood out. In the Q2 2026 Master Plan Outlook report, the MPC recorded the largest year-over-year percentage increase in last 12-month sales among qualifying MPCs with at least 200 sales in the previous 12 months.

Legacy Hills illustrates the value of creating several paths into a large-scale community rather than building around a narrow customer profile. Differentiated housing, offerings for multiple life stages, and amenities ranging from everyday recreation to destination experiences give the development multiple ways to appeal to buyers.

The insights in this article were taken from a more in-depth case study in Zonda’s Master Plan Outlook subscription.

#5643. 8 Resilience Moves Builders Can Make Before Extreme Weather Hits

When extreme weather hits, small construction details can make a big difference in how well a home performs.

According to Fred Malik of the Insurance Institute for Business & Home Safety (IBHS), research continually points to roofs, openings, and structural connections as potential failure points. Damage in these areas can allow wind and water into a home and trigger larger, cascading losses.

For builders, stronger construction can also help reduce disruption for homeowners, limit warranty-related costs, and protect a company’s reputation for delivering durable homes.

“Resilient, durable buildings are usually the result of making several intentional decisions,” Malik says.

Here are eight steps builders can take to improve resilience ahead of severe weather:

Rather than approaching roofing as a collection of individual products, Malik recommends treating the entire roof as one interconnected system. The goal is to keep the roof intact and prevent an initial failure from creating a pathway for additional wind or water damage.

A sealed roof deck creates an additional layer of protection beneath the primary roof covering. If shingles or other roofing materials are damaged or blown off during severe weather, this secondary layer can help limit water intrusion into the home.

Small details can have an outsized impact on performance. Builders should carefully install and inspect flashing at roof edges, roof-to-wall transitions, vents, chimneys, and other penetrations. These areas can become pathways for water if they aren’t properly protected.

Windows, entry doors, and other openings need to withstand both wind pressure and wind-driven rain. Following manufacturer installation instructions and properly installing flashing are critical to maintaining the home’s building envelope.

Garage doors represent a large opening in the building envelope and need to withstand pressures generated by high winds. Malik notes that this is important even in inland markets, where tornadoes can cause significant structural damage.

In areas exposed to more severe winds, builders should consider a professionally designed continuous load path connecting the roof to the walls and ultimately the foundation. Strong connections throughout the structure help transfer wind forces safely through the building instead of allowing individual components to fail.

In flood-prone areas, elevate or otherwise protect mechanical, electrical, and utility equipment. Keeping critical systems above anticipated flood levels can reduce damage and make it easier for homeowners to return to their homes after an event.

Programs such as IBHS’ FORTIFIED standards provide builders with a framework for putting resilience measures into practice. FORTIFIED goes beyond minimum code requirements with an emphasis on keeping the roof on, keeping water out, and tying the structure together.

The program also requires third-party documentation of critical resilience measures, including construction details that may no longer be visible once finishes and other materials are installed.

Overall, resilience isn’t dependent on a single product or construction technique. It’s the cumulative result of getting multiple details right, Malik says.

Leah Draffen is a senior editor at Builder. She earned a B.A. in journalism and minors in business administration and sociology from Louisiana State University.

#5642. Jupiter's Q3 Staking Rewards For All Wallets Opens Today, See Who Clears the 50 JUP Bar

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

50 JUP sounds like a threshold almost anyone can meet. It isn't, and today is when many stakers will find that out.

Jupiter's Active Staking Rewards (ASR) for July to September 2026 are now open to every wallet. That means a 50 million JUP pool can be claimed by anyone who qualified. The problem is that "qualified" doesn't mean what most people think. The rule isn't "have 50 JUP staked." It's "average 50 JUP across the whole quarter." Running the numbers this morning and a lot of wallets that look eligible at a glance aren't.

The round started quietly. According to the official Q3 campaign page, the campaign ran from July 1 until earning closed on September 30, and claims opened on October 12. That first week was reserved for Jupiter's own apps. Early access was limited to Jupiter Wallet and the Jupiter Mobile app, and other wallets can claim from 20 October 2026.

So if you stake from Phantom, Solflare, Backpack or a hardware wallet, today is your first real opportunity. Jupiter's documentation explains why the wallet matters. Rewards are linked to the wallet you staked from. If that wallet lives in another app, you either wait for the general opening or import the same recovery phrase into Jupiter Wallet or Jupiter Mobile.

There's no rush to the finish line yet. Reports put the claim deadline at January 12, 2027. Still, I wouldn't leave it to the holidays.

The campaign page states the rules plainly. 50M JUP will be distributed to stakers this period, ASR is calculated on a time-weighted average of your stake, and an average of 50 JUP or more staked during the quarter qualifies.

The words that matter are "time-weighted average." A wallet that held 50 JUP for all 92 days of Q3 averages exactly 50. A wallet that held 500 JUP for only a few days might average less than that. Jupiter designed it this way on purpose. The 7-day unstaking cooldown stops users from staking briefly around distribution periods to collect rewards without sustained participation.

One more detail surprised me, given the program's name. Voting has no effect on ASR, and you do not need to vote to be eligible. The "Active" in Active Staking Rewards now refers to keeping tokens staked, not to governance turnout.

Here's the simple math. It assumes the average is weighted day by day across the 92 days from July 1 to September 30. Jupiter hasn't published its exact snapshot schedule, so treat these figures as close estimates, not guarantees.

The edge cases are where people get caught. Suppose a wallet held 60 JUP from July 1 but started unstaking at the end of August. Its average comes to only about 40 JUP, so it misses. Another wallet held 40 JUP all quarter and added 30 more on September 1. It ends up at roughly 49.8 JUP, just under the line. Adding 31 instead of 30 would have qualified it.

The simplest check is to connect your wallet at Jupiter Rewards. The page will show the amount of ASR you're eligible to claim. If it shows nothing for an older address, the time-weighting is the most likely reason.

Now for the payout. As of mid-October 2026, total staked JUP topped 1.1 billion tokens, roughly 33% of circulating supply, spread across more than 357,000 wallets.

If you divide 50 million JUP by about 1.1 billion staked, you get roughly 4.5% for the quarter. A wallet that just clears the 50 JUP average would receive about 2.3 JUP. An average of 1,000 JUP works out to about 45, and 10,000 to around 455. The quarter's average total stake may have been a bit below the October figure, so actual allocations could come in slightly higher. Your campaign page shows the real number.

Don't expect the tokens to show up as spendable JUP. ASR is paid in JUP and added to your staked balance, which increases your governance power over time.

Three problems come up again and again in Jupiter's support notes:

Squads multisig users have a more manual process. The ASR documentation covers it in detail, including checking that the claim uses the Jupiter Merkle Distributor program, DiS3nNjFVMieMgmiQFm6wgJL7nevk4NrhXKLbtEH1Z2R before you approve anything.

Missing the deadline has real consequences. According to the Jupiter DAO portal, unclaimed ASR goes back to the community treasury once the claim period ends. Jupiter also says that no transfer is made on your behalf after the support deadline.

The bigger picture is a pool that's getting more crowded. Every quarter, 50M JUP goes to eligible stakers, and that figure doesn't change. With staked JUP now above 1.1 billion, each new staker gets a smaller slice of the same pie.

ASR is also the main reward Jupiter is still paying out. The Jupiter DAO voted in February 2026 to postpone Jupuary and send its 700 million JUP back to a community multisig. That leaves this quarterly distribution as the core reason to keep JUP staked.

My advice is to claim this round now and then look ahead. The October to December period is already more than halfway through. The same math applies, and each week you wait raises how much JUP you need to reach a 50 JUP average.

#5640. Why Waiting for Rates to Fall Can Create Other Affordability Problems

Mortgage rates are giving homebuyers another reason to hesitate.

The average rate for a 30-year fixed mortgage reached well over 7% in October, its highest level in 13 months, according to Freddie Mac. That followed a climb from 5.98% in late February to 6.65% by Aug. 20, figures cited in a recent U.S. Bank housing-market analysis.

For a buyer, even a small rate change can alter the monthly payment considerably. Waiting for lower borrowing costs can therefore be a reasonable decision, particularly when today’s payment would leave little room for maintenance, insurance or other expenses.

However, a lower future rate does not guarantee a cheaper home purchase.

“If rates fall enough to bring more buyers back, the benefit can be partly absorbed by stronger competition,” says Jeremy Olsher, a real estate professional and Principal at Mizner Residential Group. “A buyer might secure a better rate but pay more for the property, face multiple offers or have less negotiating room.”

Additionally, lowering rates can be a sign of economic instability, including perhaps a significant response to mass unemployment and rampant inflation. While that might make homeownership more alluring, families could feel the strain in other ways, from job loss to rising grocery bills to big losses in their retirement portfolios.

Olsher recommends considering three factors before making lower rates the sole condition for buying.

Can the payment work today? Buyers should calculate the full monthly cost under current conditions, including principal, interest, property taxes, insurance, association fees and a realistic maintenance allowance. If that total is uncomfortable, the buyer may need to wait, reduce the price range or reconsider the type of property. The calculation should work without assuming that refinancing will become available later.

“Refinancing can be an option if rates eventually fall, but it should not be the reason someone accepts an unaffordable payment today,” Olsher says. “The purchase needs to stand on its own using the numbers the buyer can actually secure.”

How long does the buyer expect to stay? Transaction costs matter more when a buyer may move again within a few years. Closing costs, maintenance and future selling expenses can make a short ownership period difficult to justify, even if the mortgage payment appears manageable.

A buyer expecting to remain for several years has more time to spread those costs and absorb short-term changes in value. Someone with uncertain employment, family or relocation plans may benefit from the flexibility of renting.

Olsher says the right question is not simply whether ownership costs more than rent this month. Buyers should consider how long they expect to remain, what flexibility they need and how much cash the purchase would leave available afterward.

What does waiting cost? Delaying a purchase is not automatically costly. In some markets, renting may remain the more practical and affordable choice. Realtor.com®’s 2026 midyear forecast projected rents would decline 1.2% during the year, potentially benefiting renters in many areas.

Still, waiting can carry personal and financial costs. A household may need to renew a lease, pay moving or storage expenses, remain in an unsuitable space or postpone a relocation. The selection of available homes can also change before rates do.

“The cost of waiting is different for every buyer,” Olsher says. “For one person, another year of renting is perfectly sensible. For another, it means paying for a home that no longer fits their family while hoping the market delivers a better combination of rate, price and inventory.”

Trying to identify the perfect week to purchase gives one unpredictable number too much control over a long-term decision. Buyers can make a more grounded choice by comparing today’s full payment, the expected ownership period, available homes and the real cost of remaining where they are.

Buyers should commit when they are financially ready. If they find a home that fits their budget today, buying lets them lock in the house before prices climb further. If mortgage rates drop significantly in the future, they can refinance their loan to a lower rate without having to compete against a massive wave of new buyers.

Michael Catarevas is a senior editor for RISMedia.

#5639. Wall Street’s AI Sell-Off Exposes a Weak Spot in the Bank of Mom and Dad

As more adult children count on the Bank of Mom and Dad to help them buy homes, Mom and Dad, in turn, may be counting on Wall Street.

That arrangement looked a little less secure on Friday, when fears about the cost of the artificial intelligence boom sent stocks tumbling.

The Nasdaq lost 2.9% on Oct. 30, its worst day since June, as investors grew worried about the billions of dollars companies are spending on AI. Intel shares plunged 28.6%, while chipmakers AMD and Nvidia fell 10.9% and 4.2%, respectively, according to Reuters.

The consequences could reach well beyond Wall Street and Silicon Valley. Baby boomers held approximately $35.2 trillion in stocks and mutual funds as of the second quarter of 2026, or roughly 55% of the household total, according to Federal Reserve data analyzed by Yardeni Research.

And some of that money is already making its way into their children's down payments. Half of parents who had helped or planned to help their children purchase a home reported drawing on investment accounts, according to an April survey by Veterans United Home Loans.

Of course, one bad day won't drain the Bank of Mom and Dad. But if the losses keep piling up, the damage could spill out of parents' portfolios. Research shows that after substantial financial setbacks, parents tend to scale back the money they give their adult children—or stop giving it altogether.

The AI boom has played an enormous role in the stock market's recent run. Since ChatGPT's launch in November 2022, AI-related stocks accounted for roughly 75% of S&P 500 returns, according to a JPMorgan analysis.

And that rally has helped swell the fortunes of a generation already poised to pass down an extraordinary amount of wealth.

Approximately $105 trillion will pass to heirs through 2048, according to estimates from the weath management firm Cerulli Associates—with baby boomers and older generations accounting for the vast majority of the projected transfer.

But some of that money is changing hands much sooner, as parents and grandparents help adult children overcome the financial barriers to homeownership.

Nearly one-quarter of parents surveyed by Veterans United expected to contribute between $50,000 and $99,999 toward their children's home purchases, while 12% anticipated providing between $100,000 and $199,999.

They're shocking sums, and years of rising stock prices may have made those commitments easier to make.

"When their stock portfolios go up, they feel more able to help with a down payment," says Michelle Riehn, a certified financial planner and founder of Money Momma. "People feel richer."

The trouble is that those feelings—and the financial resources behind them—can change when markets fall.

In a 2025 study published in The Review of Economics and Statistics, economists Jessamyn Schaller and Chase Eck examined how financial transfers between parents and adult children changed following setbacks such as wealth losses, job exits, and health problems.

They found that parents sharply reduced financial assistance following losses of wealth and earned income, particularly in households with fewer accumulated assets.

An earlier working-paper version estimated that among lower-wealth households, a major loss of net worth reduced the likelihood of parents making a financial transfer by 6.1 percentage points, or 18.7% relative to the group's baseline rate.

The research examined financial assistance broadly, not just down payments, and didn't isolate stock market losses. Still, the findings have important implications for housing, where financial help from parents can make the difference between buying a home and remaining a renter.

Already, parental transfers account for 13 percentage points, or 27%, of young households' homeownership, according to a 2025 Federal Reserve working paper.

Naturally, the next question for a generation waiting on those transfers is what happens if AI stocks continue to fall.

Friday's slide was far from the end of the AI boom. Despite losing more than $1 trillion in market value that day, technology stocks were still worth trillions, with Nvidia alone valued at roughly $4.9 trillion.

But researchers have examined what a much larger reversal could mean for U.S. households.

In September, Allianz Research modeled the consequences of disappointing AI investments triggering a broader market downturn.

Under its more severe scenario, a 25% decline in the S&P 500 would erase approximately $27 trillion in U.S. household wealth—nearly 14% of total household net worth—and help push the economy into recession.

That's a hypothetical scenario, not a forecast. And even losses of that magnitude wouldn't affect every family's ability to help their children equally.

Financial advisers say much depends on whether parents have already set aside the money they intend to give—or are counting on their investments to cover the gift when the time comes.

"There's a difference between help that was planned and requests that come unplanned," Riehn says.

Parents who have committed to helping their children buy homes often move that money into conservative investments well before the purchase, she explains. Doing so can shield a planned gift from a sudden drop in stock prices.

But when parents haven't prepared, a downturn can force tougher decisions.

"A lot of times they're selling stock to do it, and that's where it gets tricky in a downturn," says Greg Black, a certified financial planner and president of Tencap Wealth Coaching in Utah.

A parent who expected to sell appreciated investments to cover a $100,000 down payment might have to liquidate more shares after a substantial market decline. Rather than lock in those losses, the parent could decide to reduce the gift or postpone it.

"So if the down payment money is sitting in AI stocks and they drop, that gift might have to wait," Black says.

Even parents who could still afford to help may think twice. Riehn says watching a portfolio lose value can make affluent households more reluctant to part with money, particularly when their children make unexpected requests.

David Talley, a certified financial planner with Talley Wealth in Johnson City, TN, offers a counterpoint: Families with sufficient cash reserves and diversified investments should generally be able to maintain gifts that fit within their long-term financial plans.

"With the cash layer in place, the gift doesn't have to wait for a recovery," he says.

But younger homebuyers might not have that flexibility.

Allianz estimated that a 15% market correction could take six to nine months to reverse under one scenario. In its more severe scenario, recovering from a 25% decline could take as long as two years.

That extended timeline points to another potential consequence of an AI bust: Any prolonged downturn could also change what parents expect to leave their children.

In an earlier working-paper version of their research, Schaller and Eck found that a major household wealth loss was associated with roughly a 5-percentage-point decline in parents' reported probability of leaving an inheritance worth at least $100,000.

That finding measures parents' expectations, not the inheritances their children ultimately received. And the consequences of a market correction would depend partly on how much of a family's wealth is tied to the stocks losing value.

"The real exception is a family with a concentrated position in one company whose net worth has doubled in a few years," Talley says. "That genuinely changes what they can give."

And if those gains reverse, so can the amount available to pass down.

Still, Riehn cautions that inheritances operate on a different timeline from down payment gifts. Children expecting to inherit investments decades from now may have time to ride out a market downturn. Those counting on that wealth for a home purchase in the nearer future may not.

The recent AI sell-off is far from a market crash, and there's no evidence it has already disrupted parental gifts or inheritances. Instead, it highlights an uncertainty at the heart of the Great Wealth Transfer: The fortunes younger Americans expect to receive aren't necessarily the fortunes their parents will ultimately leave behind.

And until that money changes hands, the next generation has little control over how much will be there—or when it will arrive.

#5638. Former Landsea Homes President and COO Mike Forsum to Lead New Land Finance Platform

Home building industry veteran Mike Forsum has been tapped to lead a new land finance platform aimed at providing public and private home builders and developers with more flexible capital options.

Wafra, a New York-based global alternative investment manager, and Hunt Cos., a privately held real estate and investment company, have launched Strata Land Partners, with Forsum serving as CEO.

The platform has launched with projects comprising approximately 1,300 single-family lots and is designed to serve as a long-term capital partner for builders navigating land investment and development in an uncertain housing market.

Forsum brings more than 40 years of home building industry experience to the venture. Most recently, he served as president and chief operating officer of Landsea Homes. His experience navigating builders’ operational challenges and investment decisions will help shape Strata’s approach.

“Strata was built by builders, for builders,” Forsum said. “Having spent my career in home building, it is apparent that there is significant demand for a strategic capital partner that understands the industry’s operational nuances and thoughtfully supports builders in achieving their goals.”

He added that the platform’s goal is to “bridge that gap and play our part in building the new homes this country needs.”

Strata enters the market as builders look for ways to manage land exposure and capital requirements. According to the announcement, the platform will focus on tailored financing solutions that allow builders and developers to navigate changing market conditions while advancing residential projects.

Ryan Brenner, managing director and head of alternative real estate at Wafra, said Strata is also intended to help address the nation’s structural housing shortage by giving builders another source of capital to support new-home development.

For Hunt Cos., the partnership combines flexible capital with an operating team experienced in residential development.

“Strata brings together an experienced operating team and flexible capital to address a critical need in residential development,” said Chris Hunt, CEO of Hunt Cos. “We look forward to supporting the platform as it builds lasting relationships with home builders and developers nationwide.”

#5637. Where Health Care Employment Has the Biggest Footprint

Health care is more than a service for residents. It is also an important piece of the employment landscape. Preliminary August data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics shows significant differences in both the number of health care and social assistance jobs across states and the industry’s share of total employment.

In absolute terms, the country’s largest states naturally account for some of the biggest health care workforces. Unsurprisingly, California leads with over 3.18 million health care and social assistance jobs, followed by New York at 1.91 million and Texas at 1.76 million.

However, the health care industry’s share of a state’s total employment base may tell a different and potentially more useful story.

West Virginia stands at the top of the list, with health care and social assistance representing approximately 19.6% of total employment. New York follows at 19.1%, with Pennsylvania at 18.9%. Connecticut, Minnesota, and Massachusetts are also among the states where the industry accounts for a comparatively large share of employment, at roughly 18.1%, 17.9%, and 17.8%, respectively.

At the other end of the spectrum, health care represents just 8.8% of employment in Wyoming, 10.6% in the District of Columbia and Nevada, 10.8% in Alabama, and 11% in South Carolina.

That variation matters because a sizable health care sector can serve as an important economic anchor, providing a meaningful source of jobs that support the broader housing market.

Access to health care might become an increasingly relevant consideration in retirement location decisions. Affordability matters, but so do physician availability, provider access, and the distance residents need to travel for care.

Demographic trends reinforce that dynamic. Per the U.S. Census Bureau, the old-age dependency ratio, which measures the number of adults age 65+ relative to the working-age population, rose from 20.8 in 2010 to 29.7 in 2024, pointing to future pressure on health care systems, retirement programs, and elder care resources.

As the population ages, health care will matter to housing markets from both an economic and demographic perspective. The sector supports local employment, while access to care can influence where older households choose to live.

The insights in this article were taken from more in-depth research reports published in Zonda’s National Outlook subscription.

Maria Barr is a research analyst within Zonda's economics department, where she supports housing market analysis at both the national and market level. She earned a B.A. in economics and English from Middlebury College.

#5636. Why a Long Island Town’s Crackdown on Vacation Rentals May Not Fix Its Housing Crisis

The four-bedroom waterfront home on Long Island's North Fork hadn't even hit the market when Diane Mollica's colleagues began imagining another use for it.

"Several of them commented that it would be a fabulous rental property because it has all of the perks that you want on vacation," Mollica, a real estate agent with the Gambino Group at Compass, tells Realtor.com®.

It was easy enough to see their point: Beyond walls of glass stood a swimming pool, a sandy beach, and the sparkling blue waters of the Long Island Sound. Upstairs, a rooftop deck offered yet another picturesque view.

But Southold, the town encompassing much of the North Fork, wants fewer homes operating as short-term rentals.

A newly proposed permit lottery would allow just 119 properties across the town's North Fork hamlets to offer stays shorter than 30 days—that's less than one-fifth of the 640 active vacation-rental listings in October.

Officials hope the regulation would help protect residential neighborhoods from revolving vacation guests and preserve housing for people who live and work there year-round. But research from cities that have tried similar restrictions shows mixed results.

Mollica knows what draws people to the North Fork. Roughly 25 years ago, she came from Brooklyn for a weekend and ended up buying a house herself.

"What I love about the North Fork is the people are very embracing. They're very community-minded," she says.

The area has long attracted weekenders and summer vacationers, but the COVID-19 pandemic brought a wave of newcomers who began putting down more permanent roots.

"People made a mad rush to the North Fork because they saw the opportunity really to live and not to shelter in place," Mollica recalls. "They enrolled their children in school. They got to know their friends and neighbors. ... So a lot of those people stayed."

Others eventually returned to the city while keeping their North Fork properties as second homes, leaving year-round residents, seasonal homeowners, and vacationers with competing visions for the community.

At an October civic forum, residents complained about pool parties, weddings, traffic, and unfamiliar guests coming and going.

"I'm in a residential community; this is where I want to live," one resident told officials. "I don't want to live in a business district."

Then there's the growing difficulty of affording a home at all.

By the end of 2025, the median price of a single-family home on the North Fork had reached a record $999,000—more than eight times Southold Town's median household income of $116,667. Meanwhile, an estimated 54% of town renters spent at least 30% of their incomes on housing, according to U.S. Census Bureau data.

Even Town Councilwoman Alexa Suess, a Greenport native who campaigned on affordability, recently said she would have to move after her landlord raised her rent above $4,000 a month.

"I don't know anybody my age who I went to school with that is still here," she told a September housing forum.

Naturally, that friction has put a renewed spotlight on the town's massive share of vacation properties: Nearly 37% of its housing stock consisted of seasonal residences in 2020, according to the town's 2023 Community Housing Plan.

At first glance, those seasonal homes might seem like a natural solution for Southold's problems: a reservoir of untapped housing just waiting to be unleashed. But the town's own experience regulating vacation rentals reveals just how difficult it can be to turn those properties into year-round housing.

The town banned stays shorter than 14 nights in 2015, but officials have struggled to enforce the rule. Its housing plan subsequently identified vacation rentals as one possible contributor to the shortage.

Now, officials want to go further, requiring permits for stays shorter than 30 days, limiting them to 1% of single-family homes in each hamlet, and strengthening enforcement. The proposed system could begin in January 2028, although lawmakers have yet to formally adopt it.

The question is what happens to those homes once renting them out becomes more difficult.

Asked whether the cap could flood Southold's for-sale market, Mollica replies: "I'm going to say no."

Many of her clients already prefer monthlong or summer rentals, and she cautions that she works with few buyers seeking properties solely for rental income.

"Our clientele really come out to enjoy their home," she says. "They spend their summers here. They're looking forward to Thanksgiving and other holiday vacations here."

She recalls one family that moved back to New York City for personal reasons but kept their North Fork house as a second home. While they initially sought longer seasonal renters, they turned to Airbnb when finding tenants proved difficult.

"They wanted to rent it [out] ... to supplement their income in order to carry the mortgage," she explains.

And that supplemental income can be substantial.

Average summer nightly rates in Southold's vacation-rental market climbed from $463 in 2019 to $764 in 2026, a 65% increase, according to an analysis of AirDNA data provided to Realtor.com. Yet the median summer reservation lasted just three nights. The figures cover ZIP-code-based North Fork markets, including separately regulated Greenport Village.

"A 30-night minimum removes the weekend and short-stay premium, and a whole-season lease must cover all of an owner's income in a single booking," says Bram Gallagher, AirDNA's director of economics and forecasting.

It's true that owners may decide that renting out their homes is no longer worth the trouble. But that doesn't mean they'll sell or make those properties available to year-round tenants.

Alexander Marsella, an economist at Berry College, says the outcome depends on an owner's next best use of the property.

If that alternative is "a second home for the family," he says, "then restricting short-term rentals isn't going to do much to improve housing affordability."

Research from cities that have already restricted vacation rentals suggests he's right. A 2024 study of Berlin found that the crackdown targeting only commercial operators—not occasional hosts—significantly increased long-term rental supply.

New York City saw a similar disconnect. Short-term listings on Airbnb fell 87% after its 2023 crackdown, but rents barely budged and conventional rental inventory showed no unusual increase, according to Marsella's August 2026 working paper, which has not yet undergone peer review.

And Marsella suspects the effect on year-round housing could be even smaller in a seasonal market.

"If I don't see it happening in New York City so much, I feel like I would be less likely to see it happen in a seasonal market," he says.

Town officials have already acknowledged that restricting vacation rentals won't necessarily determine what happens to the properties themselves.

"Owners are going to have to make a decision about what to do with the houses," Planning Director Heather Lanza said in 2024. "They can go to summer rentals or year-round."

At Mollica's waterfront listing, that decision will soon belong to someone new.

The four-bedroom home is preparing to hit the market, and prospective buyers may already waiting.

"I have several people that are waiting for the right property," Mollica says.

Its swimming pool, private beach access, and sweeping views of Long Island Sound make it an enticing vacation retreat. But those same qualities could appeal to someone looking to put down permanent roots.

Mollica herself came to the North Fork for a weekend nearly 25 years ago and ended up staying.

The next buyer might do the same—or simply return for summer vacations. Southold's proposed rules could influence how the property is used, but whether it becomes a year-round home will ultimately be the buyer's decision.

#5635. Trend of the Month: 6 Ways Floor Plans Are Changing

Current floor plan trends don’t necessarily bring anything brand new to home design, but rather represent subtle shifts to better support how people want to live in their homes today.

Functionality and flow are driving many of the current trends, including these six:

As a result, floor plans are balancing the benefits of open-plan living with spaces that permit partial or total separation from the main living areas. Ideally, a floor plan lets a homeowner choose.

While the kitchen and adjacent living areas remain open, “what is changing is everything around that center. Homeowners still want visual generosity and togetherness, but they also need places for focused work, calls, study, rest, hobbies, or simply a quiet moment,” says Darian Wagner, managing principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture.

The key, says Justin Julian, senior principal and senior architect, DAHLIN Architecture, is not to treat open and closed spaces as opposites.

The most desirable plans “create layers between fully shared and fully enclosed space, so homeowners can adjust the degree of connection throughout the day,” says Julian.

Meanwhile, “Smaller cozy corners can remain open to the main space while using placement, furniture, partial screens, or an offset opening to create a sense of retreat,” says Wagner.

Away rooms are trending, which are simply secondary living spaces set off the main living area, with a closing door, and often increased soundproofing, devoted to peace and quiet.

Back kitchens and sculleries physically separate food prep, appliances and cleanup from the main kitchen, where much of daily living and entertaining takes place.

Upstairs retreats, homework rooms, and secondary living spaces create further separation, giving household members somewhere to do their own thing without sacrificing the openness of the kitchen and great room.

Wet rooms are not a new feature but are gaining more attention and are influencing bathroom layouts and design, no longer reserved just for higher-end homes.

“One reason is that you can use every inch of that space, which can mean a larger shower and a more spa-like feel,” says Debra Purvis with Design House.

A wet room typically is an open-concept bathroom, where a bathtub and a shower share an enclosure, sometimes separated by a glass partition from the rest of the bathroom.

Wet rooms offer great decorative potential too, with soaker tubs, steam showers, and statement fixtures. They also lend themselves naturally to other trends like tile drenching, which provides a dramatic, upscale look.

They are family friendly too. “Kids splash water out of the tub; it’s not a problem. Between the tile and floor drains, you are covered,” says Purvis.

Flex rooms offer opportunity in a floor plan without adding square footage, one reason they remain among the most sought-after features in new homes. But today’s buyers are looking for flex rooms with purpose, rather than just a blank-slate bonus room.

Practical considerations, such as outlets, storage, layered lighting, and easy access without crossing through other spaces, offer flexible futureproofing. The flex room needs to be appropriately sized and configured for the potential use too.

Location in the home indicates flex room potential too.

While two-story floor plans remain in-demand, one-story floor plans are showing modest growth.

“A one-story plan is going to be more accessible, generally speaking, which opens it up to buyers in many different life phases,” says Aurora Zeledon, director of digital content and marketing for Zonda House Plans, including Houseplans.com.

While land availability and cost might be driving the uptick in one-story floor plans, the versatility of living on one level has design upside and broad-based appeal, including 55+, multigen households, and younger families who appreciate having everyone on the same level.

One-story plans offer easier circulation, without stairs and landings occupying transitional spaces. Typically, one-story homes benefit from a stronger indoor/outdoor connection, often an anchor of the design, an in-demand feature as well.

According to the National Association of Home Builders (NAHB), two-story plans still accounted for over half of single-family home starts in 2025 nationwide, although that number had dropped slightly, while the number of single-story homes inched up. Notably, there were significant differences across regions.

Meanwhile, Zeledon reports that the majority of floor plans they have sold, dating back to 2019, are for one-story homes, including their current bestseller. However, she notes that year-to-date there has been a modest increase in one-story house plan sales, compared to last year, pointing out that much of the activity is concentrated in the South and Southeast.

As homes generally scale down in size, storage becomes essential for homeowners to retain the functionality of a larger home in a smaller footprint.

“The overarching idea is to utilize every square foot. When storage is thoughtfully integrated into the architecture, we can maximize the home for multiple purposes—and, importantly, multiple storage solutions—without making the spaces feel overly utilitarian,” says Hannah Sloan, creative marketing specialist with Unscripted Interior Design.

She reports that drop zones are gaining attention, as are Costco closets, laundry/mudroom and owner’s entrances.

Sloan says that some rooms are benefiting from space-specific storage that improves functionality, like in the primary bathroom with more thoughtfully designed vanities and built-ins. Meanwhile, fitness closets are appearing in home gyms to free up floor space for exercise.

“Then there are the found spaces—under-stair book nooks, hidden speakeasy-inspired bars, and other whimsical design opportunities. These spaces can become highly functional while also adding personality and surprise to a home,” says Sloan.

This article was originally published on NewHomeSource.com.

Heather Wright is a senior writer for NewHomeSource and Builder with a background in real estate reporting and home design, decor, and architecture. She has written for a number of print and digital publications in the lifestyle space.

#5634. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

“I once prayed just to make it through another day. Now I get to spend forever with the love of my life, carrying a little miracle we already love more than words. From heartbreak to healing. From surviving to living. From praying for my forever to building a family with him. Only God could have written this story. Here’s to forever, J ... and the sweetest little blessing we can’t wait to meet," she added.

Chrisley had kept the identity of her partner under wraps until now, having previously revealed on her podcast, "Unlocked with Savannah Chrisley,"  that she wouldn't share his name "until after I'm married."

In the latest episode of her podcast, she revealed she and Jason began their romance last July, branding it a "dream relationship."

She revealed that Galanis proposed five months into their relationship when they were in the Cayman Islands. "The ring is insane and it’s everything I ever wanted."

She then revealed that the couple connected after Jason reached out to her to praise her for her efforts to get her parents out of prison.

Todd and Julie Chrisley were found guilty in 2022 of conspiring to defraud Georgia banks out of more than $36 million in personal loans and tax evasion, before being pardoned by President Donald Trump in May 2025.

Savannah Chrisley has frequently spoken out about the toll of her parents' incarceration.

Todd, 57, was sentenced to 12 years (later reduced to 10 years) in the Federal Correctional Institution Pensacola in Florida. Julie, 53, was sentenced to seven years in the Federal Medical Center in Lexington, KY.

Following her parents' incarceration, Savannah took on the care of her brother, Grayson, 19, and her niece, Chloe, 13, while also assuming responsibility for the care and maintenance of her parents' opulent dwelling.

At the same time, the burgeoning real estate agent was tirelessly campaigning for Todd and Julie's release, issuing public pleas for government support, while alleging that her parents were being subjected to "beyond inhumane" conditions behind bars.

On May 27, her prayers were answered when Trump revealed to her in a personal phone call that he planned to pardon her parents. Just a few days later, they were released from prison.

At the time, Savannah revealed she was ready to return the hefty upkeep of their home to Todd and Julie.

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.
